#915. COP31 draft deal calls for 'immediate' shift away from fossil fuels

The preliminary agreement at UN climate talks in Turkey calls for a rapid reduction of planet-warming emissions and at least $120 billion to help countries adapt to climate change.

COP31 co-host Australia has kicked off the second week of climate talks in Antalya with a draft political deal calling for an "immediate transition away from fossil fuels" and a "tripling" of finance for climate adaptation measures in developing countries to at least $120 billion (€109 billion).

The goal of other co-host Turkey to increase electrification of the world's economies to 35% by 2035 also features in the text. The draft emphasizes clean energy but notes that "electrification can provide co-benefits regardless of the electricity mix" — an approach that has proved divisive at the talks, with many insisting that electrification be strictly tied to renewable energy.

Language around a faster phaseout of oil, coal and gas is important because fossil-fuel producing nations have repeatedly pushed back against stronger wording in previous COP decisions.

"The new negotiating text contains all the necessary building blocks for a successful outcome to the conference: from the goal of climate neutrality for all industrialized countries by 2030 to a work program that can keep the 1.5-degree limit in place," said Greenpeace Germany head Martin Kaiser on Monday.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The draft expressed "deep concern" that the 1.5 Celsius (2.7 Fahrenheit) temperature threshold agreed at the 2015 COP in Paris to avoid runaway climate change was now out of reach. It stressed the need for "accelerating action to minimize both the magnitude and duration of any temperature overshoot and to return global warming to below 1.5C as soon as possible."

Recognizing a need to address rising carbon emissions, the draft highlighted efforts to "urgently and rapidly" scale up controversial technologies to capture and store CO2 to bring down atmospheric carbon levels.

"For the first time, all the parties here are grappling with the fact that the world will inevitably exceed 1.5 degrees. Negotiators must deliver a response," said Ani Dasgupta, president of the World Resources Institute, adding that this meant going beyond slashing emissions.

"This requires scaling carbon removal through both nature-based solutions like restoring forests and wetlands, or emerging technologies that directly capture carbon from air," he told reporters.

Kaiser, however, criticized the lack of binding commitments in the draft's resolutions. He added that Europe should work with China and the most climate-vulnerable countries to keep oil-producing nations, including Russia and countries in the Middle East, from "undermining the conference's decisions and turning them into a free pass for the oil and gas industry."

Other activists have dismissed carbon capture as a "false solution" being promoted by corporations.

Cosima Cassel, an expert at climate think tank E3G, was cautiously pleased with the draft's "ambitious language" but said it appeared the broad deal would now leave negotiators to "fight for trade-offs."

"The test will be whether the final decision keeps the core elements once that process plays out: ambition on overshoot, defense of the science, clean electrification and forward progress on adaptation finance," she said in a statement.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Disagreements over financing largely relate to who should bear the costs of international climate action, whether financial support should be provided through grants or loans, and how funding for developing countries can be increased.

Representatives of developing nations and small island states, regions bearing the brunt of the climate crisis, have protested climate inaction and a lack of financial support in recent days.

"Climate finance isn't an extra at these talks: it's the condition for everything else," said Rukiya Khamis, program manager for East Africa with environmental group 350.org. "It's alarming how financial pledges by wealthy, polluting countries are dropping like a stone — COP31 must stop this with a strong outcome on adaptation finance."

"Now we must fight to keep this [adaption finance] in the final decision and ensure these promises become real, grant-based money," said Harjeet Singh of the Fill The Fund campaign, which calls on rich countries and corporations to deliver the funding needed for climate-related loss and damage, such as homes destroyed by floods and harvests ruined by drought.

"Communities are suffering devastating losses and damages today precisely because we failed to deliver adaptation at the right time," added Singh.

At 18 pages and 144 items, the draft will be the focus of lengthy discussions in the coming days as delegates try to come to an agreement by Friday. Some observers went so far as to say the document's scope was too wide to be taken seriously.

"The draft final declaration reads like a Christmas wish list," said Niklas Höhne, a climate policy expert at the NewClimate Institute in Germany. "There are even several points on which we will obviously not be able to reach a consensus, including for example the proposal that developed countries achieve net-zero emissions by 2030."

But Chris Bowen, chief of negotiations and Australia's minister for climate change and energy, appeared optimistic.

"The general tenor and tone [of the talks] has been very constructive," he told reporters Monday. "Parties have come to me with strong views about various things, as you'd expect […] [but] they've also come in the spirit of cooperation, the spirit of respect and a spirit where parties have said to me that they want to help get an outcome."

David Waskow, director of WRI's International Climate Initiative, said the draft text showed a level of "seriousness" on important issues like finance, electrification, oceans, overshoot scenarios and emissions of greenhouse gases including methane, which has a warming impact more than 80 times stronger than CO2.

"The question is whether the level of ambition on those issues is carried through into the final outcome here," said Waskow. "And that's what we need to be watching closely over the coming days."

Additional reporting by Tim Schauenberg in Antalya.

Update, November 17, 2026: This article has been updated with additional reactions to the draft text.

Newcastle are being tipped to solve their goalscoring issues this winter with a move to bring Ivan Toney back to St James’ Park.

Finding the back of the net has proved a major headache for Jaissle since taking the reins on Tyneside and following a summer exodus that stripped the Magpies of their spine, none of Newcastle’s current central striking options have managed to nail down a starting spot in his team.

Will Osula and Yoane Wissa have mustered just a single league goal apiece so far this campaign, while Matias Fernandez-Pardo is still waiting to open his account. Without a reliable penalty-box presence, Jaissle’s side have lacked a cutting edge in the final third.

Toney thrived under Jaissle during their time together in Saudi Arabia. The former Brentford frontman has been expectedly prolific in the Middle East, netting 87 times in 110 appearances across all competitions.

Any transfer negotiations may even be smoothed over by shared ownership links, as both Al-Ahli and Newcastle are majority-owned by Saudi Arabia’s Public Investment Fund (PIF).

Despite his form in the Saudi Pro League, Toney has slipped down the international pecking order and missed out on recent England squads, a setback that is expected to spark a push for a Premier League return in the New Year.

Speaking on the Everything is Black and White Podcast, The Chronicle’s chief Newcastle reporter Lee Ryder suggested the 30-year-old will be chomping at the bit to head back to English football.

A switch to St James’ Park would see Toney return to the club he departed almost a decade ago. Newcastle originally signed the striker from Northampton Town over in 2015, but made just two Premier League outings before being sent out on a series of loans. Spells at Barnsley, Shrewsbury, Scunthorpe and Wigan followed, before he was eventually sold to Peterborough United in 2018.

Having since proved his top-flight pedigree at Brentford, Toney would bring additional physicality and an aptitude for finishing that Newcastle are presently missing.

#911. The AfD and neo-Nazi networks: How close are the connections?

The Alternative for Germany party (AfD) has become a focal point for the far right. Many of its members and staff have ties to ethnonationalist or neo-Nazi organizations.

The electoral successes of the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) have brought the party closer than ever to taking power in Germany. For the 2029 federal election, it has set itself an ambitious goal: to see its co-chair Alice Weidel to become Germany's next chancellor.

This raises an even sharper question: what political ideas does the party stand for, which has been classified by Germany's domestic intelligence agency as a "suspected right-wing extremist" organization and, in several federal states, is already considered "confirmed right-wing extremist"?

Many political scientists have observed that the AfD has become increasingly radicalized since its founding in 2013.

"Viewed as a whole, the AfD is an extreme right-wing party that also displays tendencies associated with a fascist movement," said Fabian Virchow, a researcher on right-wing extremism at Düsseldorf University of Applied Sciences, in an interview with DW.

Virchow identifies different factions and strategic tendencies within the party, some of which are at odds with one another. Party leader Alice Weidel, for example, is generally seen as a proponent of a free-market approach that seeks to keep the state as small as possible. Others, by contrast, favor a strong state shaped by an ethnically homogeneous people, among them Björn Höcke, the influential far-right AfD leader in the state of Thuringia.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Virchow sees a "normalization" of right-wing extremist positions within the AfD. In his view, this has made the party more attractive to neo-Nazi circles: "Today, many people see greater room for ethnonationalist and radical right-wing ideas."

Support for this observation comes from the latest findings of the Leipzig Authoritarianism Study, one of the most widely cited long-term studies tracking right-wing extremist attitudes in Germany. The researchers behind the study have identified a rise in right-wing extremist views within German society, including a growing acceptance of ideologies rooted in the tradition of National Socialism.

Particularly striking is the finding that around two-thirds of people with firmly entrenched far-right worldviews would vote for the AfD. According to the study, the AfD has achieved what earlier far-right parties in Germany never managed: "to unite large segments of the electorate with anti-democratic attitudes behind it."

The debate has been further fueled by several recent incidents within the party. In 2026 alone, numerous AfD politicians and staff members made headlines over alleged ties to neo-Nazi organizations:

In August 2026, police carried out a large-scale raid targeting fifteen people. Authorities suspect them of continuing the activities of the so-called "Artgemeinschaft." Before it was banned in 2023, the group was considered one of Germany's largest and most influential neo-Nazi cadre organizations. Particularly explosive was the fact that two of those targeted in the raid are sitting AfD members of the Saxony-Anhalt state parliament. Their attorneys deny the allegations.

According to reporting by the German daily, Welt, four staff members of the AfD's parliamentary group in Saxony-Anhalt are former members of the now-banned "Heimattreue Deutsche Jugend" (HDJ), a neo-Nazi youth organization rooted in National Socialist racial ideology that organized paramilitary camps for young people. Two of the staff members held leadership positions within the HDJ and now work closely with AfD politician Ulrich Siegmund, who is seeking to become the AfD's first state premier in December.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Remarkably, both organizations, the "Artgemeinschaft" and the HDJ, are on the AfD's so-called incompatibility list, which is intended to draw a line between the party and extremist organizations and movements. In principle, anyone with a history of membership in such groups is supposed to be excluded from the party.

But the list appears to be little more than a dead letter. In 2020, former AfD federal executive board member Andreas Kalbitz was expelled from the party after failing to disclose his membership in the "Heimattreue Deutsche Jugend" on his application to join. Yet according to the news magazine Spiegel, he is once again working for the AfD, this time as a staffer for Saxony-Anhalt state legislator Hans-Thomas Tillschneider, who has since become deputy speaker of the state parliament.

The question of the AfD's relationship to National Socialism has dogged the party since its founding in 2013. Even in its early years, co-founder and first party leader Bernd Lucke sparked controversy when he described democracy and parliamentary politics in Germany as "degenerate," a term the Nazis used to disparage art and culture that did not conform to their ideological worldview.

In Germany, references to the Nazi dictatorship (1933-1945) under Adolf Hitler remain politically taboo because of the country's responsibility for World War Two and the Holocaust, the systematic mass murder of Europe's Jews.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

If AfD members or their staff have come under scrutiny because of past involvement in ethnonationalist or neo-Nazi organizations, they have generally sought to distance themselves from those backgrounds or from the ideologies associated with them.

But how credible are these attempts at distancing? Laura Neumann* has worked with many people seeking to leave the far-right scene. She works for "Nordverbund Ausstieg Rechts," a network of organizations that supports far-right cadres and activists as they disengage from the movement. "A successful exit is the result of a professionally guided process," she said in an interview with DW.

Neumann describes leaving the far-right scene as a challenging process of self-confrontation. "When it comes to someone leaving the movement, the first question I always ask is: How does that person talk about their past? Have they genuinely come to terms with it?"

Based on the experience of exit counselors, one principle generally holds true: the longer and more deeply a person has been immersed in far-right circles, the more difficult it becomes to distance themselves from those beliefs and affiliations.

DW requested a statement from the AfD's federal executive board regarding its handling of party members who were previously active in ethnonationalist or neo-Nazi organizations. Individual lawmakers and parliamentary staff members were also asked to comment. None responded.

The party's and its politicians' silence in the face of such allegations reflects an observation made by political scientist Fabian Virchow: "Within the AfD, there is no longer a perceived need to distance oneself from radical far-right positions. That is part of this process of normalization."

Virchow says that right-wing extremism appears to have advanced so far into the mainstream of German society that efforts to scandalize it now remain largely ineffective.

This article was originally written in German.

#909. What has changed in James Bond films over the decades

In 1962, a martini-drinking womanizer saved the world for the first time in "Dr. No." As Robert Pattinson takes on the role of 007, here's how the films evolved.

After years of speculation, Amazon MGM Studios announced on Monday that Robert Pattinson would be taking on the role of James Bond following Daniel Craig's departure after five hit films in the spy series.

This year alone, Pattinson has starred in "The Odyssey," "The Drama" and "Primetime." He is also famous for his role as "Twilight" vampire Edward Cullen.

The upcoming Bond movie will be directed by Denis Villeneuve, an Oscar nominee known for movies such as the "Dune" trilogy and "Arrival."

Based on the spy novels by author Ian Fleming, the Bond franchise — about a British secret agent known for his charm and ⁠a ⁠fondness for martinis "shaken, not stirred" — is among the longest-running and highest-grossing in Hollywood history. ​​​​​​​

The first film in the series, "Dr. No," premiered in London on October 5, 1962.

Playing the leading role, Agent 007, was an unknown actor: Sean Connery.

In the film, we are first introduced to his character as he sits in a casino across from an attractive woman who is about to gamble away her fortune. When she asks 007 his name, the camera pans to Bond lighting a cigarette. With a smoldering look in his eye, he utters the legendary words: "Bond, James Bond."

Shortly thereafter in the film, 007 receives an assignment to fly to Jamaica and investigate the murder of another M16 agent. He eventually tracks down a Chinese-German criminal scientist who is bent on destroying the US space program and achieving world domination.

In principle, this story is the basis of all of 25 James Bond films. Whether the villain is Dr. No, Blofeld, Goldfinger or Le Chiffre, they all aim for one thing: world domination. But to do so, they have to get past James Bond whose gunfire and wild chase scenes inevitably spoil their plans.

Although many fan forums consider "Dr. No" to be one of the best Bond films, the movie would never be made in the same way today.

Firstly, one could write entire books about the omnipresent sexism and machismo that the character James Bond has displayed over the decades.

Certainly there would have to be a thick chapter dedicated to the women in his films, who are typically portrayed as naive, willingly flinging themselves into Bond's arms, seeking protection. Sometimes they are sophisticated female antagonists who lose control at the thought of hopping into bed with the secret agent.

Whether friend of foe, each film had at least one Bond girl — and often more: More than 60 love interests have appeared in the films. Their names, like "Honey" or "Pussy Galore" would never be acceptable today. In more recent decades, female roles in Bond films have changed — as has Bond himself.

In the last five films in which Daniel Craig has played Bond, he is seen as a man who is tough on the outside and soft on the inside — and who is not always lucky with women.

Aside from the portrayal of women on screen, there are also plenty of other details in "Dr. No" that haven't quite stood the test of time.

Another sign of the zeitgeist in the 1962 film is that everyone smokes, which is a no-no by today's Hollywood standards. Cigarettes are found everywhere in the old film, from the casino to the hotel bar — and even the bedroom.

Smoking was commonplace in the US in the 1970s, so naturally this came across on the silver screen. In the 1970s TV series "Space: 1999" people were even depicted smoking on the moon, but by the 2000s, smoking was largely banned in many parts of the world due to its health risks.

One can also note in "Dr. No" that few people are wearing seat belts. When Bond drives off in his sports car to visit a woman, he is followed and a chase scene ensues. Bond, notably, is not wearing a seat belt.

His pursuers eventually drive off a slope and die, of course — after all, they aren't wearing seat belts either and cars didn't have airbags at the time. The vehicle explodes, prompting 007 to say, "They were obviously in a hurry to get to their own funeral."

In the older Bond films, all secretaries and receptionists are played by women, which in the 1960s, were considered standard female jobs.

Whether redheaded, blonde or brunette, secretaries are Bond's favorite targets for womanizing and they are all susceptible to his charms.

Throughout most Bond films, the agent has a romantic tension with Moneypenny, his boss's secretary, something which was not described in the original books.

In the 2012 film "Skyfall" Moneypenny is given a first name: Eve, and we finally learn her backstory. In this film, she is no longer a hopeless secretary in love, but a top-trained agent who accidentally shoots Bond and is reassigned to desk duty as punishment.

In any case, today Moneypenny's job title today would probably be "Office Manager" or "Executive Assistant" rather than "Secretary."

In the film, Dr. No tells James Bond that he is the child of a British missionary and a Chinese woman from an upstanding family. However, the character is portrayed by Canadian actor Joseph Wiseman who is wearing makeup to make his eyes look more "Asian."

While it used to be the norm in such movies to have East Asian characters played by white actors, today these cases of "yellowface" are frowned upon — just as it would be to wear blackface, putting black makeup on one's skin to portray a Black person.

If there was a "Dr. No" remake in the future, a Chinese actor would be more likely to play this role.

Daniel Craig already paved the way in modernizing James Bond by stripping away campy gadgets, punchlines and invincibility, replacing them with a grounded, psychological and emotionally vulnerable portrayal of a post-9/11 spy.

Now it is up to Robert Pattinson to revisit the famous MI6 agent. Film critics believe his background will allow him to add dark sophistication and nonconformism to the iconic espionage role.

Throughout his career, Robert Pattinson has managed to combine roles in blockbuster hits and indie gems, from Bruce Wayne in "The Batman" to a disposable worker who is cloned every time he dies in "Mickey 17."

Pattinson already has experience with classic spy archetypes: As the mysterious Neil in Christopher Nolan's sci-fi action thriller "Tenet," he assisted the protagonist in a time-bending espionage mission. He is also known for his eccentric personality and deadpan humor — qualities that could be useful for a modern Bond.

This article was translated from German by Sarah Hucal. It was first published in 2025 and updated following news of Robert Pattinson's casting as James Bond on November 16, 2026.

That is why Bassey ticks so many boxes for Man United’s new era under Pochettino.

Turning 27 on New Year’s Eve, the Nigeria international is entering his prime years as a defender. And having racked up more than 100 Premier League appearances since arriving in west London from Ajax in 2023, he brings the sort of battle-hardened top-flight pedigree Man United are crying out for.

In doing so, he removes the adaptation risk that has plagued so many overseas Old Trafford arrivals. His commanding display in Fulham’s 1-1 draw away at Manchester City on Saturday makes the appeal obvious; Bassey has good recovery pace, is dominant in physical duels, and comfortable defending wide channels.

Bassey won't cost the earth either as his initial four-year contract at Craven Cottage expires next summer, and although Fulham hold an option to extend his stay by a further 12 months, his contractual situation keeps any potential fee firmly within reach for a club of Man United's stature and commercial acumen.

Fulham are understandably eager to tie him down to fresh terms, but the lure of spearheading Pochettino’s Old Trafford reboot may prove hard to resist.

In FourFourTwo's view, if Bassey maintains his current level over the coming weeks, don't rule out a January approach.

Ethan Nwaneri's Arsenal career appears to be floundering, with the on-loan Borussia Dortmund teenager facing a further transfer setback.

Nwaneri returns to his parent club tonight in the Champions League with the Bundesliga giants and is eligible to face Arsenal despite still being owned by the Gunners.

But beyond this campaign, his future remains uncertain, with manager Mikel Arteta even recently alluding to the teenager's struggles at Signal Iduna Park.

Nwaneri became the Premier League's youngest-ever player in 2022 at the age of 15 – with Max Dowman later taking that record – before establishing himself in the 2024/25 season as a serious option on the right wing for the Gunners.

But after going out on loan at Marseille last term and heading to Dortmund this time, the teenager is yet to impress, with Arteta even admitting this week that “moments are not enough” for Nwaneri in his development and that consistency must follow.

A report from Sport Witness, likewise, reads as bad news for the 19-year-old, with the Gunners now pursuing a move for Gilberto Mora as soon as January.

Mora was the youngest player selected for the 2026 World Cup and has impressed hugely in his native Mexico, courting the attention of virtually every big club in Europe.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

In attacking midfield areas, Arsenal already have the likes of Martin Odegaard, Mikel Merino, Eberechi Eze and Max Dowman – with the latter two options on the wing – and should Arsenal bring in another teenage talent, Nwaneri's first-team opportunities would appear even scarcer.

FourFourTwo understands that the Gunners were open to offers for the starlet over the summer, opting to retain him and develop him at one of the best finishing schools in European football, though the paths of Nwaneri and Hale End colleague Myles Lewis-Skelly have been drastically different, thanks, in part, due to competition for places.

With Liverpool also circling for Mora, however, the Gunners may well have to present a particularly enticing package to secure the 18-year-old.

According to the report, the youngster has a release clause of around €25 million, making any move for him particularly costly – and suggesting that the Gunners could well incorporate him into their first team immediately.

Nwaneri, meanwhile, is valued by Transfermarkt at €25m. Arsenal return to Champions League action tonight against Dortmund at the Emirates Stadium.

#904. How Arsenal can expose Man City’s clear weakness to tighten grip on title

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

Mikel Arteta bolstered a strength with Bruno Guimaraes alongside Declan Rice, but, as Richard Jolly explains, Enzo Maresca splashed £125m on Enzo Fernandez and still lacks ‘balance’ in midfield

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

For Manchester City, life after three Champions League-winning midfielders began in earnest against Arsenal in August. They were a goal down after 23 seconds. It was an inauspicious start for Enzo Maresca and Elliot Anderson alike.

A reunion with Arsenal on Sunday could be deemed a meeting of managerial midfielders, in Maresca and Mikel Arteta. Each learned from Pep Guardiola, who won the European Cup as a Barcelona player and manager and then in charge of City. But it is also a first Premier League clash since Bernardo Silva and Rodri joined their mentor in decamping from the Etihad Stadium in the summer. Arsenal may not have been sorry to see any go; if Guardiola’s resignation could facilitate an era of dominance from Arteta, and if it may have already begun with last season’s Premier League title, a further factor could be the departures of the City captain and Spain’s World Cup-winning skipper.

If City have been confronted with the question of how to replace the irreplaceable, there are different answers. One is simply that it is impossible: they are irreplaceable. Another is: expensively. City committed £326m to three midfield recruits, in Anderson, Ayyoub Bouaddi and Enzo Fernandez. A third is: incoherently, at least so far. Perhaps it is unfair to expect newcomers, both in the dugout and the centre of the pitch, to bring the same cohesion and chemistry as predecessors who became the faces of longevity and continuity, but thus far they have not.

A further subplot, arguably, is that Arsenal boast men who represented an alternative line of succession at City: not merely Arteta, Guardiola’s first assistant in Manchester, but Bruno Guimaraes, who was of interest at the Etihad in 2024, but when City chose not to activate his release clause, and Declan Rice, the target who preferred to join Arsenal in 2023. Arguably the England vice-captain was the best central midfielder in the Premier League even with Rodri and Silva; without them, and despite Pascal Gross’ extraordinary start to the season, he definitely is.

But if Arsenal won the war last season, City prevailed in the battles, based around the formidable double act of Silva and Rodri. They faced the Gunners three times; but for Gabriel Martinelli’s injury-time equaliser at the Emirates Stadium, they would have won all three. Rodri’s prowess then may have come at a cost: it was his third start in a week, and he only began two more games in the next three months. City had barely a third of the ball, in an anti-Pep performance, but were superb out of possession.

In March’s Carabao Cup final, Nico O’Reilly’s box-crashing brace earned him the man-of-the-match award, but victory was underpinned by the midfield platform constructed by the Portuguese and the Spaniard. Finally, in City’s Premier League win at the Etihad, when victory seemed to shift the initiative to them in the title race, Silva was talismanic and terrific, turning in one of the best of his 460 performances for City. Two astonishing defensive interventions, one running back with Kai Havertz, the other winning a header against the rather taller Viktor Gyokeres, led Erling Haaland to compare him to Fabio Cannavaro.

That influence, that drive, that capacity to perform in major matches: perhaps it was inevitably irreplaceable, just as Rodri’s Golden Ball-winning World Cup showed no other defensive midfielder can be as good as him. The first three-and-a-half months of Maresca’s reign have shown City lack anyone who is knitting the team together as well as Rodri and Silva did. A susceptibility to the counter-attack could be a flaw in the Guardiola years, but has been more so without the two men charged with cutting them out.

It has been compounded by some of the stranger structural issues. Fernandez has spent some of his time in the inside-right channel, some apparently with designs of being a No 10. Anderson has often been isolated. He has been excellent, but even a £116m midfielder can only cover so much ground on his own.

Maresca has tended to use the word “balance”, reflecting City’s quest for it. The most obvious answer involves introducing Bouaddi alongside Anderson: the times Fernandez has played with most positional discipline have at least involved some of the bigger games, whether away at Porto, in a Manchester derby when down to 10 men or at Anfield. But City’s openness in midfield was exploited by Paris Saint-Germain: Bouaddi, a half-time remedy, brought improvement.

There is a sense that City may have complicated the equation with the Enzo reunion, Maresca’s £125m move for his former Chelsea ally Fernandez. The Argentinian’s fondness for operating in the final third can impact upon Rayan Cherki and Phil Foden; instead of a third possible No 10, City could have done more with another player with the skillset of Guimaraes or his old Newcastle sidekick Sandro Tonali, players who can be a No 6 or a No 8, in the mould of Anderson.

But maybe the task for Fernandez, Anderson, Bouaddi and Maresca always threatened to be thankless. Coming after Rodri and Silva in midfield or Guardiola in the technical area ran the risk anyone would be an automatic downgrade. And maybe Arsenal will underline that.

#903. NASA's Voyager 1 reaches a light-day away from Earth

When just saying 'hello' takes a two-day round trip, you're a light-day, or 26 billion kilometers, from Earth. Only one human-made object has ever traveled that far — and its journey into interstellar space continues.

Hate long-haul flights? Well, imagine having to travel 3,300 years to get to your destination.

Imagine departing in 1977 and arriving in 2026, on November 18 at 11:16 a.m. Central European Time to be precise, and then, not stopping but continuing the journey.

NASA's Voyager 1, a spacecraft launched almost half-a-century ago, has traveled a light-day from Earth.

A light-day is the distance light covers in 24 hours — about 26 billion kilometers (or around 16 billion miles). Put another way: Light does in one day what it took the spacecraft 49 years, two months and 11 days to do.

But Voyager 1 is not only far away, it is also traveling at an incredible speed of 61,000 km/h (38,000 mph).

When Voyager 1 launched, it was in sync with a planetary alignment that was as rare as the spacecraft itself — one that happens only once every 176 years. It was the alignment Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune, which scientists wanted to investigate.

Once the original mission was accomplished, Voyager 1 used the planets Jupiter and Saturn to perform a gravitational slingshot.

It flew close to each planet, got pulled and accelerated by their massive gravity, and swung around faster than before. And that is how Voyager 1 has achieved its speed.

In the vacuum of space, nothing slows you down.

On Valentine's Day 1990, from beyond Neptune, Voyager 1 took the only portrait of the solar system from the outside ever made by a spacecraft.

In 2012, it became the first human-made object to reach interstellar space.

Its journey is ongoing. In about 40,000 years — long after its plutonium power supply dies out — it will still be flying and pass by the star Gliese 445, which is more than 17 light-years away from Earth.

That's light-years, not light-days. A light-year is the distance light travels in a year. It will take Voyager 1 about 18,000 years to reach the one light-year milestone.

Voyager 1 is destined to wander the Milky Way "perhaps eternally," as NASA puts it.

The spacecraft is the first human-made object ever to be one light-day away from home.

"If you want to say 'hello' to Voyager, you send your message and then you go home and you wait two days before you finally get a response," says Suzanne Dodd, the mission's project manager at NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory.

But you do get a response. Even today it sends back data that helps scientists on Earth.

"[It's] still working great, sending back data from a region of space no other human-made craft has ever explored," says Kareem Badaruddin, the mission manager at JPL.

No story about Voyager 1 seems complete without mentioning The Golden Record, a phonographic record, that is part of the spacecraft's cargo.

The spacecraft is carrying other Earthly objects as messages and artefacts from Earth for extraterrestrials. But the Golden Record is what we tend to focus on because it contains soundbites representing languages and cultures from around our planet.

We're told it's very unlikely that any intelligent lifeform will ever receive the cargo or even know how to play The Golden Record.

But if they do get the record and work out how to play it, the first thing they will hear is a controversial voice — not one of Earthly unity, as was the original idea. Those are the words of Kurt Waldheim, a former UN Secretary-General (1972-81) and Austrian President (1986-92), whose concealed wartime past as a German army officer in the Balkans surfaced a decade after Voyager 1's launch. It was alleged Waldheim had participated in Nazi crimes.

#902. Emery unhappy with ‘unfair’ referee but Aston Villa are toothless

Six months after the glory of that Europa League final, Aston Villa’s return to Istanbul proved a chastening night of disappointment.

Unai Emery’s team have undergone a significant rebuild since that stirring night in May and this was another occasion where Villa 2.0 were exposed as a work in progress.

Emery’s run without a win has extended to six matches in all competitions and Villa’s Champions League campaign does not promise to get any easier, with Paris St-Germain up next.

There was always likely to be a period of transition this season, as six of the heroes from the Europa League final’s starting XI were sold over the summer.

Despite some encouraging signs before the last international break, and three successive Champions League wins, Villa are now enduring a difficult run.

Their second-half performance in particular was poor, and Galatasaray secured victory with the evening’s first shot on target.

The deadlock is FINALLY broken 🙌 Deniz Gül gives Galatasaray the lead after a scramble in front of the net. 📺 Watch live on TNT Sports & HBO Max https://t.co/fRCRh6tXYB https://t.co/SplkgZC63p

Emery was booked late on as his frustrations got the better of him. His team appear short of creativity and, when Nicolas Jackson struggles, are toothless in the final third.

Though Villa did frustrate the Turkish champions for long periods on a slow, substandard pitch, this was a second successive defeat in the Champions League. Emery now faces a daunting double-header against PSG and Borussia Dortmund. They may still have enough to qualify for the knockout stages, but Villa fans of a certain vintage will insist their team never do it the easy way.

Emery was unhappy with the performance of German referee Daniel Siebert and said: “I am disappointed a little bit. After their goal, it was impossible to play. They wasted time. They added only five minutes. OK, finish the match. We don’t want to play more, I don’t think the referee was fair there. Two years ago we lost to Brugge and Monaco away [in the Champions League]. Today I can compare this match to those matches.”

Alejandro Garnacho, the Chelsea loanee, did not travel and was absent from the match-day squad for the fourth game in a row. Emery said: “Today the players were here who I think are the best players to be here with us.” It was far removed from the magical scenes of the Europa League showpiece across the city.

Villa’s fears before kick-off centred on the playing surface, with the pitch recently relaid after extensive maintenance, but it had no real impact on the result. Galatasaray defeated Liverpool twice in the Champions League at Rams Park last season and can be awkward opponents.

In a game of few chances, Villa were intent on frustrating both Galatasaray’s players and supporters by slowing the game down, restricting the home team’s threat by playing five in defence.

Galatasaray were lacking inspiration but were given an injection eight minutes into the second half. The flashpoint came after a crude challenge from Davinson Sánchez on Villa’s Brazilian winger Alysson.

Sánchez, the former Tottenham defender, escaped a booking but an angry John McGinn responded by colliding with Aleksey Batrakov near the touchline. Both players were given yellow cards by Siebert, and McGinn was infuriated that Batrakov avoided more extreme punishment for kicking out at him.

That aggravation only served to fire up Galatasaray and there was a sense of inevitability to their goal 13 minutes from the end. Villa were under pressure and failed to clear a corner, with Deniz Gul punishing Jackson’s error to head the ball over the line after a deflection off Tyrone Mings.

Seven minutes of added time failed to spark Villa into life by creating a late chance and they returned home without registering a shot on Ugurcan Cakir’s goal.

Villa’s downturn in form continues with a Champions League defeat which owed everything to their shortcomings going forward. They settled well in a hostile atmosphere, but allowed all their possession to drift into sterility, and the second half was just plain poor. A low-quality game settled by a messy goal, but credit to Gul for putting his head where it hurts.

Villa will surely finish the week outside the top eight, with home games against PSG and Borussia Dortmund to follow.

The referee has allowed the game on beyond the five additional minutes, but a Harwood-Bellis loose pass stalls Villa in their own half.

They soon break out into midfield space though, but with all the time in the world Barkley’s pass was a touch behind Hemmings and Sanchez was able to get a toe to it.

Of all the venues in the Champions League where a referee might be inclined to blow his whistle as soon as possible, this might be the one so time is running out for Villa.

Lucas Torreira has taken a kick on the ankle, and he limps off to be replaced by Ilkay Gundogan, who has played just 75 minutes this season.

Villa then find some space down the left but Singo blocks Maatsen’s cross which was aimed towards Jackson.

Ross Barkley the fourth Villa player booked on the night. There will be five minutes added on, which surely does not represent all of the stoppages, but Uefa’s approach to timekeeping resembles freestyle jazz.

Villa eventually worked a position to cross the ball from that free-kick, but Lindelof’s header back into the six-yard box was too close to Cakir and the goalkeeper pounced on the ball. Time running out for Villa.

The goalscorer Gul is back on with a bandage around part of his face.

Mbaye with a dangerous ball into the box but he was offside in any case.

The pitch is slowing the game down which is helping Villa. There was a weird booking for Nicolas Jackson late in the half so it would be no surprise to see him taken off by Emery either at half-time or very early in the second.

A controlled and composed 45 minutes from Villa, but in truth Galatasaray have put them under very little pressure. McGinn, Manzambi and Jackson have produced some smooth flicks and touches, but there has been a lack of devastation in the final third. That has been the missing element for Villa so far. For all the talk of the atmosphere, they should be beating this team.

Nicolas Jackson has been booked, and Alysson loses the ball cheaply to put Galatasaray away on the counter-attack. Mings is up early to head the corner away. The home team continue to look pretty toothless.

Elmali’s cross from the Galatasaray left is woefully overhit and Suzuki claims, but it was a poor pass from Harwood-Bellis that instigated the attack. Villa soon restore order with a spell of possession.

Unsurprisingly, the best pass of the match so far has come from Zion Suzuki.

The Villa goalkeeper has just pinged a pearler over 40 odd yards to Alysson on the right wing.

Galatasaray find some joy with quick switches of play with Villa’s defensive shape quite narrow, but Akgun’s chipped cross was overhit.

Joao Gomes then takes an extra touch inside his own box, but moves the ball on before he is caught in possession.

Torreira than clatters Gomes, not his first foul on the night, but somehow he escapes a booking.

McGinn is picking up some midfield positions that are hard for Galatasaray to pick up, but a couple of Hollywood passes from there have not come off.

Better attacking play from the home team, but Mings was well positioned to head clear a deflected cross.

Villa with another slick move, and this one had more attacking punch at the end of it. Maatsen delivered a wicked low cross and Manzambi was waiting for a tap-in but Sanchez made a last-ditch challenge. No doubt that Villa are the better team.

For a moment it looks as if Manzambi had missed a glorious chance but the flag belatedly went up for offside against Jackson who collected the ball wide right when well ahead of the play.

Villa are doing a very good job of frustrating both the Galatasaray players and their supporters so far.

They are slowing the game down and producing some neat interplay in advanced positions.

Johan Manzambi, in particular, is covering a lot of ground.

Suzuku rushes off his line to sweep up a through ball, but Alysson had also tracked a run all the way. Singo passes forward quickly but Galatasaray’s playmaker Batrakov cannot put the ball under his spell.

John McGinn with a chance to deliver a free-kick from a crossing position, but Galatasaray win the header at the back post. Villa continue to be comfortable in the game, without really working the goalkeeper Cakir. The home crowd are restless, Galatasaray have yet to muster a menacing attacking.

Villa moving the ball well inside Galatasaray’s half with some neat interplay between Manzambi and Jackson when they are in close proximity, but there is no telling pass or shot at the end of the move.

Lovely turn from John McGinn between the lines but Galatasaray’s defender Bardakci intercepted his through ball. Manzambi started wide left on the team sheet, but Maatsen’s runs forward are allowing the Swiss to play in a narrower position.

Akgun wins a free-kick for Galatasaray, who have grown into the contest in the last few minutes. Torreira and Batrakov swapping positions in midfield, and Singo is an impressive player at right-back. The delivery from the free-kick is poor though.

Galatasaray did beat Liverpool twice in this competition last season so cannot be taken lightly tonight.

The pitch does appear to be cutting up a bit in some areas already.

Jackson perhaps unfortunate not be awarded a foul in the left corner, but this has been a bright start by Villa.

Their front players Manazmbi, Alysson and Jackson all combined in a one-touch move after Suzuki played long before the Villa striker was flagged offside.

Lovely pass from Zion Suzuki inside the opening minute, picking out Harwood-Bellis who was free down the right. He found Manzambi unmarked in the middle before Maatsen’s progress down the left was halted. Villa enjoy drawing a press, so it could suit them if the home team are aggressive.

Villa get the game under way, and from the aerial view you can see the seams between patches of the pitch.

A cacophony of hoots, howls and whistles will greet the Villa players, and the same will be true of their every touch of the ball. Aleksey Batrakov, likely to play in behind Yilmaz for the home team, has been identified as Galatasaray’s potential danger man.

Alejandro Garnacho has now been left out of the Villa squad for four games in a row.

He trained at Bodymoor Heath on Monday so does not appear to be injured.

It is looking pretty bleak for the Chelsea loanee, and the comparisons with Liverpool’s Harvey Elliott last season are impossible to escape.

Villa have made a solid start on their return to the Champions League, winning three and losing one.

Victory here would give them a fine chance of progress to the knock-out stages, and provide Unai Emery with some insurance.

Villa face a daunting pair of home games against Paris St-Germain and Borussia Dortmund in their next two league phase matches.

No problems, no. We must play in all pitches, even synthetic we play in the Champions League. It’s not perfect but it is good enough to play football.

Very competitive [on Galatasaray], they are at home so, so intense with their supporters.

We must play focused, together, try and set our game plan as much as possible. We must try and dominate in the way we must build the team.

Six months after the glory of winning the Europa League final in Istanbul, Aston Villa are back on the banks of the Bosphorus.

A potentially tricky match awaits against the Turkish champions, with much of the pre-match scrutiny on the state of the pitch.

Villa were unable to train on Rams Park on Monday as the club is undertaking repair work to the surface.

A positive result and no injuries would represent a great evening for Unai Emery.

Emery appears to be using the versatile Manzambi in a wide left starting position with McGinn in the middle in front of Gomes and Kamara. Mings for Pau Torres is surely all about rotation, with Villa going to Ipswich on Tuesday night. Harwood-Bellis could play at right-back in a similar set-up to the one Villa deployed at Old Trafford.

Lucas Torreira was signed by Arsenal in 2018, Unai Emery’s first summer as head coach. Gundogan has not played many minutes at all this season, but is back on the bench. Osimhen and Leao missing a significant chunk of the season is a major disappointment.

Aston Villa supporters have happy memories of Istanbul after May’s Europa League final, and they return to face Galatasaray this evening in a fixture which could forecast their Champions League prospects.

It has been par for the course for Unai Emery’s team in Europe so far, with victories over Club Brugge, Fenerbahce and Viking and a defeat at Barcelona aligning with the form book.

Nine points from 12 leaves them inside the top eight at the halfway stage of the league phase, but tougher challenges are ahead with PSG and Borussia Dortmund to come after tonight’s game.

Since a statement victory over Manchester City, it has been a frustrating time for Villa either side of the international break. They were dumped out of the League Cup by Bournemouth, were second-best in a home draw with Fulham, threw away a pair of two-goal leads at Old Trafford, and were held by Sunderland at the weekend.

Though Villa put six past Galatasaray’s city rivals Fenerbahce at Villa Park, away games against Turkish opposition can be different beasts, as Liverpool discovered in the last round of Champions League matches.

Galatasaray’s two major attacking threats, Victor Osimhen and Rafael Leão, are both absent with injuries. Davinson Sanchez and Lucas Torreira are former Premier League players in their squad. Galatasaray have won two of four Champions League games, losing to Barcelona and Sporting Lisbon, but they are top of the Turkish Super Lig.

Villa will be without right-back Matty Cash owing to a concussion sustained during the international break with Poland, but will hope to have Victor Lindelof available again after he missed the Sunderland draw with illness.

Emery’s team were unable to train at Rams Park yesterday in order to give a troublesome pitch maximum recovery time after emergency renovation work.

“If we could have trained in the stadium of Galatasaray, maybe we would have decided for the same situation, but it’s not changing our routine,” Emery said. “How the pitch is going to be tomorrow is important, but it’s not an excuse because it’s [the same] for both teams. Hopefully the pitch will be as best as possible.”

#901. London’s people-first approach to smart-city development

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Benjamin Plackett is a science journalist based in London.

A virtual-reality model of London’s main financial district, the City of London, has mapped the size and location of every building.Credit: Mike Kemp/In Pictures via Getty Images

London has risen to fourth place in the IMD Smart City Index 2026, up from sixth place in 2025 and eighth place in 2024. The index — which is published by IMD, an independent Swiss business institute — draws mostly on residents’ perceptions of infrastructure and technology, not a tally of sensors. That focus on perspective is important, says Trevor Dorling, managing director of DG Cities, a private urban-innovation consultancy spun out of the Royal Borough of Greenwich local authority, which works to make better use of data and introduce new technologies in the southeast London borough.

“We increasingly describe our work as ‘city innovation’ rather than ‘smart cities’, because in many people’s minds ‘smart’ is associated with gadgets and gizmos,” says Dorling. “The aim is to use technology to create better places for people. It shouldn’t be the technologists who define what ‘better’ is, but the communities that live there.”

There is plenty of evidence that London has the resources and knowledge to apply research solutions in such a people-centred way. In the 2026 Nature Index Science Cities table, London is ranked 21st overall, but it jumps to 5th place for health-sciences output, for instance.

The Smart Mobility Living Lab, created by a consortium of public and private organizations, including DG Cities, spans 24 kilometres of roads in Greenwich and the Queen Elizabeth Olympic Park in Stratford, and is one example of London’s efforts to create societal impact with its innovation.

The area has more than 1,000 different road features, from speed bumps and pedestrian crossings to one-way systems and bridges, that allow companies to test new vehicles and services in busy, real-world complexity. “The driving force for this was the rapid development of self-driving technologies and exploring the opportunities this presented for safety and accessibility, as well as the challenges,” says Dorling.

Trials to test self-driving shuttle buses and delivery vans have put the technology in public view, with residents invited to ride in the test vehicles, an openness that Dorling says has helped overcome scepticism and brought local authorities into the development process at an early stage.

London’s digital-twin projects are similarly pragmatic. The local authority in Harrow (northwest London) uses high-resolution drone imagery to inspect and measure roofs and buildings remotely and to build interactive maps of parks. The council used this approach in April 2026 to make a 3D model of Headstone Manor and Museum — a restored medieval complex and local-history museum — saving £12,000 (US$16,260) by avoiding a conventional roof survey with scaffolding and manual inspections.

In London’s main financial district, known as the City of London, a virtual-reality model created by the local authority in collaboration with researchers and digital spatial mappers has captured the size and location of every building, window, lamppost and traffic light within the area to within two centimetres of accuracy, allowing planners and the public to properly scrutinize building proposals.

Elsa Arcaute, a complexity science researcher at University College London, cautions against too much faith in digital twins, as a city with all its complexity and interplay between urbanity, nature and human behaviour cannot be completely duplicated.

#900. How Mauricio Pochettino can solve Man United’s bad luck problem

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

United have suffered from freak misfortune in each of Pochettino’s first two games in charge but there is a way the Argentine can mitigate against the effects

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

Mauricio Pochettino could only resort to basic logic. “It’s difficult to understand,” the new Manchester United manager said of various moments in his team’s chaotic 2-2 draw at Sporting CP. You could even extend that description to the logic of the performance.

For a match characterised by so much error, and often absurdity, United were actually encouragingly competent.

The basic organisation was better. The application was more intense. They probably should have won the game. And yet the reason they didn’t points to one of Pochettino’s bigger challenges, to go alongside imposing a tactical idea on this team.

Because, from one perspective, United were simply undone by blind bad luck. That statement arguably applies to each of Pochettino’s first two games, which is why it’s hard not to have at least some sympathy for the new coach.

Against Liverpool, an entire first gameplan was undone by a controversial early red card for Leny Yoro that the FA have said should not have stood – amid considerable controversy. Against Sporting in the Champions League, among other decisions, a possible late winner was overruled by what felt a spurious decision.

With both, there was a sense of the odds being unfairly stacked at crucial moments. Pochettino had few other options against Liverpool and few remaining minutes against Sporting.

The very outlook from his first two games could have been entirely transformed. And it is that outlook which is especially crucial right now, given how low on confidence the team has been.

Their mood could have been transformed, too, and at a fragile moment.

Pochettino can do nothing about luck, after all; about the basic bounces of the ball – quite an irony given Bruno Fernandes’ second goal.

That’s despite this being a club that arguably perpetuated the idea you make your own luck more than any in modern football. It was the entire lesson of the Ferguson era, especially the mythic treble season of 1998-99.

That United side, more than maybe any other European champions, just imposed their will on game after game. They never accepted setbacks or losing positions. They kept going until they manifested victory, regardless of anything else.

The idea that this represented ‘making their own luck; was of course a myth, though. There were many moments when they got extremely fortunate, in a manner they could do nothing about.

That applies to everything from Dennis Bergkamp hitting a weak penalty in that FA Cup semi-final replay to Mehmet Scholl’s chip dropping onto the post rather than the inside netting in the Champions League final.

Many in football, and especially in their analytics departments, would caution that the effect of luck in football remains extremely under-appreciated.

It may even be the next most important factor on the game after wages and recruitment.

United’s whole 2026 could be cast as a case study. In Michael Carrick’s first five months, so many borderline moments went his way. In his last five, so many went against him.

The real issue was the effect, and the momentum.

Because, if Pochettino or any other manager obviously have no control over their luck, they can control how they respond to it. This was probably the real lesson of the Ferguson era. It wasn’t making your own luck, it was making your own path in response.

United suffered multiple setbacks but just didn’t let it affect them. There was a Govan ironworks resilience, that has been entirely absent in this team.

That’s how so many games have become so bad, when the 2026 version of United have simply looked beaten. It could be seen in this Sporting game.

Although United did start well, their belief dropped after the double penalty and they buckled.

As one insider said after the game, “there have just been so many ‘head’s gone’ defensive moments this season”.

It speaks to that fragility. And that, as much as the tactics, is what Pochettino has to address. He needs to restore belief. It’s just as well this is known as one of his best qualities, regardless of the questions about how advanced his tactics are in the modern game.

There were signs he has made a start, which is why the way these opening two games went seems such a specific setback. Work was undone in the most unlucky ways that also had the most disproportionate effect.

The irony is that part of building resilience is to now dwell on that, to try and build a tunnel vision.

Pochettino is said to feel he can do that with the majority of this squad, despite the doubts about personnel.

And that’s what this is all about: dispelling doubts. His United might not be able to make their own luck. But they can forge a new resilience.

Real Madrid look in ominous form under Jose Mourinho, with the 15-time Champions League winners chasing a tenth straight victory in all competitions for the first time since December 2021.

However, dig a little deeper and Los Blancos are not as bulletproof as they appear. Mourinho's men staged late rescue acts to come from behind to beat Roma and AEK Athens last month, while they fought back from 1-0 down to edge past Celta Vigo 2-1 in La Liga on Saturday, courtesy of goals from Jude Bellingham and Carlos Espi — the latter's third late winner this season.

It suggests that this Madrid side have plenty of character and individual quality, but perhaps are not putting in the 90-minute performances that their form would suggest. That being said, they will expect to extend their perfect home record to nine wins in nine games this term.

Kylian Mbappe will become the second-youngest player to hit 75 Champions League goals if he scores for the fifth successive match in the league phase, while Vinicius Junior is set to start after he was named among the substitutes against Celta.

SEE ALSO How to watch Champions League 2026/27

PSV Eindhoven last faced Madrid in the quarter-finals of the 1988/89 European Cup, when the Dutch side were reigning champions and Los Blancos were in the middle of a 32-year trophy drought on the continent's biggest stage.

Tonight's visitors have progressed beyond the last eight only once since then, while their opponents have won the competition nine times in that period — and that gulf is likely to be reflected at the Bernabeu.

While PSV are top of the Eredivisie, they have taken only four points from their opening four league phase games, with their best result a 1-0 win at Porto last month. That was sandwiched by a 1-0 loss at RB Leipzig and a 2-1 home defeat by Club Brugge, having drawn 1-1 with Shakhtar Donetsk on opening night.

They are without captain Mauro Junior after he suffered a muscle injury in the 4-1 victory against NEC Nijmegen on Saturday, while Adamo Nagalo, Jerdy Schouten, Sami Ouaissa and Alassane Plea are also sidelined.

Madrid's perfect home record and star quality makes it difficult to see anything other than a comfortable win for Los Blancos.

#898. Champions League power rankings: Real Madrid surge – while rivals hit by injuries

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

Real Madrid remain the lone team with an 100 per cent record, while only PSG and Arsenal are now also unbeaten after a shock loss for Bayern Munich

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

Real Madrid will head to Arsenal in matchweek six of the Champions League with the only 100 per cent record remaining in the competition after Jose Mourinho’s side made it five wins from from five this season.

The 15-time winners have found form just as a couple of their main rivals have been dealt major injury blows, too, with Bayern Munich’s Harry Kane suffering an ankle injury and Paris Saint-Germain losing Desire Doue to an ACL injury, adding to the absence of Khvicha Kvaratskhelia.

It means that will back-to-back winners PSG remain top of our standings, the competition is looking rather open underneath them – as the league phase table begins to take shape and the fight for the top-eight and play-off places intensifies.

We compiled our 36-team power rankings by combining team’s previous performance in the Champions League, their results in the competition so far, and the likelihood of them going all the way this season. Agree or disagree with our standings after matchweek five? Let us know and have your say in the comments below.

Luis Enrique’s back-to-back champions have seen their star-studded attack devastated by the injuries to Khvicha Kvaratskhelia and Desire Doue, who are both likely to be out for the rest of the season due to ACL issues. While Ousmane Dembele remains, as well as a brilliant midfield three, Enrique will have his work cut out if PSG are to remain as dangerous and retain their title this season. They dropped points for the first time in the Champions League this season as Roma secured a 2-2 draw at the Parc des Princes.

Even with Lamine Yamal and Raphinha rested, the goals kept flying and a double from Anthony Gordon in the 4-1 win over Sabah made it 69 goals in 18 games in all competitions this season from Hansi Flick’s side. The LaLiga champions are well placed to finish the league phase as one of the top seeds for the knockout stages, but the big question remains how their defence will stand up against one of the top teams. Conceding four in defeat against PSG means there is still much to prove.

The arrival of winter is perhaps leading to some frustration, particularly in front of goal. Arsenal remain unbeaten but they were punished for not taking their opportunities as they dropped points at home to Borussia Dortmund, a result which means their place in the top-eight is not assured yet ahead of tough games against Real Madrid and Real Betis.

Real Madrid have come into a remarkable run of form, with a thumping win over PSV making it 10 wins in a row in all competitions under Jose Mourinho. It’s funny, in the Champions League, Real Madrid have trailed several games yet have maximum points. Now, the 15-time Champions League winners are not just managing to find a way, but they are blowing teams off the park.

Before Andoni Iraola’s first season, it felt like so much depended on the potential of Alexander Isak and Florian Wirtz coming good in the Liverpool attack. Well, the signs of the past few weeks have been hugely promising as Isak and Wirtz continued to build their partnership in the 3-0 win at Club Brugge, with the Reds bouncing back from their shock defeat at Fenerbahce last time out.

The major concern for the German champions is the fitness of their Ballon d’Or holder Harry Kane, who will now be out until the “business end” of the season due to an ankle injury. Bayern have plenty of games to play until then and the question is whether they can get through to the top eight without Kane to avoid an additional play-off round. A stunning 2-1 defeat at Lille, which featured some calamitous defending and a truly remarkable Aleksandar Pavlovic own goal (honestly, go and check it out...), saw Bayern drop to 15th in the table.

Three defeats from four in the Premier League have well and truly taken shine off an impressive start for Enzo Maresca’s side, while uncertainty off the pitch remains as well. After another sloppy performance against Napoli and the returning Kevin De Bruyne means it is now 10 games in a row without a clean sheet. City now face a mouthwatering trip to Barcelona and likely require a result to avoid dropping out of the top eight.

Up at the top of the table with the likes of Real Madrid, PSG and Barcelona, the Champions League debutants are certainly making a name for themselves. Cesc Fabregas’s stylish side didn’t quite hit the same heights against AEK Athens after their nine-goal dismantling of poor Lens, but look what comes next. Those games against PSG and Barcelona at the end of the league phase, after a tricky trip to Real Betis, are going to be fascinating.

After starting with back-to-back defeats, Inter have responded with three consecutive wins. There was more good news in the 2-0 win over Stuttgart as Lautaro Martinez marked his return from injury after a month on the sidelines with a goal.

Sure, they absolutely bottled it against Real Madrid and Manchester United, throwing away leads on both occasions. Sure, they’ve got five points from five games in the Champions League and sit outside the top 24 in the league table. But a 2-2 draw at Paris Saint-Germain continued Roma’s impressive season under Gian Piero Gasperini; they remain unbeaten in Serie A and now have a more favourable run of games in the Champions League. On performances alone, they’ve earned a place in our top 10.

Are the Premier League’s London clubs at an advantage? Arsenal prepare to put that unique theory to the test

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Having made their longest Premier League away trip of the season to Newcastle last week, Arsenal can settle into familiar surroundings for the festive period: the Gunners don’t leave London again until mid-January when they travel to Hull.

Between now and then, Arsenal’s longest away day takes them just 22 kilometres to Brentford - Google Maps says the average person could walk from the Emirates to the Gtech in under four hours, never mind a professional footballer.

That’s the third of 11 straight games in the capital for the Gunners, which will become 12 if they’re drawn at home in the third round of the FA Cup, beginning with Tuesday’s Champions League clash against Borussia Dortmund. Recent history suggests an interesting theory about such home comforts.

Eleven games into their title defence, Arsenal sit second in the Premier League away table with four wins, one draw and one defeat from six games on the road. Not that it’s anything new for the Gunners to occupy such heights: they’ve boasted the top flight’s best away record in each of the last four seasons.

And that comes with the territory of being a London club. Across the last 10 Premier League campaigns not impacted by pandemic crowd restrictions (so excluding 2019/20 and 2020/21), only once have more clubs from London had a bottom-half away record than a top-half away record. That was last term, when four of the seven London clubs finished in the bottom 10 of the away table (Crystal Palace, Brentford, Fulham and West Ham).

In each of the other nine seasons in question, at least 57 per cent of the Premier League’s London clubs have finished with one of the best 10 away records in the division; in 2016/17, all five of them did (Chelsea, Tottenham, Arsenal, Palace and West Ham).

So, is it an advantage to be a London club?

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

There’s not really a simple answer to that question (sorry), but we can still pull together some interesting takeaways.

This season, the average Premier League club will travel 153 kilometres for an away fixture. For two clubs, that average climbs to over 300km: the league’s two most north-easterly sides, Sunderland (350km) and Newcastle (347km), and the most south-westerly, Bournemouth (317km). Conversely, one side will travel a touch under 200km on average: Coventry (198km) – in that sense, you might consider the Sky Blues the ultimate Midlands club.

But the top-flight’s six London clubs all sit in the bottom eight of the league in terms of average away travel distance, with Palace travelling the furthest (227km) and Spurs the least far (202km). And the very fact that those sides account for just over a quarter of the division means short trips are a regular occurrence.

And for Arsenal, this 11-match stretch that sees them go no further than Brentford could not fall at a better time than the notoriously hectic festive period – certainly when it comes to maximising recovery time between fixtures, which come thick and fast an average of one game every 4.2 days between now and January 5 (though it’s worth noting that turnaround is still below the UEFA-recommended minimum window of five days between matches).

Could the timing of Arsenal’s London residency, so to speak, prove crucial to another successful Premier League title push? Well, they’re already six points clear at the top and look like they could walk it, given Manchester City’s dramatic recent drop-off, but minimising time spent on the road during one of the busiest stages of the campaign seems unlikely to work to their detriment.

That being said, a quick word on Chelsea: the Blues have left London three times all season but are languishing in mid-table in the Premier League and are out of the Carabao Cup. So, maybe there’s something to be said for getting out of town on a more regular basis. Besides, it’s not like elite-level players these days are travelling in anything less than luxury, is it?

Tom Hancock started freelancing for FourFourTwo in April 2019 and has also written for the Premier League and Opta Analyst, among others. He supports Wycombe Wanderers and has a soft spot for Wealdstone. A self-confessed statto, he has been known to watch football with a spreadsheet (or several) open...

#895. Mauricio Pochettino ‘so proud’ of Man Utd players despite schoolboy errors against Sporting CP

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

Bruno Fernandes scored twice but a Senne Lammens blunder cost the Old Trafford team victory in Portugal

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

Mauricio Pochettino was proud of Manchester United’s performance and his players’ early progress in the action-packed 2-2 draw at Sporting Lisbon in the Champions League.

The former Argentina international began his reign with a chastening 4-0 loss at rivals Liverpool on Sunday, when Leny Yoro’s early – and subsequently overturned – red card was the catalyst for Anfield agony.

More frustration followed on Wednesday, when Senne Lammens gifted Sporting a penalty converted by Luis Suarez shortly after denying him from the spot before Bruno Fernandes’ double with the help of a bobble put United in front.

But Suarez would level in the second half after nudging Lammens when attempting to gather a high ball and Pochettino’s hopes of a first win ended when home goalkeeper Kaique Pereira’s own goal was ruled out.

Szymon Marciniak adjudged Patrick Dorgu to have fouled him having been sent to the monitor on a night when the referee’s early whistle meant a disallowed first half Amad Diallo goal could not be overturned.

Youri Tielemans was incorrectly booked for his role in that incident and picked up a second booking at the end of an eventful night that saw Pochettino focus on the positives in Portugal.

“I am so proud of our players, my players,” Pochettino told TNT Sports. “It was a really tough game.

“I like the team during 90 minutes, the personality, the character. And it’s true that it’s difficult to find some game that (you will) be more punished.

“We were punished a lot in different actions that were key, but I think everyone that watched the game saw all the action.

“Only what I can say is I feel proud about the players. I think we today showed the way that we want to play. It’s only one week working together. I feel so proud. I told them after the game.”

Referee Marciniak’s poor performance will dominate the fallout to the draw at the Estadio Jose Alvalade, as will goalkeeper Lammens’ latest shaky display in a season replete with individual errors by United players.

“Always we need to do double effort,” Pochettino said. “We need to concentrate more and focus more and try to (do) recovery better, do all the effort.

“I think in this type of situation we start to fix also with results, but with (a) performance like today that is for me is the best medicine to prepare the next game.”

Pochettino’s frantic start to life in charge continues on Saturday afternoon at Old Trafford, where he will take charge of United for the first time against Brentford.

The embattled Red Devils have just one win to show from their opening 11 Premier League matches and languish 19th in the standings.

“I think we need to encourage and we need to really believe in our play,” Pochettino added. “We need to believe more and more and more.

“I think we need to give the capacity and the tools to perform and of course improving things.

“But that is the way that we need to show our aggression, like in the second half. We recover a lot of ball in the opposite half.

“We were aggressive, and I think I think that is the way that we want to play.”

#894. What has happened to Senne Lammens this season?
