But with uncertainty shrouding the club – following an independent commission finding City guilty of over 100 breaches of serious financial rules across a nine-year period – things may be about to become even more unstable, should the six-time Premier League champions pull the trigger on their manager already.

Maresca started fantastically after taking over from his former mentor, winning his first seven Premier League games – including a defiant 3-0 thumping of Liverpool at Anfield following the news that City had been found guilty and were facing Premier League sanctions.

But the Eastlands outfit went on to lose the following three games in the league, drew against Fulham at the weekend, and had to rely on a late Rayan Cherki equaliser against Napoli last night in order to scrape a point in the Champions League.

Fichajes in Spain are reporting that Maresca “will be fighting for his job” if he doesn't beat Arsenal this weekend, with the Gunners having already outclassed his side 3-0 in the Community Shield earlier this season.

A defeat at the Emirates Stadium would widen the gap between the pair to a seemingly unassailable nine points, with Liverpool and surprise package Brighton & Hove Albion shaping up to be the champions' biggest threats in completing back-to-back league championships for the first time in almost a century.

Despite the autumnal wobble, however, FourFourTwo understands that there are no plans at present to part with Maresca.

Fofana joked about missing a penalty and insinuated he was happy to sit on his lucrative Chelsea contract in the explosive interview

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

Xabi Alonso says Wesley Fofana has apologised to Chelsea after giving an explosive interview without the club’s permission.

A two-hour conversation with Fofana was published by French YouTuber Zach Nani on Friday, during which the 25-year-old appeared to joke about missing a penalty in Chelsea’s shootout defeat to Liverpool which knocked them out of the Carabao Cup.

He has also received a torrent of backlash for stating that he considered retiring from football during his lengthy injury lay-off, only to be discouraged by his agent because “you’ve still got so many years left on your contract, and so much money to earn” - insinuating he was motivated to sit on his current lucrative deal at Stamford Bridge.

Alonso was pressed about the interview before Friday’s trip to Nottingham Forest, revealing in his news conference that Fofana had tried to make amends with the club.

“Absolutely, we have addressed that with him and for sure it was unfortunate,” Alonso said.

“He apologised, he knows it was not right the moment, it was not right the content, we are here to take things seriously and he said that it's not going to be repeated and we know that it's something that we don't want, these kind of things and they are not going to be repeated for sure.”

Asked whether Fofana would face any further sanction, such as be dropped from the squad, or if the case was closed, Alonso replied: “Closed.”

Fofana has struggled for form as part of Chelsea’s porous defence in recent weeks and, alongside Levi Colwill, came under criticism for his part in the club’s damning 4-1 defeat to Leeds last weekend.

Chelsea have been hurt by the absence of summer signing Maxence Lacroix with a hamstring injury and Alonso confirmed he is still not yet fit to make a return.

“It's one less week than the last game so we are closer to recovery but not for this game,” Alonso said.

Joao Pedro also remains sidelined as he nurses a thigh problem, alongside winger Jamie Gittens and defender Jorrel Hato, though Alonso did confirm Moises Caicedo will be involved after enduring an injury scare against Leeds.

A clip of Jude Bellingham standing up for a female reporter who was interrupted during a post-match interview has gone viral.

BBC Sport’s Spanish football reporter Elizabeth Conway attempted to ask Bellingham a follow-up question in the mixed zone - where media gather to interview players - after asking him about his second-half goal in Real Madrid’s 5-1 win over PSV Eindhoven on Tuesday.

Her second question was interrupted by a male reporter, leading Bellingham to say, “Sorry, she's got one more”, before answering Conway’s follow-up.

The clip of the interview spread widely on social media after the Champions League game, which meant Real Madrid - who had gone 1-0 down in the first half before storming back - extended their 100% winning record in this season’s league phase.

Conway told BBC Radio WM the mixed zone is “utter carnage” and can be “intimidating” as one of few women working in sports media, saying: “You've got elbows you've got microphones, you've got cameras, you've got massive tall men reaching over you.

“I'm one of very, very, few female reporters and one of very, very, few English reporters there, so trying to make a stand for yourself and get in a good position is so important.”

Of Bellingham’s interjection, she said: “It's shown him yet again being respectful, polite, and really respecting me as a journalist.”

The 23-year-old was widely praised on social media for how he handled the situation, with comments reading “A whole lot of class” and “a role model for young men”.

Bellingham scored in the 60th minute and provided the assist for Vinicius Junior’s late goal, with Federico Valverde and Kylian Mbappe, who scored a brace, also on the scoresheet.

The England star was part of a triple change at half-time and made an immediate impact, with his inventive goal coming from a touch with his left foot before he chipped it up with his right and volleyed home from 25 yards.

Real Madrid top the group stage standings after five games played.

Newcastle United's owners PIF are seeking fresh investment to help the club achieve its infrastructure goals

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

At first glance, headlines stating that Saudi Arabia’s Public Investment Fund (PIF) has put 25 per cent of Newcastle United up for sale were always going to draw intrigue and perhaps even alarm on Tyneside.

Five years on from the much-heralded takeover that ended Mike Ashley’s unpopular regime, any suggestion of the club’s sovereign wealth owners cashing in naturally invites fears that the project is running out of steam.

However, this proposed transaction is actually one of the more encouraging developments for Newcastle supporters in months.

First and foremost, PIF are not packing their bags and walking away from St James’ Park.

Rather than offloading existing shares to pocket a profit, the club is issuing brand-new equity - with US investment bank J.P. Morgan appointed to find an external partner.

This means not a single penny from the sale will flow back into PIF’s coffers - they are not recouping on their investment. Instead, funds raised through the share issue will supposedly be injected into Newcastle's ongoing projects.

PIF will see its majority stake diluted rather than exiting the club, remaining firmly in the driving seat as owners with majority control.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

While fans have grown increasingly frustrated by delays around major infrastructure upgrades, the club, led on the executive side by chief executive David Hopkinson, remains engaged in long-term plans to either substantially redevelop St James’ Park or build a brand-new stadium altogether, alongside the construction of a state-of-the-art training complex.

Bringing in additional investment allows Newcastle to raise hundreds of millions in fresh equity to accelerate those builds, sharing the heavy financial lifting.

After a difficult summer that saw stars like Bruno Guimaraes, Sandro Tonali and Anthony Gordon depart to help balance the books, developing Newcastle’s infrastructure and off-pitch revenue streams is the only sustainable way to compete with Europe's elite.

Since original consortium member Amanda Staveley sold her shares and left the board in 2024, ownership of the Magpies has been split between just two parties: PIF holds an 84 per cent majority stake, while the London-based Reuben family - represented on the board by Jamie Reuben, via RB Sports & Media - owns the remaining 16 per cent.

Issuing new shares to cover a 25 per cent stake will dilute both PIF and potentially the Reubens proportionally, leaving PIF with comfortably over 60 per cent of the club and still overall control.

Joe joined FourFourTwo as senior digital writer in July 2025 after five years covering Leeds United in the Championship and Premier League. Joe's 'Mastermind' specialist subject is 2000s-era Newcastle United having had a season ticket at St. James' Park for 10 years before relocating to Leeds and later London. #870. Germany star ruled out of Women’s World Cup 2027 after accepting doping ban

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

Laura Freigang has been suspended after three whereabouts failures

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

Germany forward Laura Freigang will miss next summer’s Women’s World Cup after accepting a suspension over failure to comply with doping regulations.

The Eintracht Frankfurt captain was accused of failing to provide a drugs test or submit her whereabouts for testing on three occasions between March 2025 and February 2026, thereby breaching the World Anti-Doping Code.

She reached an settlement agreement with WADA, Germany’s National Anti-Doping Agency, and the German football federation over the case, which has resulted in a 16-month ban backdated to 8 June 2026, the day she was notified of the case against her.

It means she will not be eligible to return to football until 8 October 2027. She will miss the Women’s World Cup, which runs from 24 June to 25 July, in Brazil.

The 28-year-old can return to training two months before the expiry of the ban.

Eintracht Frankfurt announced the news on Thursday, with the club to “soon begin discussions to establish the structuring of their future contract [with Freigang] in light of this suspension”. Freigang’s contract runs until 30 June next year.

Freigang released a statement on Instagram saying: “It is important for me to emphasise once again that at no time was there any suspicion of doping against me.

“The last few months have been extremely hard for me. Further proceedings would have meant high financial, mental and emotional burdens for me. That's why I chose this way, in the hope of finding some calm, clarity and perspective for myself.”

She added: “It breaks my heart not to be able to be on the field, helping my team and being able to live the everyday life that I love so much.”

None of Eintracht Frankfurt’s results since her ban began in June are affected.

Katharina Kiel, director of women’s football, said: “The agreement that has now been reached provides clarity and planning certainty in a process that is unique to Eintracht Frankfurt – for us as a club, but above all for Laura.

“The way she and the team have handled the situation over the past few months, and the way Laura personally led by example on the pitch during a very difficult time, deserves the utmost recognition.

“At Eintracht Frankfurt, we have witnessed the strong sense of unity that characterises this club. We will calmly discuss the future and the details of our working relationship with Laura.”

Freigang has 45 caps for Germany and was a member of the squad which reached the Euro 2022 final. She has been at Eintracht Frankfurt since 2018.

Fast forward half a century and the Reds head into their third meeting with the Belgians after thrashing rivals Manchester United 4-0 on Sunday, in what was surely their best result of the Andoni Iraola era.

The six-time winners are above tonight's opponents only on goals scored, so a defeat would not only see them leapfrogged by the Belgians but also allow a cluster of teams to steal a march in the race for the top eight. Liverpool won their opening three matches in the league phase but suffered a shock 3-2 defeat at Fenerbahce in gameweek four, so they cannot afford to slip up again.

Ryan Gravenberch remains an injury doubt with a heel issue, while Cody Gakpo is unlikely to recover from his calf problem in time. Conor Bradley, Hugo Ekitike and Giovanni Leoni are also still sidelined.

This is likely to be a tougher game for Liverpool than some people may think, but we are backing them to claim a narrow win.

#867. Tosin Adarabioyo: ‘No one can chat s*** about Cole Palmer’

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

Interview: Adarabioyo, speaking at the launch of his trading card shop, issued a passionate defence of his former Chelsea team-mate Palmer amid criticism of his attitude

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

Tosin Adarabioyo has leapt to the defence of former Chelsea team-mate Cole Palmer amid criticism of the Englishman’s attitude.

Palmer came under fire for a viral interaction with Joao Pedro after Chelsea’s bruising 4-1 thrashing by Leeds last weekend, brushing off the Brazilian after opting not to acknowledge the home fans who booed the team at full-time.

The 24-year-old is going through a difficult patch at the moment, having been left out of Thomas Tuchel’s England squad again for the November internationals after the German manager claimed “he misses too opportunities to impress”.

This led to questions over Palmer’s commitment to the England cause, something club team-mate Morgan Rogers emphatically refuted as “nonsense” and “a lie”.

And Tosin, who moved to from Chelsea to rivals Tottenham in the summer, has now become the latest to publicly back Palmer, with whom he shared two seasons at Stamford Bridge.

“No one can chat s*** about Cole,” Tosin said.

“For me, he's one of the best players I've ever seen. You can say what you want. Honestly, you guys can say what you want. He's a top level player. He will continue to get better.”

Asked whether he was surprised about Palmer’s omission from the England squad, he replied: “Yeah, for sure. Of course, I'm surprised. For me, he's the best No 10 in the Premier League.”

Tosin also echoed Rogers’ sentiment in regards to doubts over Palmer’s hunger to play for the Three Lions, with the Chelsea forward struggling to get back in favour with Tuchel after missing out on the World Cup, before his return to the international fold in September was swiftly curtailed by injury.

“False, false, false,” Tosin added. “I know Cole's dreams, his aspirations. So, yeah, it's completely false.”

While Tosin will passionately defend Palmer against his critics, this doesn’t spare the Chelsea man of a friendly jibe, especially in the wake of Tottenham’s first win at Stamford Bridge in eight years last month.

Palmer was sent off in the 2-0 defeat to their fierce rivals and Tosin, who missed the match through injury, was sure to savour the triumph at his mate’s expense.

Asked if the pair shared some post-match banter, Tosin laughed: “Cole's my guy, man - yeah, of course. But I'll keep that secret.”

Palmer was among a number of Tosin’s team-mates, past and present, supporting him at the launch of his trading card shop, Card Cop, in London. The retail space in Borough Yards will open to the public on Thursday 26 November.

The Spurs defender, who is an avid collector, is joined by the likes of former Blues team-mates Reece James and Levi Colwill, as well as West Ham defender Kyle Walker-Peters, in investing in the business.

Along with the investors, Chelsea’s contingent at the launch party included Rogers, Emmanuel Emegha and Jamie Gittens, while the likes of Dominic Solanke, Micky van de Ven, Archie Gray and Ben Davies came down to support their relatively new Spurs colleague.

“It’s a testament to what we're like as a team,” Tosin said. “We're all very close and very supportive of each other. The boys didn't have to turn up today, but they did. It's amazing. I'm very thankful to them.”

After a dire start to the season, feeling the hangover of their near-miss with relegation last term, Spurs have finally found their groove under Roberto De Zerbi and are now just one point off Chelsea after four wins in five.

Tosin puts the uptick in form down to the team’s Marbella training camp during the first international break of the season, which was crucial in forming a bond within the team.

“It's our trip to Marbella,” he said. “We had a great time. We bonded together. We learned a lot about each other, and we're all striving to put this club where we think it belongs.”

The more things change, the more they stay the same - Watford is an unmanageable club

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Some things are certain in life; death, taxes and Watford sacking another head coach.

At 11:51am on Sunday morning, the news everyone expected had arrived and Alessio Dionisi was relieved of his duties as Watford head coach after five months in charge, following a dismal 4-0 away defeat to Sheffield United, which left the club just one place above the relegation zone.

It was the latest in a series of lifeless performances from a Watford side that have looked ill-equipped for Championship football from the moment the season started.

Now, at a time where Watford need Championship experience more than ever, owner Gino Pozzo has turned to former Romania boss Edward Iordanescu, a man that has had 13 jobs in 15 years, never managed more than 60 games at any team and most importantly, never played or coached in England or in one of Europe’s major leagues.

Given Watford’s reputation with head coaches, many would joke Iordanescu’s appointment sounds like a match made in heaven.

For Hornets fans, though, it’s an act of desperation from a club that has no plan, structure or hope.

In truth, Dionisi is the latest in a series of head coaches who have been let down by owner Pozzo, chairman Scott Duxbury and technical director Gianluca Nani, who seem incapable of building a squad or supporting a head coach.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

Things could have been so different for the Italian, because at the start of the season, there was clearly something there. Watford were excellent in their opening day win over Southampton - playing with real flair and intensity in the first half - and followed that up with draws against Wrexham and West Ham. It was clear the players respected the Italian.

However, the warning signs were already there. In the summer, Dionisi and supporters were told that Watford would prioritise experienced players in the transfer market. None arrived.

Nestory Irankunda, Imran Louza and Giorgi Chakvetadze - three key players - were sold and not replaced, with Watford starting the season with just two centre-backs on the club’s books and two fit central midfielders.

The Italian sounded increasingly exasperated as his calls for reinforcements fell on deaf ears until the final few days of the window, where Watford eventually panicked and brought in Stephy Mavididi, Soumaila Coulibaly and Branimir Mlacic on loan. Myron Boadu and Michail Antonio arrived on free transfers.

Most of those players arrived unfit and come September, Dionisi was struggling to fill the bench as injuries took hold. The Italian never really recovered from embarrassing defeats to Burnley and Cardiff City, deploying a back five in recent weeks as he attempted to make the Golden Boys harder to beat.

Quite frankly, Watford are unmanageable. Not even Pep Guardiola would be successful at Vicarage Road, because no head coach is given the opportunity to implement a style of play when they have to contend with poor recruitment, a leadership vacuum and a dressing room with seemingly poor attitudes.

Rob Edwards was promised he'd be backed in the transfer market come hell or high water by chairman Duxbury in the summer of 2022. Most of the signings he received didn't fit his system and he was sacked within two months of the season starting.

After Edwards, Slaven Bilic thought he'd be able to sign players he wanted in the January transfer window. He received Joao Ferreira and Henrique Araujo - both of whom never looked suited to Championship football – as well as Ryan Porteous, Wesley Hoedt and Britt Assombalonga. Bilic was gone by March.

Then came Chris Wilder, who repeatedly called out the poor attitude within the dressing room and wasn't given a contract extension when his deal expired in the summer of 2023. After the wheels came off under Valerian Ismael, Tom Cleverley was promoted to head coach in 2024 and despite a thin squad, united the players and fans, having been a popular player at Vicarage Road during his playing days.

Once again, though, January arrived and Cleverley didn't get the options he so dearly needed, meaning Watford's form dropped off and he was sacked, somewhat harshly, at the end of the season.

Just last season, the popular Javi Gracia returned for a second spell in charge and had Watford in the play-off spots by January. He was promised additions, but none were forthcoming and ultimately the Spaniard decided the job wasn't worth his time. Gracia resigned, returning to Spain to spend time with his family.

In short, it's time the Watford ownership took a long, hard look at themselves, rather than the head coach. Has Iordanescu been appointed because no one sensible will take it? Any head coach worth his salt in England - and possibly now Italy, too - knows what they’re walking into.

In a recent interview with Roy Moore from the 1881 Movement, Pozzo tried shifting accountability for the club’s downfall, which can be traced back to the FA Cup Final in 2019. Since then, numerous decisions have, in the eyes of supporters, led to the erosion of the club's identity - fans have had enough.

Empty statements, the constant churn of players and head coaches, and what appears to be a lack of any real structure or plan - supporters are fed up.

The fact Watford closed their Under-21 setup, downgraded their academy and sold off the women's team this summer was a huge source of disappointment for fans, too, given the club’s rich history of bringing players through their youth system.

Unless there is a sudden change of approach overnight, Watford are only heading one way and that's down to League 1.

Bradley is a sports journalist and Watford fan, who previously spent seven years working for talkSPORT. In his spare time, he is the commentator for Non League side Harefield United. Previously, he worked for Newsquest, covering both Watford and Leyton Orient for the Watford Observer and East London Guardian Series newspapers. He has also had pieces published in the Daily Mail and Watford's matchday programme.

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

The England international has extended his stay with the club until 2029

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

Leeds striker Dominic Calvert-Lewin has signed a new deal, taking his stay with the club until 2029.

The England international joined Leeds on a three-year deal after leaving Everton as a free agent in 2025, and has now extended for another two and a half years.

He scored 15 goals in all competitions last season and so far has six in this campaign, having rebooted his career following a difficult spell marred by injuries at Everton, and earned a recall to the England squad.

Leeds said: “Leeds United are delighted to announce Dominic Calvert-Lewin has signed a new contract with the club.

“The England international has put pen to paper on a two-and-a-half-year deal at Elland Road, keeping him in West Yorkshire until the summer of 2029.

“Everyone at Leeds United is thrilled Dominic has signed a new deal and we look forward to seeing him continue to impress in the famous white shirt.”

Calvert-Lewin has started all 11 top-flight fixtures of this season and scored in the statement 4-1 victory over Chelsea on Saturday. Leeds currently sit seventh in the Premier League, four points off the Champions League places.

He won the Premier League’s Player of the Month Award in December after scoring in six consecutive matches - becoming the first Leeds player to win the award in 24 years.

His performances were recognised by Thomas Tuchel, who called him up to international duty for a 1-1 friendly draw with Uruguay in March, and he retained his place the squad for Nations League matches against Spain and Czechia.

His latest England appearance was against Spain earlier this month when he stepped off the bench to win his 15th cap in the Three Lions’ 3-2 win.

#864. Pockets in compacted DNA tune gene activation

Abhinand Lal is in the Institute for Integrative Biology of the Cell (I2BC), French Alternative Energies and Atomic Energy Commission (CEA), French National Centre for Scientific Research (CNRS), Paris-Saclay University, 91190 Gif-sur-Yvette, France.

Daan Noordermeer is in the Institute for Integrative Biology of the Cell (I2BC), French Alternative Energies and Atomic Energy Commission (CEA), French National Centre for Scientific Research (CNRS), Paris-Saclay University, 91190 Gif-sur-Yvette, France.

Large regions of chromosomes are organized into a state known as heterochromatin. This densely packed form of DNA represses gene activity. Curiously, some families of clustered genes can be activated even though they are packed as heterochromatin. Writing in Nature, Buckley et al.1 report findings that explain this paradox: they show how opposing mechanisms that control the organization of heterochromatin promote the stochastic activation of genes in the protocadherin (Pcdh) gene cluster, thereby supporting proper nervous-system development.

#862. Brighton bounce back with Conference League win as Hearts suffer last-gasp defeat

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

Osman scored twice and set up another for Charalampos Kostoulas in a 4-0 win

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

Ibrahim Osman scored his first Brighton goals as his side returned to winning ways by cruising to a 4-0 success over 10-man Universitatea Craiova in the Conference League.

Talk of the high-flying Seagulls potentially being shock Premier League title contenders this season was dampened slightly by Sunday’s surprise 2-0 defeat at Hull.

But Brighton were back to their best against Romanian champions Craiova at the Amex Stadium, with winger Osman putting the Seagulls ahead in the third minute.

Jack Hinshelwood stepped over the ball following Ferdi Kadioglu’s low cross from the right before being played in by Charalampos Kostoulas and squaring to leave Osman with a simple tap-in.

Matt O’Riley had the ball in the net in the 27th minute but the effort was ruled out for offside against Chema Andres, but Maxim De Cuyper scored Brighton’s second six minutes later.

Things went from bad to worse for Craiova, who currently sit top of their domestic league, as defender Vladimir Screciu was sent off in the 39th minute for stamping on O’Riley’s ankle.

Osman set up Kostoulas for the third goal before quickly claiming his second with a fine individual effort as Brighton made it 10 points from four games in the competition.

The 21-year-old should have had another assist but his inviting low cross was blazed over the open goal by substitute Femi Azeez, who later curled narrowly wide.

Azeez’s glaring miss mattered little as Brighton comfortably extended their unbeaten home record to eight games ahead of attempting to put the league campaign back on track when Newcastle visit on Sunday.

Elsewhere on Thursday night Hearts’ Conference League hopes suffered a hammer blow as Folarin Balogun’s stoppage-time goal consigned them to a 3-2 defeat at home to Monaco.

Theylooked on course to pick up their second league-phase point after stunning first-half strikes from Jordi Altena and Sabah Kerjota either side of goals from visiting pair Folarin Balogun and Edian Diop.

But in the last of four added minutes, USA forward Balogun got himself free in the box to slot home and maintain Monaco’s perfect record in the competition.

Hearts will now require high-scoring victories over Borac and Pafos in their last two games to have a chance of scrambling into the top 24 and qualifying for the knockout phase.

#861. Wirtz follows rich Liverpool heritage with star showing in win over Brugge

It had to be this way. Liverpool No 7s have historically defined matches against Club Brugge, so it was entirely appropriate that Florian Wirtz preserved that rich heritage.

The late Kevin Keegan thrashed home a free-kick at this stadium 50 years ago to win Liverpool the Uefa Cup and Sir Kenny Dalglish was the hero at Wembley in 1978 when his deft finish ensured the European Cup was retained.

That jersey means those who have subsequently worn it have had high standards to keep. Although this fixture did not carry the heft of past occasions, it was symbolic that Wirtz, the incumbent, decorated this contest and propelled Liverpool a step closer to the knockout phase.

On another night Alexander Isak would have expected his two goals to take the headlines, but he would have appreciated more than anyone the magic spells that Wirtz kept casting. The Swede had a glorious view of the strike that essentially secured three points in Belgium’s frozen north.

The idea of Brugge playing in the biggest club fixture of all, sadly, seems fanciful now given how much the footballing landscape has changed. But they are a progressive side, full of attacking wit, and they had ambitions and, on another evening, would have done some damage.

How often, though, do you see sides these days undo their good work by being overambitious when playing out from the back? Yann Sommer has had a distinguished career, the Swiss goalkeeper has played for Bayern Munich and Inter Milan, but he is 37 and his aberration was decisive.

He put Kyriani Sabbe in all manner of trouble with a loose pass, Bradley Barcola picked the right-back’s pocket and nudged it on swiftly to Dominik Szoboszlai, who in turn fed Isak. With the goal at his mercy from six yards, the striker was never going to miss.

“He is in a great moment,” Andoni Iraola, Liverpool’s head coach, said of his striker. “When the team is playing well and getting good results everyone looks better. In the second half we defended lower and knew there would be space to exploit. In one of those moments, he killed the game.”

Liverpool are not perfect, by any means, but the closer you watch them, the more obvious it is that they are grasping what Iraola wants. They will be a good team when it does click, but these are just the first steps of the journey. The first half proved it.

Some moves broke down with a misplaced pass and Brugge were often let off the hook when they were guilty of over-elaboration. Iraola wants Liverpool to be ruthless, but his mood soured for a period, not least when Victor Muñoz injured his knee in an incident when he was trying to win back possession.

“A knock on the knee and we have to test it,” Iraola said. “That was the worst part of the night. It is very early to tell but it was very painful at that moment. He was better after the game.”

So, too, was Iraola, who was especially pleased that Liverpool recorded their first Champions League clean sheet of the season and, in the process, stopped Brugge – who had scored in 19 consecutive games – from finding a way through.

There were several reasons this was the case: Jérémy Jacquet, for instance, never put a foot wrong – what a smart signing he has proved to be. He more than did his bit to retain order in the absence of Virgil van Dijk, who was given the chance to catch his breath before the Merseyside derby.

It was tough for Liverpool in the second period, as Brugge attacked the end of the stadium where their noisy ultras created a cacophony. Yet they handled the situation well, even if Iraola looked ready to combust at one stage, receiving a yellow card for protesting too much to the officials.

“I saw the referee beforehand, I know him from Spain and I knew this was coming,” Iraola said.

Perhaps his ire was fuelled by Liverpool squandering a fabulous chance on the hour to kill things off. A move that featured Wirtz and Isak exchanging passes with pinball precision ended with Szoboszlai bearing down on Sommer, but his shot was too close to the veteran.

He had to score and the grimace that followed had nothing to do with heavy strapping the Hungarian had on supporting his right knee. That miss would have been exacerbated in the 69th minute had Alisson Becker not made a superb save to deny Félix Lemaréchal, plunging to avert the danger.

Jürgen Klopp will not want any credit, but some seeds he planted have started to bloom. Similarly, Andoni Iraola will not ask for recognition, but his constant encouragement is reaping dividends.

Past and present do not always mix in football, yet in Florian Wirtz’s case, the manager who once took Liverpool to the summit of the game and the one who wants to return them to that exalted position in the future have proved to be the perfect blend.

Liverpool have travelled over to Belgium to take on Club Brugge on matchday five in the Champions League. These sides have met competitively three times before and they have all come in finals, resulting in famous nights for Liverpool. In 1976, Liverpool beat Club Brugge 4-3 on aggregate across two legs to win the Uefa Cup. Then, Kenny Dalglish scored the only goal of the game at Wembley back in May 1978 as Liverpool won the European Cup for the second straight season, becoming the first English side to do so.

Liverpool, who have won 13 of their previous 17 matches against Belgian sides, won their first three Champions League games, beating Atletico Madrid, LASK and Villarreal but lost 3-2 away at Fenerbahce on matchday four despite leading twice in that game. After tonight’s game in Belgium, Liverpool’s remaining games in the Champions League are against Porto, Inter Milan and Lens. Andoni Iraola’s side come into this game with a spring in their step after thrashing rivals Manchester United 4-0 at Anfield on Sunday.

“A win [against Manchester United on Sunday] is always great but you do not have time to celebrate with this schedule,” Iraola said. “By Monday, we were already watching analysis of Club Brugge. I have enjoyed analysing them [Brugge], they are very energetic and have had an incredible run of games. I think we will have to be at a very good level, otherwise it is going to be very difficult. They have players who can make the difference and obviously we do as well, so I expect quite an open game. We are both aggressive, both want to press, there will be spaces and hopefully we can win the one-vs-one battles.”

Club Brugge have made a strong start to this season’s Champions League; after losing their first game to Aston Villa, they have since won their next three, including wins over Inter Milan, Lens and PSV. That puts them on the same number of points as Liverpool and are just one place behind. In the Belgian Pro League at the weekend, they thrashed Mechelen 5-1 and they sit second in the Belgian top flight, one point behind Union SG.

“I am proud of the players and what they have achieved against Aston Villa, Inter, Lens and PSV,” Club Brugge boss Ivan Leko said. “We know we should be grateful to be here, but we really want to try to show that Belgian football is fun to watch and we can win matches. I am proud, but I know we are a big club. You are only as good as your last match. We know what happened in the past, so there is also a nice connection between both clubs and the supporters. It is a special fixture to play, but we are not here just to enjoy the Champions League; we want to win and that is what we are going to try to do tomorrow [tonight].”

Team news from Belgium to follow shortly.

The Europa League game between Besiktas and Israel's Hapoel Beer-Sheva was suspended for around 30 minutes on Thursday when police clashed with fans of the Turkish club after they displayed a banner in support of Palestine.

The game, being played on neutral ground in Batumi, Georgia, was halted in the 26th minute but restarted after the interruption.

Turkey’s Haberturk broadcaster said Georgian police used pepper spray against the Besiktas fans, who also unfurled a Palestinian flag, prompting referee referee Morten Krogh to stop the game with the score 0-0.

In a statement, Besiktas accused the Georgian security forces of using “disproportionate” force against supporters before and during the game.

Georgian police entered the stands and ⁠used pepper spray on Besiktas fans, Turkish outlet NTV reported.

“We strongly condemn the security forces for their use of disproportionate force against our fans,” the club said. “We also extend our best wishes for a speedy recovery to all our fans affected by these incidents.”

The report added that Turkish fans chanted “Down with Israel” and that Besiktas players and director of football Onder Ozen spoke to supporters before play restarted to calm the situation.

The Turkish Football Federation condemned the treatment of Besiktas supporters on X, saying they were subjected to unacceptable behaviour and discrimination. It said it would press for an investigation.

The TFF’s statement read: “We strongly condemn the unacceptable attitudes, conduct and interference directed at Beşiktaş supporters, both inside and outside the stadium, before and during our club’s UEFA Europa League match against Hapoel Beer-Sheva in Georgia.

“No practice that disregards the universal values of sport, human dignity, mutual respect and the principles of fair play, or that involves discrimination, exclusion or security failures, can be tolerated.

“Nor can there be any question of remaining silent in the face of such conduct, which endangers our supporters’ safety and targets their fundamental rights and freedoms.

“As the Turkish Football Federation, we declare unequivocally that we will follow this matter to its conclusion to ensure that the events are fully investigated, those responsible are identified and the necessary sanctions are imposed without delay.

“There must be no tolerance for covering up these events, allowing those responsible to evade accountability or permitting similar violations to recur.

“We emphasize that we stand firmly with our club, Beşiktaş, and our supporters, who faced a series of problems, particularly serious security failures, and extend our best wishes for a speedy recovery to all our supporters subjected to interference and mistreatment.

“Let no one forget that we will not remain silent in the face of disrespect, discrimination and security violations directed at representatives and supporters of Turkish football.

“We will act decisively on national and international platforms to ensure that all necessary steps are taken, particularly with UEFA, and that those responsible are held accountable.”

Fenerbache also posted in support of their Turkish rivals.

The ⁠officiating team and the Besiktas players ‌left ​the pitch before ‌the game restarted.

Earlier, the Besiktas players refused to shake hands with their Hapoel counterparts, the state-run Anadolu Agency reported.

Hapoel Beer-Sheva and Israel FA had not commented on the incident at the time of publishing.

#857. Ten-man Bournemouth battle back to score Europa League victory at Celta Vigo

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

The Cherries lost Bafode Diakite to a 23rd-minute red card but battled back from going a goal behind to win in Spain

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

Bournemouth moved a step closer to automatic qualification for the Europa League last 16 after coming from behind with 10 men to win 2-1 at Celta Vigo.

It was a remarkable 10th victory in a row in all competitions for Marco Rose’s side and it might have been the most satisfying of the lot for the manager, coming as it did after his team had found themselves a goal down and a man down at half-time.

The visitors looked in trouble when, minutes after Iago Aspas had curled Celta in front, Bafode Diakite was red-carded for a poorly timed tackle.

Bournemouth might have folded then, but instead they came roaring back, Alvaro Rodriguez heading them level almost immediately after the start of the second half.

A draw would have been an excellent result in the circumstances. Substitute Rayan had other ideas, waiting at the end of a rapid breakaway to sweep in the winner 12 minutes from time.

Victory against Viktoria Plzen in December will almost certainly now be enough to earn direct passage to the last 16.

Pablo Duran had the ball in the Bournemouth net after 10 minutes after it spilled back to him off Michele Di Gregorio, the goalkeeper relieved to see the offside flag go up against the Celta striker.

The stand-in keeper redeemed himself minutes later with a solid save from an outrageous bicycle kick by Aspas. It would have been a remarkable goal but the Celta great would not be denied. Bournemouth failed fully to get the ball away, and from the edge of the box Aspas curled a beauty in off the far post.

Bournemouth had gone behind in the first half of their last game in this competition at Sparta Prague. That night, the balance was tipped almost immediately in their favour by a red card for the Czech side, but here it was Rose’s team who found themselves down to 10 men.

Diakite made an honest attempt to win the ball but was late and his studs landed on the ankle of Couhaib Driouech. An initial yellow card was overturned following a VAR check and Bournemouth were on the ropes.

It had been the most challenging half of their debut European campaign, but within minutes of the start of the second period, they were level.

Amine Adli was left in space outside the box to send over a wonderful cross to the far post. Arriving there was Rodriguez, sneaking ahead of his defender to get a head on the ball and nod in the equaliser.

A wonderful counter-attack brought the Premier League side their winner. Adrien Truffert showed good strength out on left to outmuscle Sergio Carreira, and he fed the ball up to Marcus Tavernier. He might have shot himself but instead moved it on to Rayan who swept home.

It might get worse before it gets better for Manchester City fans

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Never be the man after ‘the man’, the saying goes. Football history is stippled with cautionary tales of managers who followed an all-time great, only to discover that they were doomed from the very beginning.

Manchester City have stumbled through a bruising autumn under Enzo Maresca, uncharacteristically so. It is impossible not to wonder if the Etihad Stadium is experiencing its very own version of Manchester United's 2013/14.

For a decade, Pep Guardiola bent English football to his will, turning Man City into a relentless, trophy-winning machine. Succeeding a figure who loomed so large over the east side of Manchester was never going to be straightforward. Few, though, expected the drop-off to feel quite so jarring, or quite so familiar.

David Moyes arrived at Old Trafford in 2013 tasked with prolonging Sir Alex Ferguson’s dynasty, meanwhile Maresca was handed a three-year contract this summer to keep Guardiola’s juggernaut in motion. Four months into the job, the steering wheel is juddering uncomfortably.

Man City’s recent results make for grim reading compared to the standards set over the last 10 years. A 3-1 defeat away at Nottingham Forest earlier this month was double-take worthy, before Saturday’s 1-1 home draw with Fulham - rescued only by an Elliot Anderson volley - saw them lose yet more ground in the Premier League title race.

On Tuesday night in the Champions League, Man City needed an 86th-minute Rayan Cherki strike just to salvage a 2-2 draw at home to Napoli, currently eighth in Serie A and 14 points off the pace.

Ahead of Sunday’s trip to league leaders Arsenal, Maresca's men look a shadow of the team that so recently struck fear into the Gunners' title hopes.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

Predictably, the question of Maresca’s future has already begun to take on more of a 'when rather than if' feel. Reports emerged this week suggesting the Italian is fighting to save his job barely a third of the way into his debut Etihad campaign. Sack talk at Manchester City circulating at all, never mind in November, speaks volumes about how rapidly things have changed.

There are parallels between Man City’s recent slump and Moyes’ 10-month spell across town, too. Like Moyes, Maresca inherited a squad undergoing significant churn after an era of dominance.

To bridge that gap, City made a throng of big summer purchases, bringing in additions such as Elliot Anderson, Enzo Fernandez, Iliman Ndiaye and Ayyoub Bouaddi.

Much like Moyes’ integration of Marouane Fellaini and Juan Mata into a fading champion side, Maresca’s new-look Man City feels disjointed - caught between Guardiola’s positional automatisms and a new manager’s attempt to stamp his own authority on the dressing room.

That disconnect quickly becomes apparent when the team aren't getting results, breeding doubt among players accustomed to certainty and success. All of which begs the question: was Maresca always doomed to fail?

Following Guardiola was always going to be an exercise in managing impossible expectations while rebuilding in real time. Perhaps the Etihad hierarchy believed their structure would insulate Guardiola’s successor from the same sort of post-Ferguson collapse that swallowed Moyes' efforts - which in hindsight weren't all that bad. Perhaps there is a lesson there for Man City chiefs to heed.

Joe joined FourFourTwo as senior digital writer in July 2025 after five years covering Leeds United in the Championship and Premier League. #855. One person had a worse night than United keeper – the wretched referee

By the end of another utterly chaotic 90 minutes in the Manchester United soap opera, there was only one person who had endured a worse night than Senne Lammens.

Watching this game back will make for grim viewing for the United goalkeeper who, having been one of the club’s shining lights last season, is steadily becoming enveloped in a crisis of his own in this most torrid of campaigns.

But Roberto Rosetti, Uefa’s chief refereeing officer, might also want to sit Szymon Marciniak down after this and pick over the Polish official’s own nightmare performance. Marciniak denied United two goals, both of which should have stood, and in doing so ended up shining an even more brutal lens on Lammens’s calamitous display.

United’s Belgian goalkeeper was responsible for both of Sporting’s goals. He needlessly conceded a penalty in the first half, after a rush of blood to the head, that was converted by Luis Suárez, just 75 seconds after he had saved a spot-kick from the Sporting striker.

United had recovered from those bewildering few minutes to lead early in the second half, courtesy of two goals from captain Bruno Fernandes against his old club.

But, 10 minutes from time, Lammens committed the kind of howler that becomes worse and worse with every viewing. In doing so, he handed Sporting an equaliser and ensured United remain without an away win this season.

Lammens could have come to meet Iván Fresneda’s cross 100 times and probably dropped the ball only once. It was his and United’s misfortune that it should happen here. Suárez could barely believe his luck, although his finish was still accomplished, an acrobatic overhead kick from close range.

Senne Lammens with a gift for Luis Suárez to equalise for Sporting 🤯 📺 Watch live on TNT Sports & HBO Max https://t.co/fRCRh6tXYB https://t.co/kOQ6HImlVc

One of the stars of last season for United, Lammens is being dragged down with the rest of them this time around. He had looked hesitant from the moment he was almost caught dealing with a back-pass by Suárez in the opening minutes. It set the tone for what was to come.

As if Mauricio Pochettino did not already have enough on his plate, United’s new head coach now has a goalkeeper problem.

Of course, this would not have been as costly a night for Lammens had Marciniak not made such a mess of things himself. United may have been their own worst enemies again, but there was little doubting Sporting were given a helping hand here by some truly wretched refereeing.

The worst of it was the denial of a perfectly legitimate equaliser late in the first half after Youri Tielemans was penalised for a perceived foul – it was nothing of the sort – that the referee had initially not blown for.

And then moments after Suarez made it 2-2, the Sporting goalkeeper Kaique Pereira flapped at Fernandes’s corner and punched the ball into his own net. Kaique’s blunder was already in motion by the time Patrick Dorgu barged into Kaique. But Marciniak was ordered to the pitch-side monitor by Piotr Lasyk, the VAR, and from there, he weakly decided Kaique had been infringed upon by Dorgu. It was a big let-off for the goalkeeper and the hosts.

To compounded United’s frustrations, they were then reduced to 10 men late on when Tielemans, who had been booked for protesting over the first disallowed goal, received a second yellow card. It means United have now had four red cards and conceded five penalties in their last five games and, four weeks shy of Christmas, are still searching for a win on the road.

The irony was that, amidst the chaos, there was a lot Pochettino will have liked about the performance. It was far from perfect but United at least had a structure, coherence and confidence about them for long periods. But for Lammens’s shocker and some dubious refereeing, United would surely have claimed just a fourth win this season.

The problem with this United side is they never seem too far away from an act of self-sabotage. Pochettino insisted on the eve of this game that his team were not fragile, but that assessment was challenged in the crazy 160 seconds when United conceded not one but two penalties.

In truth, they could feel hard done to by the award of the first in the 29th minute. Geny Catamo went down far too easily – and very late – after Lisandro Martínez swung out a leg. There was contact but it was of the very minimal variety. Martínez rushed off to Marciniak to remonstrate but his pleas fell on deaf ears. There was a sense of justice, then, when Lammens saved Suárez’s feeble penalty.

You would have thought that would be a confidence booster for Lammens, but in no time he had gone from hero to zero, with worse to follow.

A ball was swept in behind Noussair Mazraoui and Maximiliano Araújo gave chase. There was no need for Lammens to come careering out of goal but that is what he did. When he clumsily blocked off Araújo in the process, Marciniak wasted little time brandishing a yellow card and pointing to the spot. This time Suárez made no mistake from 12 yards.

What will please Pochettino is United did not crumble again from there. In fact, they rallied and would soon be nursing a sense of injustice for the second time in four days.

Already outraged by the circumstances around Leny Yoro’s rescinded red card against Liverpool at Anfield on Sunday, Pochettino now had to contend with some perverse refereeing from Marciniak.

Tielemans had slipped a pass through to Amad Diallo, with his momentum carrying him into Gonçalo Inácio. Marciniak did not blow his whistle, presumably because in the moment he did not feel a foul had been committed. But after Diallo’s shot was saved and a split second before the Ivorian headed the rebound into the net, the Polish referee blew his whistle.

Tielemans could not believe what he was seeing and, to add insult to injury, was booked for his protestations.

After the match, Pochettino claimed United were punished by the referee’s decisions.

The Argentine was again in a state disbelief at some refereeing decisions, even though he appeared at pains not to land himself in hot water with Uefa.

“It’s difficult to find a game where you get punished [so much] in one game. We were punished a lot in key actions,” Pochettino said.

On the foul awarded against Tielemans, he added: “I think everyone knows all that was… impossible [to understand]. You know, it’s difficult to understand why that happened on the field.”

What Pochettino demanded was a strong start after the interval, and he got just that. A third penalty award of the night this time went United’s way. Amad cuts inside and rolls a shot not far wide of the far post, and then he is caught offside. There is a goal or two in this game for United if they can avoid falling down any more manholes. Sporting look weaker than the previous few years in Europe.

Amad puts the ball in the net, but the referee inexplicably blows for a foul against Tielemans and books the United man for his protestations. The ball was there to be won, and Tielemans went to ground to poke the ball through for Amad, but the referee decides the follow through on Inacio was a foul. Terrible call – Tielemans won the ball and kept his studs down.

Why has the referee not blown up immediately for a foul by Tielemans on Inacio? Amad scores and then he awards the free-kick to Sporting. So odd.

Marciniak did not appear to think it was a foul in the moment – it did not look like one – yet resolves later it is. Poor officiating. Second time in the game Sporting have benefited.

It's hard to know why this was ruled out 🤯 📺 Watch live on TNT Sports & HBO Max https://t.co/fRCRh6tXYB https://t.co/Pat8nzJiVW

Last-ditch defending from Yoro to scoop the ball over his bar, after a flick beyond the United defence released Fresneda. Lammens punches fresh air from the corner, but United get away with it. Having been so comfortable, they are on the ropes.

No team in Europe's top five leagues has conceded more goals across all competitions than Man Utd (35) this season 😬 https://t.co/NrSOypegmj

Araujo is proving a scourge for United down the Sporting left, Amad needs to do more to help Mazraoui. The ball over the top is on every time, and Sporting’s right-back Fresneda is also not shy of a burst forward. They are the twin threats for Sporting.

United’s capacity for self-sabotage is extraordinary. Lammens looks like he’s got United out of jail after a soft penalty award against Lisandro Martinez but then two minutes later the United goalkeeper gives away a penalty himself and this time Luis Suarez makes no mistake from the spot.

That was a better penalty, right-footed to the goalkeeper’s right and into the bottom corner. United trail.

Man Utd are behind in Lisbon 😬 Luis Suárez converts from the spot at the second attempt moments after Senne Lammens saved his first 💥 📺 Watch live on TNT Sports & HBO Max https://t.co/fRCRh6tXYB https://t.co/BqDPDsRJc7

What a crazy few minutes, from hero to zero for Lammens. It was a cracking diagonal pass to release the pacy Araujo over the top, and he always looked favourite to win the race against the goalkeeper. Knocks the ball over Lammens, who then cleans him out. Yellow card and a certain penalty.

A really poor penalty from Sporting’s top goalscorer and a simple save for the Belgian. It was a soft penalty, and on the balance of play so far United will feel that is a just outcome.

Catamo with dancing feet in the area, and the referee decides Lisandro Martinez has tripped him. It was a belated fall and minimal contact, but I suspect it will be sufficient for VAR to confirm the decision. There was a stretch of the leg towards the player from Martinez.

Cumbersome play on the halfway line from Yoro where he was very nearly robbed of possession by Suarez. But then Yoro makes an important intervention, stooping down to head the ball clear of the on-rushing Araujo, who was flying forward from left-back.

Quaresma with some good defending to halt the progress fo Mbeumo into the box, but United continue to look comfortable without working Kaique in the Sporting goal. Their start to the game should build confidence, though.

United have a better shape about them with and without the ball, and Sporting are quite happy to stand off when United have the ball. Fernandes found by a cutting Mainoo pass, but Tielemans’ pass was intercepted. Then Tielemans did well to recover possession but Zirkzee was crowded out.

United respond with their own spell of sustained spell of possession, when they have the ball Tielemans and Fernandes are advanced of Mainoo with Mbeumo and Amad wide.

Yoro picks out Zirkzee with an excellent diagonal ball and it was a smooth first touch with the outside of his boot, but Zirkzee slashes over from a tight angle.

Sporting starting to find their combinations around the United box, Andersen crossing from the right and Araujo volleying over at the back post. Catamo takes on a speculative shot from distance and he blazes over.

Sporting with their first concerted spell of possession deep in United territory, and after Mazraoui fell awkwardly Araujo was able to chip a cross to the back post. Mazraoui may have fallen on his shoulder, and Diogo Dalot has been sent out to warm up.

Aside from that shaky moment from Lammens, this has been a fairly confident United start in the circumstances. They are playing forward with purpose and looking to turn the Sporting defence, and the run of Zirkzee was found by Mainoo but he had strayed offside.

Much as Pochettino favoured with the US, it’s a four in possession and a three out of possession.

Ooof, horrible early moment for Lammens who is very nearly charged down on his goal-line by Suarez after dallying on the ball. The ricochet went in United’s favour and they survive the scare.

The early signs are that United are playing a back four of Mazraoui, Yoro, Maguire and Martinez, with Amad on the right. Tielemans and Mainoo in the middle of the pitch, and Fernandes and Mbeumo taking turns to move left. Quite hard to decipher at the moment.

After Sporting fans stand to sing their pre-match anthem O Mundo Sabe Que (The World Knows That), to the tune better known as My Way, the game begins.

Sporting tend to save their best for the Champions League and, as tends to be the case, there is unbalance across this United XI. Expect this to be tough.

Cristiano Ronaldo, Nani and Bruno Fernandes were all depicted on the Tifo unfurled by Sporting fans before kick-off. All former Sporting players who would leave for United. Only one of those can impact things on the pitch for United tonight, though, much as Pochettino would have loved to be able to call upon a Ronaldo or Nani, who is here in an executive box watching on.

We try to deal with different situations and manage the squad. The most important thing is too add some fresh legs in every game because the schedule is tight. Massive effort from the team to play with 10 men, we have to manage that it’s very important.

We start from zero and we have to give them the opportunity to compete. Everyone has to think he can compete for a place. In a period that is so busy we need every player believing they can perform.

It’s a great opportunity for Josh [Zirkzee] to show his quality. It’s an important game for him to start to think he can be a very important player for the team.

Manchester United, always the pressure is there, you compete for big things, one or another competition it is to win. That is the history of the club.

I was under the misapprehension that Peter Schmeichel and Michael Laudrup were Euro 92-winning team-mates with Denmark, but in fact Laudrup had a three-year hiatus from the national team and opted to stay away from the tournament when Denmark replaced Yugoslavia. One more in the win column for the Ewing Theory (that says teams can improve without their star player).

Laudrup told FourFourTwo: “As we weren’t able to qualify, I decided to focus 100 per cent on Barça. Yugoslavia went on to win the group, but because of the war, Denmark were suddenly given their place. People asked me if I wanted to go, but I didn’t want to join at the last moment, even though I could have. I felt it wouldn’t have been fair.”

Shaun Derry, the former Crystal Palace and QPR player, is in attendance to cheer on son Jesse who is on loan at Sporting from Chelsea. Heck of a loan move for a 19-year-old, and good to see him in fine fettle after that horrible head injury he suffered on his full Premier League debut season.

“Of course, minutes have been minimal for Jesse, but nights like this you can’t beat,” Derry said. “There are some great young players that he is learning alongside.”

“He wasn’t making his bed a year ago, now he has to cook his own dinner and get himself to training.”

Wandering around the Jose Alvalade Stadium before kick-off and Cristiano Ronaldo’s face and old No 7 is pasted on the outside of the building.

How Pochettino would love a prime Ronaldo in his team but we’re in as very different era now to the one when United went into this competition with a firm expectation of winning it. It’s two wins and two defeats so far in the Champions League for United this season although you suspect they’d be happy to come away from here with a point.

They have yet to win away from home this season and Sporting, who have won three of their four European games, are third in the Portuguese league. Watch out for Colombia striker Luis Suarez and Italy midfielder Issa Doumbia, who have six goals between them in the Champions League this term.

Sporting XI: Kaique, Fresneda, Quaresma, Inacio, Araujo, Andersen, Altimira, Doumbia, Catamo, Suarez, Luis Guilherme

Subs: Rui Silva, Callai, Ioannidis, Simoes, Vagiannidis, Zalazar, Irankunda, Lima, Derry, Ba, Felicissimo, Goncalves.

Mauricio Pochettino has made four changes to the side that were beaten 4-0 at Anfield by Liverpool. One of those is enforced, with the suspended Matheus Cunha making way for Joshua Zirkzee, who gets his first start of the season. Harry Maguire comes in for Matthijs de Ligt, who was abysmal against Liverpool, and Noussair Mazraoui replaces Diogo Dalot. Amad Diallo is in over Patrick Dorgu. Mainoo and Tielemans have struggled as a partnership all season but Pochettino again persists with that midfield pairing with Bruno Fernandes ahead of them.

Manchester United XI: Lammens; Yoro, Maguire, Martinez, Mazraoui; Tilemans, Mainoo; Amad, Fernandez, Mbeumo; Zirkzee

Subs: Darlow, Heaton, Amass, Dalot, De Ligt, Heaven, Shaw, Santos, Mount, Lacey

After the game [against Liverpool], we were all very disappointed. But what I felt in the dressing room is a group of players that really care, that really want to ⁠perform, that are going to do everything for the club and to change that dynamic.

It’s always an opportunity to change the dynamics, especially ​after we have had a ‌loss. The best thing that could happen to us now is [to] win. But that will require performance. We have ‌to perform ​at our ⁠best, collectively and individually.

They need to finish 24th or higher to avoid elimination. They only have two fewer points (after four games) in the Champions League than they do in the Premier League (after 11).

Few Manchester United fans expected a positive result from Mauricio Pochettino’s first game in charge at Anfield, but the bar will not be set so low for Sporting in the Champions League this evening.

The manner of the 4-0 defeat against Liverpool, even accounting for Leny Yoro’s early red card, was dispiriting but not unexpected. The next few weeks will reveal how Pochettino intends to get a grip on the job.

When it comes to United’s Champions League prospects, the comeback win over Roma at the tail-end of Michael Carrick’s tenure made their position less perilous, but avoiding outright elimination is the first target.

United are 19th in the table, with the top 24 teams going through. Those between ninth and 24th go into a play-off round before the last 16. After Sporting away, United host RB Leipzig and Bayern Munich before a trip to Villarreal so there are stiff tests to come.

Sporting are well-placed after three wins from four, but their Champions League schedule is rather one-sided: in their final three matches they travel to Roma, before playing Barcelona and Manchester City. They reached the quarter-finals of the competition last season, losing narrowly to Arsenal over two legs.

They are third in their league, having been weakened by the summer sales of Geovany Quenda (to Chelsea), Morten Hjulmand (to Atletico Madrid) and Ousmane Diomande (to Nottingham Forest). The vast majority of goals are scored by Colombian striker Luis Suárez.

Bruno Fernandes, United’s captain, returns to his former club tonight and there is hope Luke Shaw could be back at left-back. Pochettino must decide whether or not to stick with Matthijs de Ligt, who was extremely rusty at Anfield but may need the minutes.

Yoro’s one-game suspension was overturned by the FA, and he would have been available for this one in any case.

#854. Sunderland ‘disappointed’ after banned Jagiellonia Bialystok fans enter Stadium of Light

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

Police and stewards were called to handle a disturbance within a home area of the ground during the early minutes of the game

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

Sunderland have expressed their disappointment after a number of Jagiellonia Bialystok fans gained access to home sections at the Stadium of Light during Thursday night’s 1-1 draw.

UEFA had issued an away supporter ban against Jagiellonia for Thursday’s match on Wearside.

However, police and stewards were called to handle a disturbance within a home area of the ground during the early minutes of the game.

A club statement said: “Sunderland AFC is disappointed that a number of Jagiellonia Bialystok supporters were present in home areas of the Stadium of Light during tonight’s UEFA Europa League fixture.

“Jagiellonia Bialystok were subject to a UEFA away supporter ban for tonight’s Matchday 5 fixture, following a disciplinary sanction imposed by European football’s governing body.

“In the build-up to the match, the club had put measures in place in line with this sanction and maintained regular communication with our supporters, Jagiellonia Bialystok and UEFA. Unfortunately, Jagiellonia Bialystok failed to engage and cooperate on this matter.

“We are disappointed that these measures and communications were disregarded by some visiting supporters and will review the circumstances surrounding their entry to the stadium.”

Sunderland struck early in the second half through Timur Tutierov’s header, his second goal in the competition, but Kamil Jozwiak levelled only minutes later after capitalising on a mistake at the back.

A point means the Wearsiders stay in the knockout phase play-off places after being held to their second draw from five games in the competition.

Sunderland remain without the injured Brian Brobbey and Granit Xhaka, and Regis Le Bris made six changes from their goalless Premier League draw with Aston Villa on Saturday.

Jagiellonia showed an early flash of danger when Nik Prelec weaved into the box and played a low cross into the area, but Roefs held the resulting clearance.

Sunderland caused problems when Angulo found Enzo Le Fee and the midfielder had his strike deflected narrowly behind.

Slawomir Abramowicz was forced to push away Fofana’s menacing shot before the half evolved into a scrappy affair.

A sudden burst of energy from the hosts saw Trai Hume chip over and Le Fee was at the heart of another solid attack.

The Frenchman went around Abramowicz before playing a low ball across the box towards Angulo lingering in front of an open goal, but his strike from close range was blocked by Yuki Kobayashi.

An enforced change six minutes before the break saw Luke O’Nien introduced for Omar Alderete and moments later Roefs was called into action to palm away Szmyt’s free-kick just outside the box.

On the stroke of half-time, Jagiellonia struggled to clear their lines and Hume blasted wide of the upright.

Sunderland brought on Jules Ahoka and Thomas Meunier at half-time and just two minutes after the restart they went ahead.

A good team move stemming from Chris Rigg’s break down the middle resulted in the ball reaching Le Fee and his cross from the right was deflected by Taras Romanczuk in to Tutierov to nod home at the back post.

However, their lead was short-lived when Jozwiak pounced on a tame attempted back pass from Reinildo Mandava and rolled past Roefs in the 52nd minute.

Another sloppy defensive error allowed Jozwiak to again latch on to the ball, but Roefs tipped the resulting shot behind.

Sunderland’s frustrations continued when Fofana’s half-volley was stopped and Angulo blasted a free-kick straight into the wall before Rigg’s low shot was comfortably scooped up by Abramowicz.

Both sides went close in the 90th minute when Reinildo’s header was saved by Abramowicz, and Jeremy Agbonifo broke for the visitors but was denied by Roefs as the game fizzled into a draw.

Arsenal could lose a first-team defender who has fallen out of favour with manager Mikel Arteta.

The Gunners boast arguably the best backline in Europe at the moment, having conceded the fewest goals in the Premier League this term (just seven), and goalkeeper David Raya has already kept seven clean sheets in 11 fixtures.

Part of Arsenal's strength at the back is in their depth – but that could be seriously impacted with interest in a star who hasn't been getting in the team as much of late.

Following a back injury at the 2026 World Cup to William Saliba, the Gunners moved to bring in quality cover in the shape of England international Ezri Konsa.

Konsa has been an instant hit at the Emirates Stadium, and with Arteta now boasting eight senior players competing for places – Konsa, Saliba, Gabriel and Cristhian Mosquera in the centre, with full-backs Jurrien Timber, Ben White, Riccardo Calafiori and Piero Hincapie all capable in the middle, too – the problem is giving each of them playing time.

Sport Witness have now relayed a report from L’Interista that claims Inter Milan are interested in Mosquera, who started the Gunners' first three games of the season in all competitions but hasn't featured much of late.

The Spaniard filled in for Saliba before the Konsa deal was completed, but went off injured against Aston Villa in the second league game of the campaign, paving the way for Konsa to make his debut.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

The 29-year-old has kept his place alongside Gabriel ever since – and despite Saliba returning to fitness and featuring on the bench recently, the former Villa star has remained a mainstay of the team.

This has left Mosquera out in the cold as the fourth-choice, and though the ex-Valencia man can play across the backline, White and Timber have rotated for the right-back slot, while Calafiori and Hincapie have shared left-back, leaving him with very few minutes since the start of the campaign.

Mosquera only signed last summer, but with ESPN reporting the transfer fee to be just £13 million, Arsenal may well consider flipping the 22-year-old for a steep profit, with the report claiming Arsenal want around £30m for his signature.

The champions also have a homegrown talent in the form of Marli Salmon, still just 17 years old but having already impressed both centrally and at right-back.

FourFourTwo understands that Arsenal have no interest in selling Mosquera in January but could reassess the situation next summer.

Mosquera is worth €40 million, according to Transfermarkt. Arsenal host Manchester City this weekend when Premier League action resumes.

#852. China’s AI-powered smart-city model is going global

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Jacob Dreyer is an editor for business, economics, politics and law at Palgrave (a subsidiary of Springer Nature) based in Shanghai, China. The views expressed here are his own.

To understand the Chinese smart city, it helps to know that twenty-first-century infrastructure, technology and policy increasingly makes the whole of China a single, interconnected economic unit. Trains, planes and autonomous vehicles shuttle about, with the centre of megacities such as Shanghai and Shenzhen merely being in the middle of ‘one-hour circles’ for commuters that allow them to reach anywhere in the wider urban area with ease. Previous barriers to the internal movement of workers, such the hukou system, which restricted access to public services based on a person’s birthplace, are being removed, making it easier for people to compete for jobs across the country. And all the while, the Internet supercharges these shifts to a nationwide marketplace, backed by an ever-expanding supply of data centres. Sichuanese farmers of organic lemons now livestream from rural villages on apps such as Xiaohongshu or Douyin as they compete for city restaurateurs to buy their products.

So, if the goal of a ‘smart city’ is to use big data and AI to outsource governance functions, keeping everything running smoothly, then maybe we should think of China as a single city, with its different provinces and megalopolises as neighbourhoods with their own special roles. For instance, three of China’s megacities each have their own important function: Beijing regulates and invests in fundamental research; Shanghai is home to multinational corporations, frontier research in AI and biotech, and finance; and the Greater Bay Area, including Shenzhen and Guangzhou, is home to innovative manufacturers, such as electric vehicle producer BYD, tech giant Huawei and consumer electronics firm DJI.

China’s 15th five-year plan unveiled earlier this year sees the country in this way, too, by entrusting certain functions to different cities and regions, and with rural areas also playing an essential role. In the northeast, farming is increasingly carried out with the use of drones and big data by state-owned companies such as Beidahuang. In Inner Mongolia and Xinjiang, data centres are powered by abundant solar and wind energy, where they calculate how the self-driving cars of China’s eastern seaboard should navigate roads or process the AI that helps to keep the country’s state-of-the-art high-speed train network running on time.

This approach on data is embodied by 东数西算 (roughly translated as ‘east data, west compute’), a national-level strategic project to channel data from developed eastern regions to resource-rich western regions for processing and storage using eight data-centre ‘hubs’ located across the country. Eastern megacities generate the vast majority of China’s data and AI requests, but they bring skyrocketing land costs, power shortages and cooling difficulties that make hosting data centres unattractive. Instead, the solar farms of Xinjiang’s deserts and the wind farms of the Mongolian steppe are used to provide renewable, cheap energy to data centres.

One key example is Ulanqab in Inner Mongolia, which has been transformed from a traditional farming region into a prominent data powerhouse, earning the name ‘Grassland Cloud Valley’. The energy costs in Ulanqab are low, because the government has been installing massive renewable capacity, relying on the area’s abundant wind and solar resources. Mongolia is cold for most of the year, so data centres use standard air cooling rather than massive air-conditioning set-ups — effectively, they just cover the servers with plastic and leave the door open for wintry winds to circulate. Major firms such as Huawei, Alibaba, Kuaishou and Apple have constructed large-scale cloud bases in Ulanqab. The region houses China’s largest intelligent computing centre for autonomous driving (Fuyao), built by Xpeng Motors and Alibaba Cloud, which has helped make it 170 times faster to train self-driving models. It means an autonomous taxi driving around Beijing is effectively being controlled by servers in the far-away desert of Inner Mongolia.
