New Manchester United manager Mauricio Pochettino may well be about to address the dreaded left-back problem that has hampered the club for years

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Manchester United plan to address their issues at left-back by signing a player dubbed ‘the next Riccardo Calafiori’, following another poor result away at Sporting.

The Red Devils dropped two points in Europe last night away in Lisbon, with new manager Mauricio Pochettino winless in his first two games in charge, as the scale of the task at hand becomes clear.

With Manchester United 19th in both the Premier League and the Champions League's league phase right now, Pochettino is under pressure to deliver quickly, with January earmarked for much-needed new signings.

Once again, United have struggled at left-back this season, with veteran Luke Shaw injured for much of the campaign.

Lisandro Martinez started the 4-0 defeat to Liverpool in Pochettino's first fixture, while Diogo Dalot has played out of position to cover there this term, with no obvious candidate to step in during Shaw's absence.

Sport Witness, however, have relayed a report from Gazzetta dello Sport, which claims that United have “already made moves” to sign Juan Miranda of Bologna.

The Spaniard signed for I Rossoblu following the sale of Riccardo Calafiori to Arsenal, and has impressed in Serie A with similar attacking instincts and reliable performances in manager Raffaele Palladino's backline.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

While Bologna are looking to tie Miranda down until 2030, there is significant interest from both Pochettino and Newcastle United, who see the 26-year-old as an option to alleviate the burden on Lewis Hall at left-back.

FourFourTwo understands that the Red Devils have a modest budget for January and may be limited in what they can do in the transfer market – meaning that cost-effective signings like Miranda may be the way forward, should Pochettino wish to strengthen.

After finishing third in the Premier League last season, manager Michael Carrick welcomed four new faces to Carrington in the form of Andrey Santos, Carlos Baleba, Youri Tielemans – all midfielders – and backup goalkeeper Karl Darlow, along with the returning Marcus Rashford, following his successful stint on loan with Barcelona.

While the lack of depth in defence and attack has been obvious this season though, United's midfield acquisitions have been questioned too for their lack of dynamism, with Carrick ultimately paying for the side's atrocious form with his job after just 10 league games.

United have won just three matches all season in all competitions.

Miranda is worth €15 million, according to Transfermarkt. Manchester United face Brentford this weekend when Premier League action resumes.

#850. Crystal Palace edge out 10-man Real Sociedad as Sunderland frustrated again

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

Jon Martin was sent off for Real Sociedad as Thomas Frank earned a first victory in charge of the Eagles

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

Crystal Palace delivered Thomas Frank a first victory after they came back to beat 10-man Real Sociedad 2-1 in the Europa League.

Dean Henderson was kept busy in the first half, making several stops to ensure it was all to play for after the break in south London, where Frank took charge of a home game for the first time.

Mamadou Sarr broke the deadlock in the 66th minute, but the contest turned on its head when Jon Martin was sent off with a second yellow card for tugging down Jean-Philippe Mateta six minutes later.

The Frenchman fired in the resulting penalty before second-half substitute Dwight McNeil tapped home from Jorgen Strand Larsen’s overhead kick.

Yeremy Pino had a chance to put the game away with a stoppage-time penalty but he was denied by Unai Marrero, and the hosts had to grind out a nervy finish, with Henderson producing his biggest save of the night to deny Orri Oskarsson at the death.

The result moves the Eagles into a play-off position, after starting the evening just outside of it, in 25th.

Sunderland were left frustrated again in their Europa League campaign after drawing 1-1 with Jagiellonia Bialystok at the Stadium of Light.

The Black Cats enjoyed the best of the first-half chances through Malick Fofana and Nilson Angulo, but the visitors had an opportunity when Robin Roefs saved Kajetan Szmyt’s free-kick.

Sunderland struck early in the second half through Timur Tutierov’s header, his second goal in the competition, but Kamil Jozwiak levelled only minutes later after capitalising on a mistake at the back.

A point means the Wearsiders stay in the knockout phase play-off places after being held to their second draw from five games in the competition.

Camilo Duran came to Celtic’s rescue in Europe again after coming off the bench to head a late winner against Torreense in Portugal. The Colombian striker peeled off to the back post to meet a cross from fellow substitute James Forrest and send a downward header into the net in the 85th minute.

Duran’s 15th goal of the season earned a 2-1 victory over the Portuguese second-tier side and put Celtic on six points in the Europa League after his double off the bench inspired a comeback win over Besiktas last time out.

Celtic took the lead in the ninth minute when Javi Vazquez sliced Jota’s cross into his own net with Yang Hyun-jun right behind him.

But the Portuguese Cup winners levelled 10 minutes later after some sloppy defending. Both Kieran Tierney and Colby Donovan had chances to deal with bouncing balls after Alex Alfaro hit the bar from 22 yards but they could not clear and Haiti international Dany Jean volleyed home.

Celtic dominated second-half possession but clear chances were at a premium until Duran struck.

Terry Venables arrived at Middlesbrough in 2000 to work alongside manager Bryan Robson in an unconventional setup

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Mark Schwarzer has revealed that he feared a difficult reunion with Terry Venables when the former Australia manager arrived at Middlesbrough – only to find that the coach was willing to put their past disagreement behind them.

The pair had fallen out over Schwarzer’s availability for international duty in 1997, when the goalkeeper chose to honour a commitment to Boro rather than join an Australia squad under Venables.

Schwarzer had reason to worry about the potential for awkwardness when Venables was appointed to work alongside Bryan Robson at the Riverside in December 2000, tasked with helping Middlesbrough to beat the drop.

Schwarzer told FourFourTwo: “I was worried when Terry came in, because his previous job had been manager of Australia.

“I’d just joined Middlesbrough when we had that League Cup semi-final at the same time as an Australia call-up.

"Terry had made it clear that if he called you up, he expected you to be there

"Bryan Robson asked him if I could stay because it was one of the biggest games in Middlesbrough’s history.”

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

“Terry initially agreed, then three days beforehand called and said I had to choose. I told him I’d made a commitment to my club. He didn’t pick me again, including for the World Cup play-off against Iran.

“When he arrived at Middlesbrough, I wondered if there might be a problem. To his credit, he was brilliant. He basically said 'These things happen, let’s move on'."

Instead of allowing the dispute to linger, Schwarzer says Venables did a fantastic job of working out how to get Middlesbrough back in form

He said: “He made a huge impact at Middlesbrough. He spoke to everyone about what they thought was going wrong, then made his own mind up about how to address it.

“Terry was exceptional at not undermining Bryan. Robbo was still at the front of things but had this incredible coach to learn from. If Terry hadn’t come in, we would have been relegated.”

Boro eventually finished the 2000-01 Premier League season in 14th, well clear of the drop.

#848. The Spygate reunion that proves Southampton and Tonda Eckert got off lightly

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

Southampton face Middlesbrough for the first time since the ‘Spygate’ scandal - but with Tonda Eckert still in a job and Saints flying high, Will Castle questions whether justice was really done

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

When Southampton were kicked out of the Championship play-off final four days before football’s richest game, there was a bubbling dread that things were about to spiral.

‘Spygate’ had rocked English football to its core. It started with an intern, camera in hand, failing to adequately hide behind a tree outside Middlesbrough’s training ground, birthing the cartoonish image that will forever be the thumbnail of this scandal. What subsequently unravelled was far more sinister; a pattern of cheating by Saints that was driven by those at the very top. As the club was put under the spotlight, they also admitted to espionage against Ipswich and Oxford before being caught red-handed spying on their play-off semi-final opponents.

Tonda Eckert wasn’t simply complicit in sending staff out to spy on rivals; it was initially stated that he spearheaded the plot. Findings of the League Arbitration Panel investigating the scandal laid bare of the Saints boss’ influence in “a contrived and determined plan from top down to gain a competitive advantage”, which left junior staff feeling “compelled to do what they were very uncomfortable doing because they considered their jobs would otherwise be at risk”.

“Deplorable” was the word used to describe this scheme, and it resulted in an unprecedented punishment. Saints were expelled from the play-off final and stripped of their shot at promotion back to the Premier League, along with the £200m in riches that come with it. They were also handed a four-point deduction for the start of the 2026/27 Championship season. The club called this "manifestly disproportionate to every previous sanction in the history of the English game". But it felt like this was only the start.

Eckert, who at just 33 had been building a reputation as one of English football’s most promising young managers, was at serious risk of seeing his rise completely derailed. The FA swiftly opened an investigation into the German and a lengthy ban from football was on the table for bringing the game into disrepute. Had he been slapped with a months-long suspension, Southampton - who wanted to stand by their manager - would have been forced into unwanted turmoil in the dugout.

Instead, Eckert - who took responsibility and admitted the misconduct charges - escaped serious punishment. The FA’s findings were not as harsh as the EFL’s, stating that while he authorised said spying, there was less of a culture of pressure. The contradiction raised eyebrows. He was given a six-week suspended ban and a £28,000 fine.

Now, two months on from this verdict and six months since ‘Spygate’ erupted, Eckert will lead his side into their first post-scandal meeting with Middlesbrough. He’ll do so having just signed a new contract.

There is a fair argument to say Eckert, as an individual responsible for his own behaviour, got off lightly. In any other job, suspicions of such an abuse of power could result in the sack. Southampton chose to back him, which is their prerogative - Eckert has the best win rate of any Saints manager since the 1890s, so it’s no surprise they wanted to avoid losing the German. But both club and manager are fortunate that the FA opted against a full measure, which would have effectively taken his future out of their hands.

Still at the helm, Eckert has been empowered to oversee a recovery at St Mary’s, to the point where the shockwaves of ‘Spygate’ are no longer really being felt. The four-point deduction was swiftly made up at the start of the season and the club are now seven points off the top and very much in the promotion hunt. Their formidable home form sets them apart, unbeaten in 18 on their own turf.

Tipped for a season of chaos in the summer, they welcome league leaders Boro almost back on their perch by November. The visitors might feel a tinge of injustice at just how quickly they’ve managed to return to this point, especially with Eckert still pulling the strings.

Eckert hinted that hostilities between him and Boro boss Kim Hellberg had been quelled in his pre-match press conference on Thursday. The Swede said he had sleepless nights due to the “disgraceful” actions of his opposition, but Eckert stated the pair spoke on the phone earlier this year and that both will go into Friday’s clash with only the end result in mind. "We've had a conversation on the phone and we saw each other at the EFL day before the season,” he said. “We are two managers who will try to win a game and that's it."

Boro are out for redemption this term. Their last-minute ticket to the play-off final went in vain when hearts were broken by Ollie McBurnie at Wembley. They look well-placed to go one better this season, though, fuelled by a fantastic summer transfer window which saw them bring in, among others, the league’s current top scorer Will Lankshear from Tottenham.

But for all their sins, Saints still harbour the feeling that they emerged from this scandal wronged by their sanction; akin to a poor man’s Weimar Germany after World War One. Before Eckert learned his fate at the hands of the FA, chief executive Phil Parsons claimed the club had “taken enough” punishment, chiefly their play-off expulsion. He complained about the legal fees and the money being lost by local businesses, almost as if to drive pity for the club. And while he stated: “We don’t want to be seen as a victim of this,” that is the narrative that is held in parts of Southampton.

Ultimately, however, Saints were let off the hook to the extent where the club could keep Eckert and rejuvenate before the New Year. Any victim sentiment is borderline deluded, and that’s evidenced by the state of play going into a ‘Spygate’ reunion. This is a promotion six-pointer; after all that’s happened, Southampton should count themselves lucky to be in such a promising position.

#847. 'I hate it' - Brady reacts to stunning Rodgers claims

Sky Sports NFL's Jason Bell says Aaron Rodgers is 'losing respect' after claims that head coach Mike McCarthy was 'snoring' in a quarterback meeting in an explosive interview; Steelers president Art Rooney II comes out in "100 per cent" support of McCarthy after team releases Rodgers

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

Has Aaron Rodgers played his final game in the NFL? Was he wrong to publicly criticise Mike McCarthy? Seven-time Super Bowl champion Tom Brady says he "hates" the situation, insisting "nobody wins when the family feuds".

Rodgers sent shockwaves through the NFL on Thanksgiving Eve as he used an interview on The Pat McAfee Show to claim McCarthy had been "falling asleep in meetings" while suggesting his entire team believed a change was required on the sideline.

It came after Rodgers was benched for Friday's match with the Denver Broncos following two straight defeats, with Mason Rudolph due to start under center.

The Steelers later released Rodgers 11 weeks into what is set to be the final season of the 42-year-old's career.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

"The sanctity of an NFL locker room, it's a very sacred place and we shouldn't ever lose track of that as players. It's a privilege to be in that locker room," said Brady during the broadcast of Thursday's Thanksgiving game between the Dallas Cowboys and Philadelphia Eagles.

"You're fighting with your team-mates. You're fighting with your coaches. You're always acting as a team together. Shouldn't always be the place for private things to become public.

"A Hall of Fame career and he's a tremendous player and has nothing to do with his play style. I was fortunate to be around a lot of great team-mates over the years and what made a great team-mate to me was you cared about your team-mates and your coaches and you cared about what the team was trying to accomplish."

NFL: Tom Brady comments on Aaron Rodgers situation

'That was sick!' | Milton winds one up to get Smith 50-yard touchdown!

Brady referenced his own relationship with former head coach Bill Belichick, with whom he won six of his seven Super Bowl rings as part of a historic New England Patriots dynasty.

"That supersedes any Individual aspect of your game that you want to promote. I was in a great locker room, I played for my team-mates, I played for my coaches. Nobody wins when the family feuds," Brady continued.

"I wasn't a perfect player. He [Bill Belichick] wasn't a perfect coach. But we did some things in the game that we're so proud of now and even me being four years removed from the game the things that matter more than winning a Super Bowl or trophy is my relationships with my team-mates my coaches.

"That's going to transcend anything you do on the field, so it's just unfortunate. I hate it and I hate to be even talking about it. It's a privilege of the NFL, you want to inspire the next generation of athletes and you always want to do it the right way."

The four-time MVP quarterback is 'losing respect' following his explosive claims about the McCarthy, according to Sky Sports NFL's Jason Bell.

"First of all, I don't want to be on Aaron Rodgers' bad side. Let's start there. We all make mistakes, right? We all do things that aren't necessarily right in the moment," said Bell.

"But when I look at him as a player, he wasn't playing well. He wasn't helping his team.

"And you could could see him and his head coach arguing on the sideline with with each other. They weren't getting along.

"Whatever happens behind closed doors, that goes down, but the response to it is where I'm losing a little respect.

"In that locker room is a sanctuary. Some things we just don't let out. We don't have those conversations in public - it's a respect thing.

"If Rodgers was playing MVP football like he did before, he could say all these things and get away with it, but you have to know where you are in your career."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

Rodgers suggested in his appearance on The Pat McAfee Show that the prospect of being benched had never been mentioned during recent conversations with McCarthy.

He accused McCarthy of snoring during meetings and rebuffing Rodgers' suggestions that he needed to make more of an effort of connecting with the Steelers' defensive players.

Rodgers added that the "final straw" came during half-time of a game when McCarthy closed a team talk by shouting 'one, two, three, Packers!'.

Rodgers and McCarthy spent 13 seasons together with the Packers from 2006-2018, reaching the playoffs nine times and winning one Super Bowl. They were reunited this past offseason when the Steelers hired McCarthy following the departure of Mike Tomlin.

"I'm not sure what's next for Aaron Rodgers. He will figure out that for himself over the next handful of months, or whatever his particular process is," said Super Bowl champion and Sky Sports NFL expert Ndamukong Suh.

"But I want to go back to what Jason [Bell] said in the way that you handle your business, especially from the perspective of a star. There's a way you go about handling things.

"Those things should be handled behind closed doors before trying to get ahead of the story - on either side. Have a conversation, have an understanding, and then go from there and address it.

"Going out to the media and doing all of these different things, The Pat McAfee Show, it's great for them and great for ESPN, but it's not the proper way I would want to handle that particular scenario."

Responding to Rodgers' comments, McCarthy admitted to his "embarrassing" moment when mentioning the Packers during half-time of their defeat to the Philadelphia Eagles in Week 11.

Steelers president Art Rooney II defended McCarthy on Thursday in an interview with the Pittsburgh Post-Gazette, insisting he supports him "100 per cent".

"I just want to say that I have 100 per cent confidence in Mike McCarthy and I expect he'll be our coach this season, next season and beyond," Mr Rooney II told the Post-Gazette.

"The big thing, what happened this week, is insubordination can't be tolerated in any organization. When you start getting ultimatums, you can't live with that. There's maybe a time and place after the season if he wanted to kind of unload.

"He talks about wanting to be a good teammate, but you don't do that to your teammates a couple days before the game, that's for sure."

Rooney II underlined his belief that events in the locker room should be kept within the locker room, and downplayed Rodgers' comments regarding concerns for McCarthy's health.

The Steelers are 6-4 as they prepare to face the Denver Broncos (8-2) on Black Friday.

Terry Bradshaw, who won four Super Bowls as quarterback for the Steelers, criticised Rodgers for his lack of leadership and turning on his team-mates.

"I'm sorry that Aaron Rodgers had to do this," said Bradshaw on Fox Sports. "I'm sorry that he had to go public with all his gripes and complaints. Am I surprised? Absolutely not.

"To my opinion he's a strange guy anyway and the one thing you don't do, all of us athletes up here, none of us turn on our team-mates, we don't turn on our coaching staff, we don't turn on our ownership, we show class on the way out. Aaron Rodgers didn't do that.

"He said, 'when I'm through playing here in Pittsburgh, I'll disappear and you'll never hear or see from me again' and I hope this is one time he's telling the truth.

"When you're the quarterback, you are the leader. Whether you want to admit it or not, you are the leader.

"Had trouble in Green Bay as their leader, had trouble in New York with the Jets as their leader and certainly in Pittsburgh."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

Rob Gronkowski said Rodgers does not prioritise his team unlike his former quarterback Tom Brady, who also had disagreements with coaches.

"I don't think he plays again in the NFL," said former Patriots tight end Gronkowski on Fox Sports."When there's a guy like Aaron Rodgers that's available there's too much smoke. It would take away from the objective and that's to win games."Aaron Rodgers and Tom Brady, they're both Hall of Fame quarterbacks. I've seen situations personally with my own eyes where Tom and coaches had disagreements but there's one thing that Tom did different. He would dissect it all and then he would hold it in and he would still do what's best for the team and for his team-mates and for the organisation. And yes the disagreements, they were lethal sometimes."But then I would see him go out and still be the best player he can be in practice and in games to help win games and win Super Bowls for the team."

Liverpool are beginning to see the very best of Florian Wirtz if recent form is anything to go by

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Florian Wirtz's £116 million Anfield arrival last summer was, on paper, a marquee addition to the Premier League, until he took to the field.

Supporters of all clubs were expectant, not least Liverpool fans. His debut campaign proved an awkward adaptation to English football, one in which the German seemed caught between systems, clearly in transition.

Fast forward to today and the player who lit up the Bundesliga with Bayer Leverkusen appears to have finally arrived on Merseyside.

Wirtz produced a standout display in Sunday’s 4-0 thrashing of Manchester United, where he scored an improvised goal to extend the Reds' lead and created 10 chances - albeit against 10 men - before finding the net again in Wednesday night’s 3-0 Champions League triumph over Club Brugge.

The underlying numbers from Gradient Sports prove this is no fleeting purple patch, either, especially after three goals in two games over the November international break.

According to Gradient Sports’ data, Wirtz’s overall player grade dipped sharply from a league-leading 91.0 in his final Bundesliga season with Leverkusen in 2024/25 to 73.1 during his debut 2025/26 Premier League campaign.

While his overall 2026/27 Premier League grade sits at 73.9, his attacking execution indicates a resurgence back toward his Leverkusen peak.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

In the Premier League this season, Wirtz has had a 48 per cent increase in chances created - jumping from 1.99 to 2.94 per 90 minutes - ranking first among all Premier League wingers and attacking midfielders.

Even more telling is his cutting edge in the final third: Wirtz's passes directly leading to a half-chance have increased by 84 per cent, from 0.31 to 0.57 per 90.

His end product in front of goal tells a similar story. Gradient data notes that Wirtz’s positively graded shots have risen from 0.24 to 0.38 per 90 - closing in on the 0.45 he posted in 2024/25. Similarly, his 1.61 shots in the box per 90 actually surpasses his final Leverkusen tally of 1.60.

So, what has initiated the turnaround? New Liverpool boss Andoni Iraola deserves credit for tweaking Wirtz's role and adjusting the team's tempo, but Anfield may also owe a debt of gratitude to Jurgen Klopp.

Since taking charge of the German national team, Klopp has turned Wirtz into his talisman; he has four goals in his last four international appearances. And it's that confidence which has bled into his club form, aided by private counsel from the former Reds manager. Wirtz revealed recently that he regularly speaks with Klopp about life at Anfield, taking on board "small, private things" from a man who knows exactly how to win over the Kop.

Armed with Klopp’s guidance and backed by the evidence of improved creative metrics in the Premier League, Liverpool’s £116m man is finally beginning to look worthy of his price tag.

#845. Defending in the Premier League has changed – and it’s causing chaos

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

There is an argument that being a centre-back for a high-pressing team is the hardest position to get right in modern football, as young defenders bought for huge transfer fees tread a tactical high wire

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

As Ronald Araujo prepared to play a long ball forward and Leny Yoro stood close to the halfway line, alarm bells were ringing in the heads of several former Premier League defenders.

Everything about Yoro’s positioning and response to Araujo sending the pass over the top went against what those former players would recognise as the principles of playing next to a centre-back partner, the rules of playing in a back four that have been passed down for generations.

Yoro did not begin to drop when it became clear that Araujo was going long. He did not anticipate the threat of danger by providing cover for Matthijs De Ligt, as he and Alexander Isak challenged for the ball. Instead, Yoro watched on, as if it was not his responsibility.

By the time he had reacted to De Ligt’s mistake, it was already far too late; in chasing Isak down and crashing into the striker outside of the box, he left Manchester United down to 10 men for the majority of their 4-0 defeat to Liverpool at Anfield in Mauricio Pochettino’s first match in charge (the Frenchman’s one-match ban was subsequently overturned after United won their appeal for wrongful dismissal).

Yoro, though, had only followed the instructions Pochettino and his coaching staff had issued him. The 21-year-old wasn’t even playing as a centre-back partner for De Ligt, as such; with United instead looking to defend Liverpool man-for-man, it was, in a sense, every man for himself. Yoro appeared more concerned with Florian Wirtz, the Liverpool creator who was positioned 15 yards away, than covering Isak with De Ligt. He was, effectively, tasked with thinking as a defensive midfielder as well as a centre-back.

To measure just how the responsibilities of the Premier League centre-back have changed, take how Gary Neville spent the closing stages of United’s defeat during his commentary for Sky Sports describing the lessons he learned in his formative years. As a youth, Neville was taught how to play in a back four by holding onto a long rope with his fellow defenders. The exercise was designed to build cohesion and form the idea that the pieces of a defensive line were inter-connected, so that when a full-back rushes out wide to close down a winger, the rest of the defence moves with them, or that when one centre-back jumps forward to attack a long ball, the other drops in behind.

Those commandments are likely to still be repeated across parks and astroturfs as youngsters learn the game today, but it sounds horribly out of date when compared to the very elite, where tactical shifts within the Premier League and top leagues can make modern football appear as a different sport – where bravery and risks are embraced and caution is cut out.

Fulham’s approach at Manchester City on Saturday was another example. Fulham had lost 17 consecutive matches against City in the Premier League and were facing the league’s best striker in Erling Haaland. Did Alvaro Arbeloa’s side look to be safe? To keep it tight and compact to get through the opening stages of a difficult away game? It wasn’t even a consideration.

Within two minutes, Calvin Bassey could be seen leaving his inexperienced (in Premier League terms) centre-back partner David Affengruber one-on-one with Haaland on the halfway line, as he pushed forward to mark Phil Foden. For Arbeloa’s gameplan to work and Fulham to press City, Bassey had to trust that Affengruber, in his sixth Premier League appearance, could be left to deal with Haaland by himself.

Bassey and Affengruber were individually outstanding as Fulham held City to a 1-1 draw, but then they had to be. There is an argument that playing centre-back for a team that looks to press high and go man-to-man across the pitch is now the hardest position in the sport. It requires defenders to not only win their individual duels against skilful dribblers but cover huge areas of space against fast forwards, often as the last one back. They have to be strong physically, have excellent recovery speed and be dominant aerially, as well as being technically sound and capable of playing line-splitting passes, or else they would be seen as a liability in possession. They have to be seen as leaders, to be commanding, brave, and an effective communicator.

And there is nowhere to hide if one of those pieces falls through. The decisions and tactical set-up that led to Yoro’s sending off at Anfield was brilliantly covered by Jamie Carragher and former Tottenham centre-back Toby Alderweireld on Sky’s Monday Night Football, but the struggles of Levi Colwill and Wesley Fofana following Chelsea’s 4-1 defeat at home to Leeds was dissected as well. “You feel like you’re watching kids play in a men’s game,” was Carragher’s assessment of Colwill and Fofana. Yet Fofana was a £75m-rated centre-back when he was signed from Leicester at the age of 21 four years ago; Colwill may have gone for a similar fee following his breakthrough season on loan at Roberto De Zerbi’s Brighton three years ago.

The value of finding a player who can meet the demands of the modern-day centre-back was underlined when Arsenal decided to spend up to £55m on 28-year-old Ezri Konsa, rather than play the first three months of the season without a suitable replacement for the injured William Saliba. Liverpool similarly went big on Jeremy Jacquet, spending up to £60m after he had barely played a full season at Rennes. The early impact of the 21-year-old, next to Virgil van Dijk, suggests Liverpool knew what they were getting; the combination of technical quality and athleticism, which has become even more valuable in a high-pressing team under Andoni Iraola.

Yet one of the reasons Liverpool landed Jacquet was because they missed out on signing Yoro two years before when he was an 18-year-old at Lille. United swooped to pay a reported £52.1m for a player who had entered the final 12 months on his contract, with Real Madrid and Paris Saint-Germain also pursuing a deal. They all saw what United did too: a young centre-back who had all the attributes needed to play as part of a high defensive line and win his duels in one-on-one situations.

Yoro can still be that player. He is, in many ways, an ideal centre-back for Pochettino, who learned at Anfield that De Ligt, post back injury, is not. Yoro will be available for United against Brentford on Saturday, attempting to rebuild his confidence on the high wire that modern-day centre-backs have to tread.

England and Arsenal striker Alessia Russo speaks about football memories and handling pressure in front of goal as she partners with Lucozade

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Alessia Russo has two European Championships and a Champions League to her name and has established herself as one of England’s most prolific strikers.

In another impressive year for the 27-year-old, she became the highest-scoring English player in UEFA Women's Champions League history with a recent hat-trick against Benfica, was named England Women's Player of the Year and earned a place in the FIFPRO Women's World 11.

Speaking to former Three Lions striker Ian Wright at the launch of her new long-term partnership with Lucozade, the England and Arsenal forward discussed how she fell in love with football and the mentality behind her performances.

Russo grew up in Maidstone, Kent and football always featured in her life.

“Football has always been a massive part of my life,” she said. “Growing up, my dad would take me to watch women’s games at Charlton, and I remember looking up to those players and dreaming of doing the same one day.

“To see how far the game has come is incredible. Women’s football is now about so much more than what happens on the pitch. It’s influencing fashion, culture and bringing communities together in ways I could never have imagined growing up.

“To be part of that journey is really special.”

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

Now one of the leading strikers in world football, Russo believes her calm approach is one of her biggest strengths when it comes to finding the back of the net.

"I've always been really laid back. I'm always wanting to win. Just because I'm not angry or shouting or screaming, doesn't mean I don't want to win and I don't want to score," she said.

"I think that calmness is something that I try and bring to the game. And I think as a striker, you have to be calm in and around the box. When things aren't going your way, I just kind of strip it back. I like to train hard and then whatever happens in the game happens.

"You can't control a whole lot as a No.9. You're quite reliant on other players. But what you can control is the moments that you do get."

The partnership will see Russo work with Lucozade Sport to better understand her individual hydration and fuelling requirements, with the 2027 Women's World Cup in Brazil on the horizon.

She will also help inform future product innovation as the brand continues its longstanding support of the Lionesses, dating back to 2006.

Ayisha Gulati is the women's football writer at FourFourTwo. Fresh from a summer covering the Lionesses’ triumphant Euro 2025 campaign in Switzerland, she brings a passion for all things WSL, UWCL, and international women’s football. She has interviewed names including Alessia Russo and Aitana Bonmati and enjoys telling stories that capture the excitement on and off the pitch.

#843. Calvert-Lewin signs new Leeds deal

Dominic Calvert-Lewin has signed a new deal until the summer of 2029 at Leeds; the striker joined the club in 2025 from Everton; he has scored six goals in all competitions this season; his form earned him a recall to the England squad

Dominic Calvert-Lewin has signed a new deal at Leeds, keeping him at the club until the summer of 2029.

Sky Sports News has been reporting that he was expected to commit his future to the club, which has now been confirmed.

Manchester United had shown interest in the 29-year-old.

Calvert-Lewin joined Leeds on a free transfer in the summer of 2025 after leaving Everton. He scored 15 goals across all competitions last season, and has scored six this season. He scored in a 4-1 win against Chelsea on Saturday.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

Since he joined Leeds, Calvert-Lewin is the highest-scoring Englishman in the Premier League (19) - three ahead of his next closest countrymen, Morgan Gibbs-White and Ollie Watkins.

His form for Leeds saw him return to the England set-up in March, and he also featured in the September/October and November squads. Calvert-Lewin was not selected for the World Cup.

Ao Tanaka is also close to signing a new contract with Leeds, Sky Sports News understands.

The midfielder is understood to have agreed terms on a deal that will keep him at Elland Road until 2029. The 28-year-old's current contract was due to expire in the summer of 2028.

Tanaka has grown to become a key figure in Daniel Farke's side this season, starting in nine of Leeds' 11 Premier League matches. They have lost just 10 of the 66 games Tanaka has started since then.

Calvert-Lewin follows in the footsteps of Ethan Ampadu, Joe Rodon, Jayden Bogle and Brenden Aaronson, who all signed new deals in the summer. Leeds are also reportedly set to trigger Lukas Nmecha's one-year extension.

Leeds are seventh in the Premier League, four points from the Champions League places. They face Coventry next in the league on Saturday.

Ahead of the weekend's match, Daniel Farke has refused to shed any more light on his own new contract talks. He signed a four-year contract when appointed in 2023 and that is set to expire at the end of the season.

He was reported to have parted company with his agent in October while reaching an agreement with Leeds in principle to extend his contract until 2029.

Farke said: "I'm the manager of Leeds United. I sign players. I don't sign managers. Since I've been here, I fell in love with the people here, and I fell in love with the club.

"And the only thing I care for is our supporters because they had to suffer really for such a long time. I want to bring success to them. I care for the players, I care for the staff and this is the way I work.

"I think this is also the reason I don't like to talk about my contract at all because I have to lead the people here.

"I'm a leader of men and women at this club and and no one wants a leader who talks about his future, about himself, or whatever. And this also not my style."

Spurs are getting things moving in the right direction under Roberto De Zerbi - but there's a missing piece to the puzzle

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Tottenham Hotspur’s resurgence under Roberto De Zerbi has breathed fresh life into the club after back-to-back 17th-placed finishes.

There is one clear deficiency in their current make-up that threatens to limit what they can achieve in 2026/27, though - they can't finish.

Despite sitting comfortably in the top half after 12 games, Spurs’ underlying attacking numbers tell the story of a side creating plenty and squandering too much of it.

Tottenham have rattled off 170 shots in the Premier League this season - the fifth-highest tally in the division - while only Liverpool and Manchester City have registered more efforts from inside the penalty area than Spurs’ 109.

But, when it comes to actually hitting the target, De Zerbi’s side slump to 14th across the top flight.

There's also an issue with their ball-striking. According to Gradient Sports’ analysts, just six of Spurs’ 170 league attempts have been graded as ‘unsaveable’ - a figure bettered by every team in the Premier League bar Everton (5).

For context, high-flying Brighton have racked up 20 unsaveable efforts, while Erling Haaland has managed seven on his own. At 3.5 per cent, Tottenham boast the lowest proportion of unsaveable shots in the entire division.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

A glance at De Zerbi’s attacking options explains why to some extent. Richarlison has been frozen out entirely and is angling for a January move, Dominic Solanke has managed just two league goals, and big-money summer arrival Omar Marmoush is yet to hit the ground running in north London.

Centre-back Jan Paul van Hecke is the team's joint-top Premier League goalscorer with two goals after 12 matches: Spurs need a centre-forward in January.

Enter Real Sociedad’s 22-year-old Icelandic international Orri Oskarsson.

Oskarsson is by no means LaLiga’s most prolific frontman, having netted four times in the Spanish top flight this term but his underlying metrics point towards a striker ready to thrive in a possession-heavy, attack-minded system.

Unlike De Zerbi’s Spurs, Real Sociedad do not dominate the ball as often, leaving their striker without service for large periods of matches. Oskarsson, though, is making every second count when his team are in possession, averaging a goal every 64 minutes that La Real actually have the ball this season.

In total, he has scored nine times across his last 13 appearances for club and country.

What makes Oskarsson particularly suited to Tottenham is how intelligently he moves to receive the ball. Gradient Sports’ data shows the Icelandic forward receives line-breaking passes 45 per cent of the time, placing him among LaLiga’s best at peeling off defenders and making himself available to creative midfielders.

That off-the-ball awareness is reinforced by the fact he has received the ball in a clear shooting position 10 times in the league this season - a tally bettered only by Barcelona’s Raphinha (13) and Real Madrid's Kylian Mbappe (11).

Once the ball arrives at his feet, Oskarsson has the penalty-box nous Tottenham lack. Ninety-two per cent of his LaLiga shots this season have been taken from inside the box, which aligns nicely with the 109 close-range openings Spurs have already generated this term. Even more impressive, out of the 25 shots he has taken in LaLiga, five have been graded as unsaveable by Gradient's analysts - just one fewer than Tottenham’s entire squad combined.

Gradient have also flagged just one occasion all season where Oskarsson opted to shoot when passing to a better-placed teammate was the superior option, highlighting good judgement under pressure and decision-making that is rare for a 22-year-old.

Meanwhile, his Expected Goals (xG) ranks sixth-highest in LaLiga - a decent return given Real Sociedad’s modest share of possession and chance creation.

And best of all, a winter deal is entirely plausible. For a Tottenham side creating plenty of penalty-box opportunities but with nobody reliable to tuck them away, Oskarsson could be one of the more shrewd January investments the market has to offer.

#839. Chelsea Q&A: Are Blues in crisis? What next for Fofana after viral interview?

Your questions answered by Sky Sports News' James Savundra on Chelsea's season, with Blues having lost three of last four in Premier League; Wesley Fofana’s unauthorised interview, the absences of Danny Welbeck and Estevao, and January transfer plans all addressed

After Chelsea fell to back-to-back losses with a 4-1 humiliation by Leeds at Stamford Bridge last Saturday, Sky Sports News reporter James Savundra examines the latest developments at Stamford Bridge.

As well as suffering a third defeat in four Premier League games, Chelsea and manager Xabi Alonso also faced the added frustration of defender Wesley Fofana giving an unauthorised interview this week, in which he laughed off his penalty miss in last month's Carabao Cup defeat to Liverpool and revealed he had contemplated retiring during his time at Stamford Bridge.

Here, Savundra addresses Fofana's future, Joao Pedro's injury, transfer plans and much more...

Jake: Is Fofana expected to face any disciplinary action for his impromptu interview? Some of the things said in that were unacceptable from a footballer, especially one involved in as much off-the-pitch controversy as him.

James says: Xabi Alonso addressed this at Thursday's press conference. Fofana has apologised following the interview. The matter has been dealt with internally and there are no suggestions that the defender is set to miss any matches.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

Whether the club look to punish Fofana with a fine is not known at this stage. Alonso made clear that this will not be repeated. It's completely understandable to emphasise with Chelsea supporters. Fofana simply hasn't justified the £75m that Chelsea paid Leicester City.

Benny: Why is Fofana still being chosen when every single fan watching football can see how poor his form is?

James says: At the moment there is a lack of real alternative options. Xabi Alonso stood behind the Fofana-Colwill axis during Thursday's press conference despite their clear struggles dealing with Dominic Calvert-Lewin and Brian Brobbey.

Liam Delap will prove a similar physical threat tomorrow [Friday] with an added point to prove. Ultimately, Chelsea trimmed down their squad in the summer in light of no European football. Maxence Lacroix would be starting, possibly ahead of Fofana right now if he was fit.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

Colwill has found things difficult this season having missed the majority of the last campaign. In hindsight, should Chelsea have sold Trevoh Chalobah? Perhaps it was time for the academy graduate to end his Chelsea chapter but he rarely let the side down.

You could feasibly play Josh Acheampong at centre-back. The youngster has been a shining light this season. Yet he looks comfortable on the right. Do you want to upset something which actually seems to be working. And if Acheampong moves to centre-back, then does Marco Palestra play as a right-back?

The Italian impressed in Serie A as a wing-back but with Chelsea opting largely for a flat back four, is Palestra defensively good enough to fulfil that role. Aaron Anselmino remains an option but hasn't played a minute for the club this season.

Chelsea manager Xabi Alonso of Wesley Fofana: "We have addressed that with him and for sure it was unfortunate. He has apologised. He knows it wasn't the right moment. The content wasn't right. "We are here to take things seriously and he said it wouldn't be repeated. We know it's something we don't want and they are not going to be repeated."

Mikey: Will Chelsea sell and buy any defenders and strikers in January? I feel we need stronger defenders with a better aerial ability and maybe a more out and out No 9 to challenge Joao Pedro and give us something different.

James says: Chelsea will spend money in January if they believe it will help them achieve their target this season - qualifying for the Champions League. They were pleased with what they did in the summer but accept that the squad still requires investment.

It seems unlikely any defenders will be sold given the lack of current options. A loan move would seem to suit Aaron Anselmino given his lack of options. The winter window is a difficult one. There's a sense that Chelsea could benefit from signing a more experienced centre-back, considering the moves for Emi Martinez, Jordan Henderson and Danny Welbeck in every other area of the pitch in the summer.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

The club have shown a willingness to tweak their transfer model and sign players for the here and now, in addition to targeting players for the future. A striker would appear unlikely given the presence of Emmanuel Emegha and Danny Welbeck. It will be interesting to watch Emegha's development if given a run of games in the absence of Joao Pedro.

The fact that Xabi Alonso opted for a false nine in three matches prior to Leeds would suggest he believes there are shortcomings in both Emegha and Welbeck's games. It feels more likely that Chelsea will revisit the forward line next summer.

JD: How has Joao Pedro's injury affected how Chelsea has been playing as an overall team, and how has Xabi Alonso had to adapt to it?

James says: The stats are undeniable. Since the start of last season, Chelsea average 1.8 goals per game when Joao Pedro plays, compared to 0.6 when he doesn't. It's quite staggering the difference that the Brazilian seems to make.

Cole Palmer and Morgan Rogers look far more potent when they are playing off him. Danny Welbeck initially started in his absence at Brentford. However, he had virtually no impact and appears to have fallen down the pecking order.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

Playing Rogers or Pedro Neto as a false-nine has been experimented with but Chelsea have looked blunt without a focal point - though Emmanuel Emegha scored in his first Premier League start which was really encouraging.

Xabi Alonso doesn't tend to give much away but he has described Emegha as being a player with "special" qualities. There's clearly an adaptation period required and Emegha missed a lot of football last season due to injury.

He was also signed prior to Alonso's arrival so it was very much a club signing. Chelsea's season has been derailed by the absence of key players such as Reece James, Joao Pedro and Moises Caicedo.

Alonso needs his big players to step up to ensure they can cope with the casualties - albeit to really key players.

Adam: Why does Alonso not start Welbeck whilst Joao Pedro is injured? Given his experience?

James says: The treatment of Welbeck has been puzzling. He performed really well in the opening two Carabao Cup matches of the season but has featured sparingly since the Brentford defeat.

It was interesting to see how late he was brought on against Tottenham despite Chelsea's need to turn the tide. The 36-year-old (happy birthday today, Danny!) clearly cannot get around the pitch with the same intensity and speed he did when he broke through at Manchester United but that was obvious when he was signed.

Alonso has deflected when asked about Welbeck's lack of minutes but perhaps his inability to press with intensity is one of the main reasons behind him spending more time on the bench than on the pitch.

He's still got a brilliant goalscoring touch - as seen last season at Brighton. He may benefit from more opportunities during a busy December period.

Tim: Should Chelsea be starting Estevao more often? If not, then what should we do with him? Where could we send him on loan if we can't guarantee minutes?

James says: Estevao has only started twice this season - both times at home. He made a huge impact on the pitch and on the supporters when he started in the win against Manchester United. His lack of physical robustness and defensive acumen would appear to be why Xabi Alonso has used him so sparingly.

However, I don't think his lack of minutes is going to be sustainable long-term. There's an argument given Cole Palmer's drop off that Estevao should get an opportunity at No 10. Chelsea see Estevao as one of their "untouchable" players and they would be extremely reluctant to let him leave.

I asked Alonso last month about whether a loan could be an option in January. The Spaniard said that it had not been discussed. Something is going to have to give at some point.

Estevao is still a teenager so has lots of learning and development left. However, he would be a key player for many of the top clubs in Europe.

He needs to find a way to force his way into Alonso's plans. A January departure is very unlikely but conversations will need to take place in the summer if his lack of football continues.

Saying that, if Chelsea do qualify for Europe next season then there should be more opportunities.

Sam: Which manager is in more need of a win on Friday, Oliver Glasner or Alonso?

James says: Both clubs feel like they are in very similar situations right now. Both signing managers to deliver a cultural reboot and sustained success. Yet both have had challenging starts.

I was at Glasner's press conference on Thursday and he spoke about lengthy conversations he had with the club owner earlier this week about January transfers and standards. Forest gave him an extremely lucrative contract and will want to give him as much time as they can.

However, given they have had five managers in the space of a year, it's difficult to predict anything at Forest.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

Chelsea have full confidence in Xabi Alonso but home defeats against Spurs and Leeds have really harmed his approval ratings amongst supporters.

It would feel like a crisis if Chelsea lost three league matches on the bounce, so I would say Alonso needs a win just a little bit more than Glasner.

If Forest can create an atmosphere at the City Ground similar to their win against Manchester City then Chelsea will really be tested. Liam Delap will be desperate to prove a point.

#838. Gut microbes can adapt to our ageing bodies

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

John A. Lees is at EMBL’s European Bioinformatics Institute EMBL-EBI, Hinxton CB10 1SD, UK.

Our guts contain around 40 trillion bacterial cells, a similar quantity to the number of cells in the entire human body1. Although the community of bacterial species in the human gut usually stays relatively stable over time2, genetic mutations in such bacteria can be associated with a measure of body size called the body mass index3. Writing in Nature, Wang et al.4 scanned the gut bacteria of some 10,000 people for genetic variation and searched for statistically significant associations with almost 250 characteristics, including age, height and cardiovascular fitness. The authors singled out one adaptation that seems to help one of the most abundant bacterial species in the human gut to resist a form of stress called oxidative stress, which damages cells and increases as people age.

#837. Joan Smalls Says Tom Brady Was "Catalyst" for Candice Swanepoel Feud

Joan Smalls addressed her and fellow Victoria's Secret Angel Candice Swanepoel's friendship fallout, confirming that the South African model's new romance with Tom Brady was the reason.

Joan Smalls is strutting away from relationships that don't respect girl code.

One month after rumors emerged that the Victoria's Secret supermodel was unhappy with fellow runway star Candice Swanepoel for dating her former fling Tom Brady, she confirmed the New England Patriots alum was at the center of their friendship breakup.

"Unfortunately, that was the catalyst," Smalls said during the Nov. 25 episode of The Cutting Room Floor podcast. "I was seeing this person for a period of eight months."

E! News has reached out to reps for Swanepoel and Brady for comment and has not yet heard back.

Though Smalls doesn't consider Brady to be an ex, she clarified that they casually dated the former NFL star on and off between 2023 and 2024. Swanepoel went on to spark romance rumors with Brady in June.

And for her part, Smalls emphasized that before ending her and Swanepoel's 15-year friendship—which she confirmed took place in April—they were each other's confidants about love and heartbreak.

"You've seen the relationships, situationships and people I've dated, and I've confided in you in these spaces and we never had a crossover," she reflected. "All of a sudden, I stopped seeing this person, and three months later, you text me and say, 'Oh, we have to speak about something,' which is usually not a conversation we normally have."

The Puerto Rican-born model—who had confirmed their fallout in scathing comments under her own Instagram posts last month—had a feeling that Swanepoel, 38, was planning to name him her MVP.

"I called her and I asked her, I said, 'Is this about him?' She said, 'Yes,'" she recalled. "We spoke on the phone very briefly, and I was just perplexed and lost for words."

The confrontation was especially devastating because Smalls said Swanepoel—who was previously linked to model Andrés Velencoso in 2022—had been a guiding light during her romance with the Fox Sports commentator.

"She helped me write text messages to this person," Smalls, also 38, said. "She knew intimate things. Potentially to my detriment, I overshared. I was just being open with a friend that I thought was a safe spac

As for how the conversation went? Smalls accused her former friend of committing a cardinal girl code sin: Dating a guy your friend was romantically involved with.

"She came across as justifying her actions," she explained. "She started diminishing my experience to make herself feel better about the situation, which I think is what infuriated me."

Smalls believed that Swanepoel—who shares two sons with ex Hermann Nicoli—refused to take accountability for being a bad friend.

"It was this whole attitude of 'I'm an adult. I don't need permission,'" she posited. "Both are actually true: you are an adult and you don't need permission. But as a friend, you should consider me in your choices. Don't consider me in your apologies."

"Then she was like, 'Well, I'm sorry, but I'm going to explore this and so is life,'" she continued. "It was just this attitude of entitlement and lack of care towards someone who's your friend and something that I would never do to you."

Looking back at the conversation, Smalls felt that Swanepoel was looking to ease her own mind.

As she put it, "She wanted me to comfort her about her bad decision so that she didn't feel guilty by her choice and then she would constantly justify it."

It was especially difficult for the model since she prefers to keep her inner circle small.

"I rarely allow people into my life, and I'm very private," Smalls added. "So, if I let you into a space that I thought you would protect me as my friend, that's the only one thing I asked for you to do. Create a safe space for me to be myself, to open up, and you can't do that."

Following initial speculations about their fallout, Swanepoel's team detailed her perspective on their friendship.

"Candice has always been exceptionally private about her personal life, with her focus remaining on raising her children," her rep Amanda Ruisi told E! News in October. "She and Joan share a longstanding history and a friendship that Candice will always respect."

As Smalls and Swanepoel navigate life after their friendship, keep reading for more famous celebrity feuds.

The Sex and the City costars had dodged feud rumors for years, but they were reignited after Cattrall decided not to return for a third movie and made comments about her SLP that raised eyebrows.

"What was your reaction to Kim Cattrall telling Piers Morgan that you were never friends just colleagues?" Andy Cohen asked Parker on a September 2017 episode of Watch What Happens Live.

As she explained, "Just...heartbroken. I mean that whole week, you and I spoke about it because I was just...I don't know I found it really upsetting because that's, you know, that's not the way I recall our experience."

"So...it's sad but I'm kind of...I don't know, I always think that what ties us together is this singular experience is the thing," she continued. "It was a professional experience but it became personal because it was years and years of our lives. So I'm hoping that that sort of eclipses anything that's been recently spoken. That many years spent doing something so special that people had a connection with is such a privileged."

And though they didn't film scenes together, Cattrall did make a small appearance on And Just Like That.

During a 2022 TikTok challenge, JoJo Siwa described Candace Cameron Bure as the "rudest" celebrity, later explaining that she felt snubbed when Bure once refused to take a picture with her on a red carpet. Shortly after the dig, however, the Full House alum apologized: "I kind of broke your 11-year-old heart. I didn't take a picture with you. Ugh! I feel crummy, I feel—JoJo, I'm so sorry."

Back in June 2021, the Hole frontwoman accused Rodrigo of copying her band's album cover for a promotional photo without giving credit, prompting the Disney alum to respond, "Love u and live through this sooooo much."

however, it seemed their hatchet was buried when Love replied, "Olivia - you're welcome. My favorite florist is in Notting Hill, London! Dm me for deets! I look forward to reading your note [winking face emoji]."

"So I just got to my dressing room and found this actual olive branch," Swift said in an Instagram video. "This mean so much."

She captioned the video, "Thank you Katy."

Panini have launched their latest WSL sticker collection at event with ex-Lioness Rachel Daly

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Panini have launched their latest Barclays Women's Super League sticker collection, featuring teams from WSL and WSL 2 for a second year running.

This is only the fourth edition of the book for the top women’s league in this country, and Rachel Daly believes the culture of sticker collecting can play its part in growing the women’s game.

As the latest collection was launched in London this week, the ex-Lioness spoke to FourFourTwo about the rise of the women's game.

Speaking at the launch, Daly reflected on her own childhood memories of collecting Panini stickers.

"For me, it goes back to my childhood,” Daly told FourFourTwo. “I collected them with my brother. We used to, every Saturday morning, go and get the stickers.

"You'd get your piles and you'd trade them and swap them at school. Just that whole feeling of sitting down and putting stickers in.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

"I'm a Leeds fan, so I always wanted to get the whole Leeds team immediately when I was younger.

"I would literally swap any of my stickers, even if I'd already got the Leeds player, just to have more.”

While Daly grew up collecting men’s players, this WSL collection offers an opportunity to introduce more fans to the women's game, something Daly believes is particularly important as the league continues to grow.

The latest album has 545 stickers across all 26 WSL and WSL2 clubs, giving fans access to collect stickers of their favourite players from across the top two tiers of English women’s football.

"The visibility of the game is massive," she added.

"For the fact that it's WSL 1 and 2, I think it's equally as important. Those players in the WSL 2 deserve the same recognition as us.

"Being able to see kids being exposed to seeing the women's game as well, it's exciting."

Daly was speaking at the launch of the Panini Barclays Women's Super League Official Sticker Collection 2027 in London. The collection is available now at retailers nationwide and online via Panini.co.uk.

Ayisha Gulati is the women's football writer at FourFourTwo. Fresh from a summer covering the Lionesses’ triumphant Euro 2025 campaign in Switzerland, she brings a passion for all things WSL, UWCL, and international women’s football. She has interviewed names including Alessia Russo and Aitana Bonmati and enjoys telling stories that capture the excitement on and off the pitch.

#835. Leclerc denies having 'No 1 clause' in Ferrari contract

Lewis Hamilton, meanwhile, confirms they remain "free to race" after talks following their collision in Las Vegas, for which Leclerc was punished by stewards; watch the Qatar GP on Sky Sports F1 this weekend, with qualifying at 6pm on Saturday and the race at 4pm on Sunday

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

Charles Leclerc has strongly denied suggestions he has a No 1 driver clause in his Ferrari contract.

The Monegasque, who has been with the team since 2019 and signed an extended deal earlier this year, was speaking ahead of the Qatar Grand Prix as both he and Lewis Hamilton faced the media again four days on from their latest clash at the Las Vegas Grand Prix.

Leclerc was given a 10-second penalty by the stewards for causing a collision as he attempted to overtake Hamilton for sixth place in Las Vegas, with the incident also earning him severe criticism from Ferrari team principal Fred Vasseur.

The Las Vegas collision came just three weeks after a fierce battle between the team-mates - with Hamilton running first and Leclerc second - on the opening lap in Mexico City cost Ferrari a likely one-two, with clear-the-air discussions required after Red Bull's Max Verstappen won that race.

Vasseur has hitherto played down the need to impose strict, pre-determined rules of engagement on his drivers to avoid future repeats. There had subsequently been speculation that, perhaps, there were contractual reasons on Leclerc's side preventing the team from formally intervening in this way.

But offered the chance on Thursday to address claims about the presence of a so-called 'No 1 driver' clause in his deal, Leclerc said: "I normally never disclose what I have in my contract, but I think this one is an important one to speak about.

"And I absolutely have zero clause that says that in my contract.

George Russell admits feud with Max Verstappen is 'avoidable' and 'unnecessary' ahead of Qatar Grand Prix

"It's never something that I was interested in and never something that I personally wanted."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

Leclerc bore the brunt of Vasseur's post-race criticism last Sunday and, asked if he agreed with the Frenchman that the crash with Hamilton had indeed been "unacceptable", replied: "That it is unacceptable? Of course.

"As a team, we cannot afford to clash between team-mates and I think that is very clear for everyone. For the clash in particular of Las Vegas, as I said, I took responsibility.

"I think there's just tension around, that we just need to dissipate and make sure that we look at more positive days in the future.

"That's all I'm looking for. But yeah, I do agree. It's unacceptable that both Ferrari clash together, of course."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

Vasseur had promised further talks with his drivers following the race in Vegas, having insisted the clashes between the pair "cannot continue".

The drivers confirmed on Thursday that talks had taken place, with both the team principal and among themselves, with Hamilton saying they had been "good discussions" and "positive".

Neither driver said they would elaborate on the specifics of what was discussed, with Leclerc stating in the official FIA news conference that he "cannot disclose" what possible "solutions" were agreed to avoid future repeats or whether any restrictions were in place for the season's final two rounds.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

Hamilton later confirmed they remained free to race each other this weekend in Qatar

"We're still free to race, and I think that's the ultimate goal of being here. We want to race, right?" said Hamilton to Sky Sports F1.

"Of course, we don't want what happened last week to ever happen, so we communicate. Charles and I had a good sit down earlier on and had our chat, and I I think moving forwards we can be fine.

"We literally focus on racing hard and fair, and continue to try and enjoy it. We do enjoy racing together, and we do have a really good relationship.

"It's obviously intense in the background, well on the outside, it seems a lot more intense than it really is inside."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

Hamilton has previously called for the team to adopt clearer guidelines on how he and Leclerc are able to race each other but, speaking on Thursday, said it was Vasseur's final call to make.

"That's for Fred to decide ultimately," he said. "I made my point clear already about them.

"So yeah, there's not really much more to say on it really. I said my piece before and and my point hasn't really changed."

Leclerc and Hamilton are in their second season as Ferrari team-mates and will at least spend one more year in tandem in 2027, with the potential for more.

Asked if he thought they could move forward in harmony, Hamilton said: "I do. We're going to figure it out.

"We're team-mates at the end of the day and we do always learn from these experiences whilst maybe it doesn't necessarily look like it.

"There will be learnings that we take from this difficult period, and I still believe in everything we're building and working towards in the background.

"I came here with the goal of taking Ferrari back to the top and it has been a massively challenging season but it's so easy to look at the negatives but I like to look at the positives this year."

Ferrari can clinch the runner-up position to world champions Mercedes this weekend in Qatar and Hamilton added: "We are fighting for second in the Constructors' Championship, we have had wins, I think we've had the best car chassis-wise particularly this year and that's down to all the amazing people back at the factory who have worked and brought upgrades. I am so proud of them.

"Did we have the straight-line speed? No. That's something we are working towards for next year. If we are able to galvanise and improve on that section, we're going to be mighty next year in my view.

"I'm just trying to look at the positives, I think everyone seems to be focusing always on the negatives, which is obviously the easiest thing to do in life. But I try to remember the positives, and we've really done some amazing things this year together."

Hamilton added: "I like to think that we are stronger. I think that if everything was just great all the time I don't think you learn anything.

"When you're winning all the time as well, you don't learn a lot through that. You learn really through the hardest times, and these are the definitely very, very challenging times for Fred, for Charles and I, but these are the moments that you really learn and grow closer together, through conversation, communicating and having those sit-downs.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

Leclerc believes his off-track relationship with Hamilton is "really strong" and they now needed to find a workable way forward when racing each other on track.

"We're just really very much focused on trying to find a solution that works," said Leclerc.

"Particularly because I really believe we are in a good momentum and if next year we are to be in a position of fighting for the championship, it's even more so important to find the right solution for both of us to bring Ferrari back to the top.

"At the end of the day, we are two, one in each car, and we need to make sure that things just work out. At the moment, it's not working.

"Then, of course, I can take the blame from one episode and whatever. That doesn't really matter. It's just important that we find a compromise and a solution that works for both."

#833. Could the Airbus €3 billion loan row reignite a US-EU trade dispute?

The US says a record €3 billion financing package for Airbus may conflict with a transatlantic aircraft-subsidy truce. EU officials insist the funding complies with market-based rules.

A fresh row over a record-breaking EU loan to European aerospace company Airbus could reopen a long-standing rift with Washington and threaten an existing EU-US trade truce.

The European Investment Bank (EIB), the lending arm of the EU, agreed in June to loan Airbus up to €3 billion ($3.4 billion) but US President Donald Trump's top trade advisor recently suggested the loan breached a 2021 EU-US agreement on state support.

"I had sincerely hoped that trade-distorting European subsidies to Airbus were a thing of the past," US Trade Representative Jamieson Grier said in late October. "For decades, France, Germany and Spain have aggressively supported Airbus, their national champion aircraft manufacturer, to gain an unfair advantage over US aerospace workers and business."

He also suggested there was a lack of transparency around the terms of the loan. The EU insists the loan does not amount to subsidies, that it is in close contact with the Office of the US Trade Representative and "will provide all necessary information," a spokesperson told DW.

An Airbus spokesperson told DW the company is "actively engaging with the relevant authorities and are happy to share more information about the loan with governments."

Airbus and the US company Boeing, the world's two largest plane manufacturers, were previously involved in a 17-year corporate trade dispute.

The World Trade Organization (WTO) ruled that both the EU and US provided the companies with state subsidies, resulting in years of tariffs, tit-for-tat retaliation and claims of victory by both sides.

A deal to end tariffs with strict provisions on state support was finally agreed in 2021 and strengthened in 2025, but the latest row threatens to reopen the dispute and could potentially threaten the wider EU-US tariff deal agreed last year, experts say.

The previous Airbus-Boeing dispute was one of the longest-running corporate disputes in history and led to billions of dollars' worth of tariffs leveled by both sides.

"Trade experts tend to hate to talk about it because there are so many ups and downs to the story, it took so long to get resolved and it always tends to creep back up again," Inu Manak, a senior fellow at the Peterson Institute for International Economics who specializes in international trade law and policy, told DW.

She says because the issue is such a "persistent thorn in the side," it has the potential to spiral, but for now the US is only signaling displeasure before things escalate. "They want to talk about this, and that conversation will need to happen before anything goes further," she said.

At the heart of the current dispute is whether the €3 billion loan from the EIB, the largest corporate loan ever authorized by the bank, amounts to illegal state support.

"The EIB loan to Airbus is a standard loan on market terms," a European Commission spokesperson told DW. "It carries interest, it must be repaid in full, and it is the type of financing the EIB provides every year to companies across many sectors."

A spokesperson for the bank told DW the €3 billion loan is "a standard EIB corporate loan, implemented under the bank's established procedures and on market-based terms." It says it considers the financing to be "fully consistent with the market-terms principle" of the 2021 deal.

A spokesperson for Airbus told DW the loan is "a standard corporate financing facility, similar to commercially available loans we've signed in the past."

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Fredrik Erixon, founding director of the European Center for International Political Economy, says the lines are still blurred when it comes to what counts as a subsidy and what is just a loan and that only a comprehensive World Trade Organization investigation could establish the full facts.

Another potential issue is how the €3 billion will be used, including the share earmarked for research and development and how much funding will support defense-related activities versus commercial aircraft development.

Inu Manak says it is impossible at this point to determine if the loan amounts to the provision of illegal subsidies or not, and that it depends on the very specific terms of the credit provided and whether or not it could be proved to be damaging to Boeing's business.

"If it's a market-based loan, if it's not providing below-market rates that would provide an unfair advantage, then it should be fine," she said. "That remains to be seen."

In Erixon's view, the situation is further complicated by the fact that the aerospace sector is "a highly murky business" due to the amount of defense contracts companies like Boeing and Airbus hold with governments and the high costs associated with that in terms of research and development.

"The problem is we've ended up in a world where there's only two large aircraft manufacturers," he told DW. "And it is a business with high upfront costs when you're going to develop different things."

He points out that while Boeing may have a legitimate grievance over this loan, Airbus and the EU can point to Boeing's own deals with the US government.

"Boeing does R&D contracts for military purposes, which end up producing technology and support for the civil aircraft program for Boeing," said Erixon. "That's also what the World Trade Organization found previously."

It was Boeing that originally asked the US trade representative back in July to intervene over the loan, linking it to Airbus' plan to develop a new single-aisle aircraft program, which could spark a new era of intense competition between the two giants. Neither the US trade representative nor Boeing responded to a DW request for comment.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Inu Manak thinks the next obvious step for the US would be to launch a Section 301 investigation, which is an official inquiry to determine if the loan "violates an international trade agreement or is unjustified, unreasonable or discriminatory, and that burdens or restricts US commerce."

She thinks the Trump administration has no interest in engaging with the WTO and believes it has the potential to threaten the broader EU-US trade agreement.

"I don't think there's a lot that can stop the US trade representative from taking action if they decide they want to do it," Manak said. "They may think there may be something else to extract from the European Union."

Fredrik Erixon agrees that "it's going to be a point of leverage that the Americans can use against Europe," adding that the dynamics underpinning the aerospace sector — that both Boeing and Airbus need greater government investment due to ramped-up military spending — is the fundamental underlying problem.

"We are getting into a state aid race, which basically means these companies just need more and more and more money," he said. "That in itself is an escalatory development."
