#751. Why KMI Panel frustrates referees too - and impacts their salary

Referees rely on the opinions of former players to determine a significant part of their annual salary

It has become something of a Wednesday morning ritual for fans. At 10am, the Premier League releases the latest votes of its Key Match Incidents Panel.

For four seasons, the KMI Panel was a clandestine operation. It was distributed to clubs only, but it would still find its way out into the public domain.

This season, it began being released to the public.

Yet little is really understood about the KMI Panel.

Why does it exist? Is it just protecting referees? And does it really mean anything?

For referees, the last question is more important than you might realise.

The votes, which ultimately say whether referees have got a decision right or wrong, create a merit table of performance - and this impacts their salary.

"It depends where you are on the list," former Premier League referee Graham Scott said. "But if you're in the middle, then it might be 25% of your take-home. So it's substantial."

For the officials, these are not decisions being taken by their bosses.

Their performance reviews are effectively outsourced to a group of former players.

The results can be inconsistent and frustrating as much for the referees as they are for the fans.

Let's take a look at how a referee's salary works in the Premier League.

A Premier League official will earn, on average, about Â£175,000 per year. The scale will run between Â£125,000 and Â£250,000.

Think that is unduly high? Referees in Spain's La Liga are the highest paid in the world, according to Marca, with an average yearly salary of Â£221,000.

Premier League officials are about on par with those in the German Bundesliga and Italian Serie A.

In England, there is a guaranteed base wage of 50%. This will differ depending on the seniority and experience of an official.

Michael Oliver would be at the top of the bracket, a newcomer like Farai Hallam at the other end.

The other 50% is based upon a set of variables, with match fees a major part.

Each on-field appointment is worth a little over Â£1000, with a VAR game slightly less.

Last season, Anthony Taylor refereed the most Premier League games, 31, followed by Chris Kavanagh, 30, and Michael Oliver, 29.

Kavanagh and Oliver worked as VAR on a handful of occasions, while Taylor did not do any.

Stuart Attwell had the most combined appointments at 52, with 25 games as a referee and 27 as a VAR.

Finally, there is the subjective element - the KMI Panel.

The votes determine the annual bonus payments for all officials.

Until 2022, referees' body Pro Ref, or PGMOL as it was known until this summer, used to do its own assessment of its referees' decisions.

But clubs grew restless, feeling referees were marking their own homework.

It is made up of five members. Three are former players and coaches, plus there is a representative for the Premier League and one for Pro Ref.

Their identities remain secret, with the former professionals selected from a pool on rotation.

What you won't see on the published version is that each incident is given a difficulty rating, ranging from one to five, which is taken into account when drawing up the referees' merit table.

All this really is, of course, is another layer of subjectivity. On top of the referees, VAR, players and coaches.

"People complain about the consistency of referees on field, of VAR interventions, or otherwise," said Scott, who now acts as the refereeing expert for the Athletic.

"But then, if you look at the KMI Panel outcomes, they're also inconsistent."

It is a view shared by Andy Davies, who retired as a Championship referee last year.

"Naturally, there will always be a level of interest given as it provides a significant part of income for the season," Davies said.

"But ultimately, the KMI Panel lacks any real credibility amongst referees."

Graham Scott was a Premier League referee for 10 years and acted as a VAR for more than 100 matches

Referees are scored on their on-field decision-making. If an error has been corrected by the VAR, it still counts as a mistake for the merit table.

Those at the top of the table will be rewarded well, while those at the bottom are not likely to receive much of a bonus payment at all.

Let's take a look at the numbers from last season.

Michael Oliver was the top referee, getting 93.5% of KMIs correct. John Brooks, Darren England and Simon Hooper were very marginally behind.

For other referees, the borderline decisions, ones which are the most subjective and sit in the grey areas, can be an issue.

One vote could be the difference between a referee being right or wrong. And a place on the merit table, impacting how much they get paid.

Last season, Sam Barrott and Jarred Gillett were both told they made four errors to a 2:3 vote.

Attwell, meanwhile, had three of the more high-profile incidents go in his favour to a 3:2 vote.

"The ones that sit in the margins can be very contentious and inconsistent," said Scott.

"You think, well, how can that be right? You know, that's not definitive, is it? It could have gone either way.

"But there seems to be a reluctance to allow that 'seen them given' sort of mentality, neither right nor wrong.

"Relying on such a small group of people to be so definitive, especially when they vote 3:2, is unhealthy and unhelpful."

As well as determining the merit table for each referee's salary, what the KMI Panel says can guide how games are refereed.

The members of the KMI Panel can be influenced by public opinion, and inconsistency means referees are often having to change the way they approach games, only to be told it is wrong.

"I have spoken to many referees, even this season," Davies said. "And they have no idea which way the panel is going to fall at times, or which way Pro Ref are going to vote because of how political it can be."

Scott used the example of holding when an attacker is offside.

In December last year, Brentford's Dango Ouattara was pulled back against Leeds. The penalty was cancelled by the VAR for offside. The KMI Panel voted 5:0 it was correct.

Last month, Arsenal were not given a penalty against Hull, when an offside Kai Havertz was pulled back by Nobel Mendy. The KMI Panel voted 5:0 it was incorrect.

"One minute we're told football expects an offside," Scott said. "Okay, we'll deliver that for you. We do it again, and they say the opposite.

"Referees get confused on the back of that mixed feedback. It just shows how the system's flawed.

"The game can afford to invest more in this process, and a properly independent approach."

For now, at least, referees have no choice but to rely on the KMI Panel to determine a chunk of their salary.

#748. Borussia Dortmund bows to fan pressure and end Rheinmetall deal

Borussia Dortmund has reluctantly ended its association with a major sponsor after long-term fan protests. They are not the first Bundesliga club to u-turn, as commercial interests clash with politics and fan culture.

Two years of fan pressure and criticism has forced Borussia Dortmund to drop a sponsorship deal with Germany's largest arms manufacturer, Rheinmetall.

The Bundesliga club will not renew its deal with Rheinmetall beyond its expiry in June 2027, at the end of this season. Dortmund chairman Carsten Cramer confirmed the news on the club's website ahead of its AGM on Sunday, which may have proved a potential flashpoint. He acknowledged that "our partnership has been controversial from the outset" but lamented the loss of income.

"It reduces our financial room for manoeuvre. We will have to reprioritize planned investments and carefully examine how we can find viable solutions."

Though he welcomed the news, one of the leaders of the fan revolt against the partnership, Michael Schulze von Glaser, warned this is likely not the end of the road.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

"I think in the end it was a victory for the fans. But I'm also a bit skeptical about what the future will bring us," the Dortmund fan and former head of the German Peace Society told DW. "Football fans in Germany always must be skeptical and always must watch what the club is doing.”

Many Dortmund fans have opposed the deal — which has seen Rheinmetall's logo on advertising boards and other surfaces at locations such as Dortmund's 83,000-capacity Westfalenstadion — from its beginnings in 2024. It was estimated to be worth between €7 ($7.68 million) and €9 million per year.

At the club's AGM that year, 556 of 855 members present voted against the deal in a non-binding vote. There were 247 votes in favour, with 52 abstentions. This, said Cramer, informed the eventual outcome.

Rheinmetall sells arms mostly to Germany, Ukraine and NATO but fans and critics feel that platforming any arms manufacturer goes against the club's statement of its core values. In that, Dortmund states its desire for "a club and a society that operate free of racism, anti-Semitism, LGBTQIA+ hostility, sexism, violence and discrimination."

To play this audio please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 audio

It has always been clear, said Schulze von Glaser, that this deal did not chime with that.

"In the end, they kill people. They are for war," he said of Rheinmetall. "The slogan of Borussia Dortmund is true love (Echte Liebe). But for me and many others, our love ends there…. I know some fans who have put fan merchandise in the trash because they were so shocked.”

In the Q and A on the club's website, Cramer said he was still a "personal advocate" of the deal but that Dortmund's commitment to the 50+1 model, which means German clubs are majority controlled by the members, meant they had to listen to fan voices. But he also warned that Rheinmetall must be an "absolute exception and an isolated case."

That set off some alarm bells for Schulze von Glaser.

"It's a bit concerning that there are constantly these attacks on professional football — a new sponsorship, investment deals," he said.

Indeed, Dortmund's climbdown is not the first of its kind in Germany's top flight. Last year, after fan and media pressure, Bayern Munich ended its commercial deal with the tourism arm of the Rwandan government before its conclusion.

Fans had objected to the promotion of Rwanda, which many felt sought to divert attention from its poor human rights record and actions in the war with DR Congo, through sporting partnerships. Two years earlier, Bayern withdrew from a similarly controversial deal with Qatar Airways.

Elsewhere in the league, Werder Bremen fans objected to their long time shirt sponsor, Wiesenhof. Many supporters took issue with the factory farming practices of Germany's largest poultry producer. Though it was not given as a direct reason for the end of a shirt sponsorship deal in 2023, it likely played a part.

Union Berlin fans have also made their voices heard. When the club signed a new shirt-sponsorship deal with Luxembourg real estate company, Aroundtown, upon promotion to the top flight in 2019, many fans were frustrated at the tie up in a city where rent prices were skyrocketing.

"It's a problem for a lot of people," fan Sven Dobberstein told DW at the time.

"We have to try to find a way between commercialization and what we have at the moment. It isn't easy."

Striking that balance can often be a source of tension for Bundesliga clubs. 50+1 ensures fans have a voice, preventing rich owners, or nation states, from taking control as they do in England's lucrative Premier League or in France or Spain. Indeed fan protests have also stopped the league signing a €1billion private equity partner and seen Monday night matches scrapped. For Schulze von Glaser, this needs to be protected.

"In Germany, the fan culture has an impact," he said.

”If there is something bad or terrible happening in your club and in the Bundesliga, there are the organized fans and they can have an impact if they want, if they stand together and, yes, they can stop the Rheinmetall deal."

#747. Duran scores late Celtic winner to keep Europa League hopes alive

Torreense vs Celtic. UEFA Europa League Round 1.

Campo Manuel MarquesAttendance: Attendance4,971.

Report from the Europa League clash between Torreense and Celtic at Campo Manuel Marques; Javi Vazquez' own-goal put Celtic in front; Dany Jean levelled before the break; substitute Camilo Duran headed in a late winner for the Hoops; Martin O'Neill's side are up to 25th

Football Journalist @AlisonGConroy

Camilo Duran came off the bench to keep Celtic's Europa League hopes alive with a vital win against Torreense.

The Colombian striker peeled away to the back post to meet a cross from fellow substitute James Forrest, guiding a downward header into the net in the 85th minute.

Duran's 15th goal of the season secured a 2-1 victory over the Portuguese second-tier side and moved Celtic on to six points in the Europa League. His latest decisive contribution follows a match-winning double off the bench in the Hoops' comeback victory over Besiktas last time out.

Celtic took the lead in the ninth minute when Javi Vazquez turned Jota's cross into his own net, with Hyun-jun Yang lurking behind him.

However, the Portuguese Cup winners hit back 10 minutes later after some hesitant defending from the visitors. Alex Alfaro rattled the crossbar with a 22-yard effort, but neither Kieran Tierney nor Colby Donovan could deal with the resulting loose balls, allowing Haiti international Dany Jean to volley home the equaliser.

Celtic dominated possession after the break but struggled to create clear-cut opportunities until Duran's late intervention secured all three points.

The Hoops' attention now turns to Hearts on Sunday, live on Sky Sports, as they look to remain top of the Scottish Premiership.

Their next Europa League match is away to Omonia Nicosia on December 10.

2: CLOSE! Alex Oxlade-Chamberlain sends in a corner, it's flicked on by Liam Scales but Hyun-jun Yang can't knock the ball in before it's cleared.

9: GOAL CELTIC! Javi Vazquez tries to clear Jota's cross but turns it into his own net.

19: GOAL TORREENSE! Alex Alfaro's effort rattles the underside of the bar, Celtic fail to make a clearance and Dany Jean fires in the equaliser.

33: SAVE! Jota's powerful strike is pushed over the bar by Adriel.

36: OFF THE LINE! More awful defending from Celtic, but Liam Scales manages to head the ball clear.

47: SAVE! Jota tries to chip the ball over the goalkeeper but he manages to pluck the ball out of the air.

53: BLOCK! Jota is continuing to cause problems for the hosts as he sends in a cross for Kieran Tierney, which is headed behind.

61: CLOSE! Jean looks to squeeze in a shot at the near post, but it's just wide.

69: CHANCE! A misplaced pass from Oliver Sorensen lets Musa Drammeh get a shot away. Thankfully for Celtic it's wide.

70: LET OFF FOR CELTIC! Trouble at the back again gives Drammeh space to get a shot away, but the former Hearts striker is inches wide.

84: GOAL CELTIC! Camilo Duran rises at the back post to head in James Forrest's cross. Celtic are back ahead.

Jota looked back to his best despite not scoring or providing an assist.

In his first European appearance for Celtic since 2025, the winger was a pest for the Portuguese side until he was replaced by James Forrest.

He created chances with some brilliant crossing with one turned in by Vazquez for the opening goal.

He has been sensational since arriving in the summer and he saved Celtic again.

But it was far from a perfect performance in Portugal.

Once again, slack defending and individual errors proved costly, allowing Torreense to remain well in the game.

Record signing Kasper Hogh started, but once again did not score. He is lacking in confidence, but how long do you stick with a striker who is not putting the ball in the net?

Celtic manager Martin O'Neill on TNT Sports:

"I'm just delighted to have won, it keeps us going if nothing else. We've got six points on the board and we've still a couple of games to go.

"From an almost impossible position, having lost the first three games, we've given ourselves some hope.

"Three points tonight were of vital importance. There's lots we can still do to improve our game."

Asked about Camilo Duran, he added: "He's just a magnificent footballer.

"15 goals and we're not into December, he's been flying. He's a terrific player, and that's two games he's come up big for us."

Celtic winger Jota speaking to TNT Sports after his first European appearance for almost two years:

"It was a long road and I did my maximum to be as fit as possible.

"Right now, it's all about enjoying life. No expectations, just be professional and having the responsibility of being a Celtic player.

"It wasn't easy. I think we just had to stick with our plan and in the end it worked out, that's the most important thing.

"We must believe [Celtic can qualify]. Every game is a different battle, we know what to do."

#744. Saving Nepal’s wild orchids — in photos

Prized for their ornamental and medicinal value, hundreds of orchids are illegally harvested and sold each year. Now, conservationist Reshu Bashyal is leading an effort to protect them.

Words by Saugat Bolakhe and photos by CJ Karki

A couple of hours drive from Kathmandu, in the hills near Chitlang village in central Nepal, a group of locals and forest officials gather in a dense subtropical woodland. Beneath a canopy of pines, Himalayan chestnuts and Nepalese alders, the group listens as wildlife conservationist Reshu Bashyal guides them through a questionnaire designed to document the signs of poaching.

Bashyal refers to this team as a taskforce — one on the hunt for illegal activity. But instead of focusing on animals, as many conservation projects do, the group’s objective is to protect flora, specifically orchids. These flowering plants are harvested and sold across Nepal’s borders.

The flowers are prized for their ornamental value, but they are also used in traditional medicines, including Chinese, Tibetan and Ayurveda healing products.

Multiple parts of the plant, including the stem and fruit, can also be used as ingredients. “It’s as if these plants have some magical properties about them,” Bashyal says.

Nepal has more than 500 orchid species, many of which are heavily harvested. Between 2008 and 2016, the country legally exported more than 47,000 kilograms of wild-collected orchids. However, discrepancies exist between Nepal’s export data and those of its trading partners, arising from issues such as mismatched and unreported trade amounts and species being sold under different names.

The trade in animal and plant species is regulated mostly under the Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species of Wild Fauna and Flora (CITES) agreement, which is designed to protect wildlife from exploitation. Although Nepal joined the convention more than 50 years ago, it did not introduce legislation to implement CITES until 2017.

The orchid Dendrobium longicornu is sought after for its black-haired canes and fragrant white and orange blooms.

The orchid Dendrobium longicornu is sought after for its black-haired canes and fragrant white and orange blooms.

All but two species of orchid in Nepal are now listed in CITES Appendix II, which includes species that are not currently threatened with extinction but could be if their trade is not regulated. The government must create a management plan and a formal assessment to confirm that harvesting a species for trade won’t harm the survival of the wild population. “We haven’t prepared such a management plan for any orchid species yet. So, their trade is still considered illegal here,” Bashyal adds. Violation of the CITES Act can lead to a fine of up to 100,000 Nepalese rupees (US$660), one year in prison, or both.

Bashyal started researching orchids in 2018, when conservation fieldwork revealed the extent of harvesting and trade of the plants.

Bashyal started researching orchids in 2018, when conservation fieldwork revealed the extent of harvesting and trade of the plants.

Bashyal demonstrates a survey technique to a member of her team.

Bashyal demonstrates a survey technique to a member of her team.

Bashyal (right) and a team from the non-profit organization Greenhood Nepal have partnered with forest officials and local community members to form an anti-poaching taskforce.

Bashyal (right) and a team from the non-profit organization Greenhood Nepal have partnered with forest officials and local community members to form an anti-poaching taskforce.

Bashyal first became involved in orchid research by chance. In 2018, while working on a conifer tree conservation project for non-profit organization Greenhood Nepal in Kathmandu, she visited several regional sites across the country and was often approached by people asking about the demand for orchids in the city. When her team investigated further, it realized that many people living in the villages were harvesting or actively trading the plants.

This illegal trading was often overlooked by authorities, according to Bashyal. Before suggesting a way to stop it, the team had to understand the market — specifically which species were being taken, their conservation status and how the supply chain operated. To do this, it visited orchid trading hubs across Nepal and spoke to harvesters, traders and enforcement officials.

The Makawanpur region of Nepal is home to orchids, yew trees and a rich diversity of other wildlife.

The Makawanpur region of Nepal is home to orchids, yew trees and a rich diversity of other wildlife.

“The local people provide information on where orchids are harvested, moved, gathered and how much they sold orchids for,” she says. During these visits, the team shared its research and spoke about the importance of conservation, which was well received, she says. “After all, an unsustainable harvesting of the orchids severely threatens local livelihood and income,” she adds.

Bashyal’s team at Greenhood Nepal learnt that several orchid species, including Satyrium nepalense and Pleione praecox, are harvested in large quantities for their medicinal value. Overharvesting an orchid species that is in decline can easily lead to its extinction in the wild, which makes understanding a species’ population and distribution crucial for creating sustainable harvesting practices.

After the field trips, Bashyal’s team created a series of policy briefs, drafted conservation frameworks and started the anti-poaching taskforce in collaboration with the region’s governmental forest management office to document illegal activity and conduct patrols.

The team is also developing comprehensive identification manuals and guidelines for regulators. Many existing manuals focus on identifying whole plants and flowers, but traded items can include the orchid’s thickened stem and fleshy underground storage organs, called tubers. Some orchids are boiled, or dried for several hours or days before being traded.

In some parts of Nepal, communities can earn a good income from harvesting and selling orchids alongside other medicinal plants. For many, medicinal plants are their sole source of income. “Simply telling the locals ‘you are not supposed to do this’ will not stop them from harvesting,” Bashyal says. For this reason, imposing a blanket ban on trade might not be effective.

Bashyal emphasizes that tracking the wildlife trade is complex and often requires navigating delicate legal territory. Researchers must also have patience when interviewing informants. “Thus, it also comes down to following research ethics, respect and treating local knowledge as a valuable resource to build trust,” Bashyal says. “Only after that, can we have data and develop any intervention.”

The forests of Makawanpur support an array of native orchids.

The forests of Makawanpur support an array of native orchids.

#743. Paris Fury retracts Tyson schizophrenia claim

Paris Fury says Tyson did not receive a diagnosis of schizophrenia; Netflix documentary has now been updated; The British Boxing Board of Control indicated it would look into comments about a schizophrenia diagnosis and could deny Fury a licence to face Anthony Joshua on December 11

Paris Fury has retracted her claim that husband Tyson Fury was diagnosed with schizophrenia.

A new Netflix documentary explores Tyson Fury's experiences of depression, anxiety and bipolar disorder, which became particularly acute after his unified heavyweight championship victory over Wladimir Klitschko in 2015.

Paris Fury made the comments about schizophrenia in an initial version of the documentary. Netflix said it has worked to "update" the footage in light of her clarification.

She has now said: "I want to clarify a statement I made in the original version of the Tyson Fury documentary. I recalled a conversation from many years ago when discussing Tyson's condition and I used the word 'schizophrenic'. Whilst Tyson did show some symptoms associated with schizophrenia, he doesn't have this condition and has never received a diagnosis.

"Mental health is complex, and it isn't always easy to find the right words, especially when you're living it with someone you love. I'm so proud of Tyson for really opening up in this documentary and want to say thank you for all the support we've received as a family."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

Earlier on Thursday, the British Boxing Board of Control (BBBoC) indicated that it was investigating the comments and could deny Fury a licence to face Anthony Joshua in Cardiff on December 11 if he was deemed unfit to fight.

Sky Sports News has contacted the BBBoC to clarify if an investigation is ongoing after Paris Fury's retraction.

A spokesperson for Netflix said: "Following new information shared by the family relating to Tyson's official mental health diagnosis, we have worked alongside them to update the documentary accordingly ahead of launch."

After his victory over Klitschko, Fury revealed he had struggled with drug and alcohol addiction and had gained weight.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

He was admitted to hospital in June 2016 with a suspected heart attack, and revealed that while in hospital he had heard voices in his head.

"Words can't explain the darkness I was in," Fury said during the Netflix documentary.

"It was like a living version of the pits of hell.

"I thought I would end up in a padded room with the door locked, and that scared me so much.

"The anxiety was crippling me. I just could not overcome it and that's when I went and saw the psychiatrist down in London. She asked me a gazillion questions, and I ticked all the boxes. Depression, anxiety, bipolar disorder."

The NHS says schizophrenia is a long-term mental health illness that is a form of psychosis.

Those suffering from the condition may, at times, be unable to distinguish their own thoughts from reality. Symptoms can include hallucinations and delusions.

The NHS describes bipolar disorder as a mental health issue where a person can experience extreme changes in their mood.

If you've been affected by anything discussed in this article, support is available; please visit Sky Viewer Support.

If you are worried about your mental health, get advice and support through your GP or call the NHS on 111.

#738. Is the AI bubble bursting just as Anthropic goes public?

The sharp sell-off in tech stocks after the US midterms and the Nvidia scandal has cast doubt on Anthropic's IPO. Yet with hundreds of billions still being invested, some think the AI party is still in full swing.

Anthropic, the artificial intelligence (AI) giant, made its Nasdaq debut Thursday in the largest share sale on record.

The Claude maker offered 980 million shares for sale at $83 (€76), yet began trading 34% higher at $111.50.

The opening price valued the five-year-old firm at around $2 trillion, well above market estimates of around $1.3 trillion.

Yet, after the first two days of trading, Anthropic stock closed Friday more than 20% below its opening price at $87.80, suggesting the hype had run ahead of what investors were willing to pay.

Anthropic's public listing is being seen as a key test of investor appetite for AI, as stock prices have swung wildly in recent months.

2026 was meant to be the year Wall Street’s trillion-dollar bet on what US President Donald Trump calls superintelligence (SI) started paying off.

In the first half of the year, it did. Many AI stocks hit record highs as US hyperscalers like Google's Alphabet, Meta and Microsoft recorded bumper earnings.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The second half of 2026, however, has brought a lot more uncertainty.

While the stock of chipmaker Nvidia pushed even higher last month, many hyperscalers and chip or memory firms have seen erratic movements in their stock prices.

Then, after the Democrats won control of the United States Congress in the midterm elections earlier this month, technology stocks sold off again dramatically.

The Magnificent Seven — including Meta, Apple, Amazon and Tesla — lost more than $1 trillion in value in a single trading day.

In a further twist, the AI sector took another hit last week as Nvidia shares plunged nearly 10% over two days.

The sell-off followed revelations that CEO Jensen Huang had an affair with a woman reportedly suspected by US intelligence of being a Chinese spy.

Huang resigned from the chipmaker, sending Nvidia's shares lower still and prompting a campaign by current and former staffers, investors and other key figures in Silicon Valley to have him reinstated.

"Is this the best timing?" asked Dennis Dick, chief market strategist at the Canada-based Stock Trader Network, in an interview with DW last week.

Dick said Anthropic's valuation depends on whether it can deliver on a forecast by Goldman Sachs of more than $600 billion in revenue by 2030.

"If you get to a company with $600 billion in revenue, [a] $1.3 trillion [valuation] doesn’t sound that bad," he told DW. "But when you’re talking about a company with currently $52 billion in revenue, it sounds like it’s overvalued."

Other analysts, like Vivek Seth, chief executive officer of Shaires Holdings, are more bullish about the Claude maker's prospects.

"Anthropic is a once-in-a-generation company," Seth told Bloomberg last week, noting how it has grown rapidly and has strong institutional backing. "Its IPO will establish a market-clearing valuation as conditions stabilize."

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Wall Street is growing increasingly cautious about the sheer size of the AI outlay, amid warnings that future earnings may not justify the huge spending.

In September, investment bank Goldman Sachs estimated that hyperscalers need around $300 billion in annual AI revenue to break even on their spending, leaving a gap of roughly $230 billion.

"We're not in Kansas anymore," Dick quipped, borrowing a line from the classic movie "The Wizard of Oz," which means times have changed. Now, he said, investors are telling companies: "Show me the money."

Other analysts, however, think it's too soon to expect the AI bubble to burst, including Kit Rees, investment strategist at London-based wealth manager Quilter, who thinks the post-election rout was a "healthy correction."

"We’re still in the very early innings of the AI build-out," Rees told DW. "There’s still a lot of excitement around this technology and investors will want to have a slice of the pie."

In addition to the roughly $800 billion invested in capital expenditures this year, AI hyperscalers plan to spend a further $1.2 trillion in 2027 and $1.4 trillion in 2028, according to Goldman Sachs estimates.

With many investors already running for the hills, Rees isn’t convinced the AI bubble will burst in the way skeptics expect. She thinks they should watch for stronger signs that the AI trade is maturing.

This could be "a slowdown in AI-related revenues for companies, or signs of less demand or less appetite for financing companies’ AI plans, be it through debt or through equity offerings," Rees told DW.

There are early signs that investors have less appetite for AI-related debt. Borrowing costs for AI infrastructure firms like CoreWeave and Oracle have soared recently. Even the cost of insuring Nvidia’s debt against default has risen 76% in a month, CNBC reported recently.

"They [Oracle] have been spending, some people say, like drunken sailors," Dick told DW. "They’ve compromised their balance sheet to a point where the stock’s fallen 65% from the highs."

That has not stopped Oracle, along with Meta, Microsoft and Alphabet, from continuing to issue new AI bonds. Since the end of last month, the four AI giants have announced deals worth $67 billion.

Rees said another sign could be any new regulations that make it harder to build out US data centers, due to pressure on local water and electricity supplies.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

In his upcoming book "AI Mania: Blather, Bluster, and the Bubble of All Bubbles," economist Gary Smith compares the AI boom with earlier frenzies around railways, automobiles, television and the internet. He warns of a "frightful crash" when the AI bubble eventually pops.

When the dot-com bubble burst in 2000, the tech-heavy Nasdaq stock market index lost nearly 80% of its value. Yet, previous bubbles have often lasted far longer than expected, making the timing of any crash hard to predict.

Joachim Klement, head of market strategy at UK-based investment bank Panmure Liberum, believes a reckoning could happen as early as next year.

"My core conviction is that the AI bubble will either burst in 2027 or in 2028, so sometime in the next two years,” Klement told Bloomberg last month.

Editor's note: This article was first published on November 13, 2026 and was updated on November 18, 19 and 20 to reflect the latest developments.

#737. Bass hits 57-yard field goal in final seconds as Bills beat rivals Chiefs

Buffalo Bills beat rivals Kansas City Chiefs thanks to a 57-yard field goal from Tyler Bass; he also hit a 54-yard field goal to level the game with 12 minutes remaining

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

Tyler Bass hit a 57-yard field goal on the hooter as Buffalo Bills improved their AFC-leading record to 10-1 with a 13-10 victory over rivals Kansas City Chiefs.

James Cook had 117 yards rushing and scored on a five-yard run and Bass also made a 54-yard field goal in the defensive struggle.

The highly anticipated fireworks between Buffalo's Josh Allen and Kansas City's Patrick Mahomes, two of the NFL's best quarterbacks, and top offenses failed to materialise.

Allen finished 10 of 21 for 81 yards with two interceptions - both coming inside the Kansas City 20. Mahomes finished 16 of 29 for 174 yards.

Buffalo have won seven straight and matched their best start to a season since 1991.

Emmett Johnson had 72 yards rushing and scored on a one-yard run for the Chiefs.

Neither offense could muster much momentum with rain falling through the evening and cold gusts that made it feel like -5.

Bass's decisive kick came after the Chiefs went three-and-out at their own 11 with 15 seconds remaining. Matt Araiza's punt was partially tipped by Joe Andreessen, leading to a line-drive ball fielded by Greg Dortch, who returned it 17 yards to Kansas City's 39 with four seconds remaining.

Bass's 54-yard field goal to tie it at 10 some 12 minutes earlier also was struck in the same direction.

Kansas City's Harrison Butker, kicking in the other direction toward the north end of the stadium, missed a go-ahead 46-yard attempt wide right with just over five minutes remaining.

In their seventh regular-season meeting since 2020, the Bills improved to 6-1, including six straight wins over Kansas City. The Chiefs, however, hold a 4-0 edge in the playoffs, including two AFC championship game wins.

After Cook opened the scoring 28 seconds into the second quarter, Allen squandered a chance to build a 14-0 lead on the Bills next possession. Facing second-and-eight at the Chiefs nine, Allen rolled to his right, appeared to have his pass slightly tipped by George Karlaftis, and intercepted by Alohi Gilman in the end zone.

It marked the first time in 43 drives inside an opponent's 20 the Bills failed to come away with points this season.

He would turn it over again in the red zone two drives later on Buffalo's first possession of the second half. On first-and-10 at Kansas City's 14, Allen's sidearm pass to Khalil Shakir was low, glanced off the receiver's hands and deflected into the arms of Nohl Williams.

Allen has five touchdowns versus seven interceptions in his past five starts.

The Chiefs continue to face questions over whether they have padded their record with weaker opponents. Of their eight wins, only one - a season-opening victory against Denver - has come against an opponent with a winning record entering Week 12. Meantime, all three losses have come against winning teams.

The Bills, meanwhile, were coming off a four-game stretch in which they feasted in playing against backup and third-string quarterbacks.

Buffalo limited the NFL's best offense to 241 yards and contained Mahomes, who entered the outing combined for 13 TDs passing and averaging 309 yards over his past four games.

Buffalo did allow their first touchdown in four outings, dating to to Derrick Henry's two-yard run in a 36-10 win over Baltimore on November 1. They were also limited to a season-low 230 yards.

#736. Carsley eyes Euros history with England U21s after draw

England Under-21s won Euro 2025 with an extra-time win in Slovakia against Germany

Lee Carsley has urged his England Under-21s to create a legacy as they aim for a third straight European title.

The Young Lions - who have won the past two European Championships in 2023 and 2025 under Carsley - have been drawn in Group A against France, Poland and co-hosts Serbia at Euro 2027.

Only Italy have won three successive European Under-21 tournaments - between 1992 and 1996 - but that was when just eight teams competed at the finals and not the current 16.

Head coach Carsley told BBC Sport: "The players I am privileged to coach and work with have a great opportunity to make history with three in a row in this format and create their own legacy within the under-21s."

He was speaking after Thursday's draw in Belgrade, with Serbia hosting the tournament with Albania.

"This group of players are in a really unique position and it will be a while before another group will be in this position," said Carsley.

"Let's go for it. Why not? Go all out to try to win it. That's what we're going to do. We have the players who can do that.

"They are highly motivated. We have seen that in the last two tournaments we have had, the players were so determined to win every game and it makes it a lot easier from a coaching point of view."

England will open their campaign against France - who they beat 3-2 in Bristol last week - on 16 June in Leskovac before facing Serbia in Belgrade on 19 June.

The Young Lions stay in the Serbian capital for their final group game against Poland on Tuesday, 22 June.

#735. Why Hoda Kotb Is "Relieved" by Thanksgiving Day Parade Postponement

Hoda Kotb weighed in after NBC confirmed that the 2026 Macy’s Thanksgiving Parade would be postponed to Nov. 28: “We waited 100 years for this parade, we’re gonna wait two more days.”

Hoda Kotb knows that sometimes stuffing happens.

After the Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade was postponed for the first time in its 100-year history, the Joy 101 founder—who was set to host the event alongside Savannah Guthrie and Al Roker—shared why she thinks pushing the event to Nov. 28 was for the best.

“It’s OK,” Kotb said on the November 25 episode of Late Night With Seth Meyers. “We waited 100 years for this parade, we’re gonna wait two more days. We’re gonna have it on Saturday. It’s gonna be a beautiful, sunsplash day.”

As the 62-year-old noted, the date change came about after it was clear the forecast on Thanksgiving Day “was not gonna be fun.”

“The winds were like tropical storm force,” she explained. “There are a bunch of kids who were marching and people with the balloons.”

But Kotb—mom to daughters Haley Joy, 9, and Hope Catherine, 7, with ex Joel Schiffman—is choosing the see the gravy boat half full.

“The good news is, to me, I’m relieved,” the Today alum said. “Saturday’s gonna be amazing. Everybody’s still hanging out. We’re gonna watch it anyway.”

In lieu of the scheduled program, NBC will re-air last year's show at 8 a.m. in all time zones, a spokesperson from the network told E! News in a Nov. 25 statement. And the change in plans won’t rain on Kotb’s parade.

As she put it, “We’re gonna watch an old parade and you won’t know the difference, OK? It’s gonna be spectacular.”

And since the team behind the Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade has “been working tirelessly for a year-plus” to perfect the event, Kotb teased that it'll be worth the wait.

“The musical acts are incredible,” she said. “It’s gonna be out of this world.”

Kotb’s comments come hours after an NBC spokesperson confirmed to E! News that the beloved event would be postponed due to weather.

“Due to the extreme weather conditions, the city of New York, Macy’s and NBC have decided, in the interest of safety for both the participants and spectators, to move the Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade to Saturday, Nov. 28,” the spokesperson shared in a Nov. 25 statement. “More details to follow.”

And while the postponement marks the first in the parade’s 100-year history, they emphasized that the show will go on.

“Thank you to the thousands of volunteers, performers and partners who create the magic millions enjoy each year,” a spokesperson told MSNOW in a statement. “We look forward to celebrating together on Saturday.”

#734. 'Laughing gas has ended careers' - so how common is it in football?

Watch: Moment Raheem Sterling arrested after car crash

It is known as laughing gas but the impact nitrous oxide can have on a professional footballer's body is anything but funny.

"I'm not going to name names but I have colleagues who know Premier League footballers who are no longer playing as a direct result of nitrous oxide [use]," said Dr David Nicholl.

Nicholl, a clinical lead in neurology with Sandwell and West Birmingham NHS Trust, was speaking after former Manchester City, Chelsea, Liverpool and England forward Raheem Sterling was handed a suspended jail term after pleading guilty to dangerous driving.

A key part of the case was that Sterling had been inhaling nitrous oxide from a balloon while driving.

His Lamborghini was seen veering across a motorway and later crashed into a metal gate. Sterling, 31, was arrested at the scene and found with six gas canisters in his car.

He disclosed to custody staff "he had a problem with nitrous oxide", the court was told.

Defending Sterling, Jason Bartfeld KC said his client "recognised the various unhealthy coping mechanisms that brought him to this position" and that he has "sought to address" these in the "most positive and effective way and with some success".

So, what is nitrous oxide, how does it affect those who take it and is its use more common in footballers than the wider population?

Footage was released of the footballer driving dangerously

Nitrous oxide's original use was as a sedative that healthcare providers like dentists could use to keep patients comfortable during procedures.

It is now legally sold for catering, medical and industrial purposes, but is frequently used as a recreational drug and is commonly known as laughing gas.

This can be abused by inhaling the gas via a balloon, leading to a short-term high causing symptoms such as brief euphoria, mild perceptual changes and uncontrollable laughter, external.

Nitrous oxide also slows brain and body responses and can displace oxygen in the lungs and bloodstream, contributing to dizziness, confusion or fainting.

It is thought long-term or excessive use can have disastrous effects on the body, from neurological harms to nerve and spinal cord damage which could lead to permanent disability.

According to medical journal The Lancet, it is now the third most commonly used drug after cannabis and cocaine in the UK, with use highest among people aged 16â24 years.

It has been increasing in popularity as a recreational drug over the past decade.

This prompted it to be reclassified as a Class C drug in 2023 after a government consultation.

Does football have a nitrous oxide problem?

BBC Sport has been told the abuse of so-called laughing gas has been widespread among professional footballers for a long time.

Former player Drewe Broughton is now a human performance coach, working with Premier League footballers and clubs around the world.

He said laughing gas was seen by some as a release.

"I think the use of nitrous oxide is really common," he added.

"It's something that can be done in private. It's something that can be hidden. You can't smell it on their clothes or the breath. It's an underground thing."

Broughton said he had been in the company of professional players when they had been using 'balloons'.

"I remember sitting in a players' house on the outskirts of Manchester, and these canisters were all over the floor," he added.

"I was from a world where people drank or they gambled or went to pubs and nightclubs. That was my first exposure to it."

Broughton has developed an app to help tackle issues with mental health and under-performance in football.

He said the reasons to use nitrous oxide had always been there: pressure on players to perform leaves them searching for an escape.

But Broughton has concerns about the toll nitrous oxide can take.

"I don't think there's the same awareness around nitrous oxide and damage to the body as there would be around alcohol or other drugs," he said.

BBC Sport has been told that some footballers see laughing gas as an alternative to harder substances because it does not stay in the body's system for more than a few hours.

Luci Hanmer, who works with Lancashire drugs and alcohol support charity 'We Are With You', said a substance like nitrous oxide was hard to detect.

She said: "Anything that you're inhaling, the effects that you're going to feel happen very soon.

"So if you are looking for that escapism, the effects are going to be quick.

"Once ingested, it doesn't last very long within your body compared to some of the other substances which can be detected for quite a number of days.

"So if you're getting a drugs test the next day for example, that won't show up."

Sterling given suspended sentence for dangerous driving

Former Manchester City defender Nedum Onuoha said more support was needed, particularly for players like Sterling who break through young.

Sterling made his debut for Liverpool and England at just 17 - before going on to win four Premier League titles at Manchester City and 82 caps for his country, including the Euro 2020 final at Wembley.

"Look at what's happened to Raheem," he said. "Look at how this led to this moment, a moment which I'm sure he's hugely embarrassed about, because I'm sure he can see how dangerous that was to not just his life, but the lives of so many people who are on the road at the same time.

"But I just don't feel like football is in a position where they think it's important to support people who have issues with nitrous oxide."

The BBC Radio 5 live pundit said the use of nitrous oxide in professional footballing circles was very common.

"I think the difference from when I was younger is that people would openly party in certain places," he said.

"Now they party where they're harder to spot. That's why you don't really see on a week-to-week basis now the scandal of somebody that's been out drinking.

"The players are doing it, but it's more sophisticated in terms of how they do it, the locations, and this is an example here with nitrous oxide."

Neurologist Dr Nicholl has been working with patients who have abused nitrous oxide for years and issued a warning to others.

"It certainly is being used by footballers, but it's pretty much the worst thing that you want to be using if you're a professional sportsperson," he said.

"It damages your spinal cord and the spinal cord is a bit like an electrical cable, where the insulation - the outside of that cable - gets stripped away.

"So what patients will complain of is difficulty with feeling on their hands or feet, or unable to walk at all.

"So, in effect, it's like a spinal cord injury. But they can also get blood clots, deep vein thrombosis, pulmonary emboli, and some patients have died."

If you have been affected by any of the issues raised in this story, information and support can be found at the BBC's Action Line website.

#733. Fofana has apologised for interview - Alonso

Wesley Fofana played all 90 minutes of Chelsea's 4-1 defeat at home to Leeds United on Saturday

Chelsea boss Xabi Alonso says defender Wesley Fofana has apologised for a controversial interview he gave on YouTube.

Fofana has been criticised for comments he made in the interview with YouTuber Zach Nani in which he appeared to joke about his penalty miss in a Carabao Cup shootout defeat at Liverpool.

He did not have permission to hold the two-hour interview, which was aired after Chelsea's humiliating 4-1 defeat at home to rivals Leeds on Saturday, but Alonso said the matter was now "closed".

"It was unfortunate. He has apologised. He knows it was not right, the moment, it was not right, the content," said the Blues boss, who was speaking before Friday's Premier League match at Nottingham Forest.

"We are here to take things seriously. He's said it will not be repeated. We don't want these kind of things and they won't be repeated."

Alonso refused to confirm whether Fofana had been punished by the club, but said "we have addressed that with him."

Interviewer defends Fofana after backlash

Okafor double delivers rare win for Leeds at Chelsea

'Fragile' and 'miles off it' - Alonso's Chelsea honeymoon is over

Fofana's comments followed criticism from fans of his performances this season, including in last weekend's humiliation at the hands of historic rivals Leeds.

But interviewer Nani defended Fofana against the backlash, saying: "People can clearly see he wasn't happy. He admits he didn't play well and says he needs to improve."

The interviewer also defended Fofana's explanation for putting himself forward to take a penalty against Liverpool, saying the defender believed it was his responsibility as one of the senior players on the pitch.

The 25-year-old France defender has often struggled for form and fitness since completing a Â£70m move from Leicester City in August 2022.

He has made 81 appearances for the club in four years, but has played nine times under new manager Alonso this season.

In that time Chelsea have struggled with defensive frailty, conceding 20 goals in their 11 Premier League games.

They are eighth in the table after falling to a third defeat in their last four league matches.

#732. Not even making a 12-man bench - what next for Garnacho?

Alejandro Garnacho is yet to start a game for Aston Villa this season

Alejandro Garnacho's time at Aston Villa has been brief - and it already looks to be over.

The latest snub by Villa boss Unai Emery was the most damming of all, with the on-loan Chelsea winger left out of Tuesday's Champions League defeat at Galatasaray.

"The players who were here I think are the best players to be here with us," said Emery.

Villa could have had 12 substitutes in Istanbul but Emery chose just 11 - including two goalkeepers - as Garnacho stayed at home.

The plan was for the Argentina international's loan move to become permanent for Â£43m should certain criteria be met.

They are believed to be based on a number of appearances staff felt were so achievable the club were in little doubt he would become a Villa player.

But now there is doubt he will ever play for them again.

Garnacho trained with Villa's first team on Monday but did not travel to Istanbul

"First start after three months. Happy to be enjoying football again."

The post Garnacho wrote on social media after a pre-season game in July has - along with anything else related to Villa - been deleted from his account.

He has played just 34 minutes in the Premier League this season, and seven of Villa's 11 games ended without him getting on the pitch.

His last appearance - just a three-minute cameo - came in the 1-1 draw against Fulham on 31 October.

Including Saturday's 0-0 draw with Sunderland, Garnacho has been omitted from the past three matchday squads - a strong sign Emery has lost faith in him.

But he may have been fighting a losing battle from the off, having arrived at Villa unfit.

Sources have acknowledged the 22-year-old was not at the level required and were surprised how off the pace he was when he signed in July.

He initially trained on his own, and questions over the signing were already being asked, with eyebrows raised by some internally given his inconsistent form for both Chelsea and Manchester United.

Yet he had been on Villa's list of targets - albeit a long list - while he was at Stamford Bridge as Emery was keen to sign a pacy winger in the summer.

Garnacho's problems were compounded by a head injury suffered in Thailand in pre-season, and even a boot camp during the international break in September and October, and scoring in friendlies against Sevilla and Southampton have not helped.

One of the issues Villa have is there is no exit clause, and both teams would have to agree to end the season-long loan deal early.

This time last year, Emery had already decided not to sign Harvey Elliott permanently in a Â£30m deal, leaving the on-loan Liverpool midfielder in limbo for the rest of the season.

And it appears Emery has already come to the same conclusion with Garnacho.

With Villa unable to find a solution with Liverpool, Elliott wasted a precious year of his career. Those close to him recognise the damage last season did, playing just nine times after being named Player of the Tournament at the European Under-21 Championship in 2025.

He is now at Valencia and is yet to start in La Liga this season.

The risk of going on loan to Villa became a topic of conversation in the game because of Elliott's plight, with sources suggesting players would think twice about joining the club. Garnacho's situation only increases those concerns.

Three times in two seasons, Emery and Villa have signed a high-profile player on loan only for it to fail.

Jadon Sancho's expensive loan from Manchester United last season - Villa paying a guaranteed 80% of Sancho's wages of more than Â£200,000 a week - ended with him having made just nine Premier League starts and scoring once in 39 appearances, with 21 of those as a substitute.

Sancho may have played more than Elliott and Garnacho - and came off the bench in their Europa League final win - but what value did Villa really get?

Of course, Marcus Rashford and Marco Asensio enjoyed positive loan spells previously - Rashford returning to the England squad while at Villa - but they are exceptions to the rule.

Nicolo Zaniolo, Clement Lenglet and Axel Disasi have joined in recent years and barely merit footnotes, while Douglas Luiz's loan return last season did not prompt a return to the heights he had reached previously at Villa.

The club have constantly complained about financial restrictions with some justification, but questions can certainly be asked about the money spent on many of their signings.

The blunt truth is there is no clear path.

Teenager George Hemmings has just signed a new deal and has earned praise from Emery for understanding the way he wants his players to work.

Ibrahim Mbaye and Alysson are also ahead of Garnacho, leaving him well behind even before regulars John McGinn, Johan Manzambi and Emi Buendia are factored in.

There was interest from abroad in the summer, with Roma keen, and it seems increasingly unlikely we will see Garnacho at another Premier League club soon.

Fifa rules allow players to play for two clubs in a season - or three if they move to a team whose season overlaps like the MLS - meaning Garnacho could feature for another, unlike Elliott as he had already played for Liverpool and Villa.

Garnacho, whose character has not been called into question while at Villa, cost Chelsea Â£40m when he signed from Manchester United in 2025 but failed to make a consistent impression, with eight goals in 43 games. When he joined Chelsea he signed a contract until 2032.

Prior to that, United boss Ruben Amorim had told him to leave.

Now nothing, it seems, will persuade Emery that Garnacho is worth persevering with - leaving the winger's career continuing to drift.

#731. Calvert-Lewin signs new Leeds deal until 2029

Calvert-Lewin joined Leeds United in 2025 after nine years at Everton

Dominic Calvert-Lewin has signed a new contract to stay with Leeds United until 2029.

The former Everton striker, 29, has five goals and one assist so far in the Premier League this season, with Daniel Farke's side sitting seventh in the table.

Confirmation of Calvert-Lewin's deal follows speculation about his future at the club, with reports that he was interesting Manchester United.

Calvert-Lewin scored 15 goals across all competitions during his first season at Elland Road after joining in August 2025, and the form earned him an England recall in March.

He was also called up by Thomas Tuchel this autumn and came off the bench in England's wins against Czech Republic and Spain.

He scored a penalty and had an assist in Leeds' 4-1 thrashing of Chelsea on Saturday.

#730. Germany's Freigang given 16-month ban over drugs test issues

Laura Freigang has scored 17 goals in 45 appearances for Germany

Germany international Laura Freigang has been suspended from football for 16 months over issues with three drugs tests.

The 28-year-old will miss the Women's World Cup next summer and is banned from all football activity until after 7 October 2027.

The 16-month suspension begins from the date of notification by the German Football Association (DFB), which took place in June.

The World Anti-Doping Agency (Wada), the National Anti-Doping Agency (Nada), DFB and Freigang reached a dispute resolution agreement.

The dispute said Entracht Frankfurt forward Freigang committed three reporting and/or testing failures between 11 March 2025 and 23 February 2026.

Freigang can return to training two months prior to the end of the suspension period but cannot play matches until after 7 October.

All personal records of appearances, goals, assists or other statistics from 23 February 2026 are nullified, though Frankfurt's results are unaffected.

This season Freigang has scored six goals and provided two assists in 11 starts in the Frauen-Bundesliga.

Since joining the club in 2020, the striker has scored 107 goals in 187 appearances and was in the Germany squad for October's friendly victories over Australia and Japan.

In a club statement, external, Franfurt said they will "begin discussions shortly to determine the terms of her future employment relationship".

Freigang's current contract is due to expire on 30 June 2027.

Frankfurt's director of women's football Katharina Kiel said: "The agreement now reached provides clarity and planning security in a process unprecedented for Eintracht Frankfurt - for us as a club, but above all for Laura.

"The way she and the team have handled the situation in recent months, and how Laura personally led by example with her performance on the pitch during a very difficult time, deserves the highest recognition.

"The identified shortcomings, despite the agreement to settle the dispute, have resulted in a suspension, which means the loss of a key player."
